R. STEPHEN DOAN

R. Stephen Doan was installed as Grand Master of Masons in
California on October 14, 1992. He was elected Junior Grand Warden in
October, I 989 and progressed through the offices of Senior Grand Warden and
Deputy Grand Master, before his election as the I28th Grand Master.
Born in Santa Monica, California on October 17, 1949, he was the
youngest man to hold the highest office in California Freemasonry in seventy
years. He grew up in a Masonic family , and his earliest memories are of being
at Triangle Masonic Hall in Venice with his parents at some Masonic event.
His father is also a Past Master of Triangle Lodge No. 548, and later served
as the Inspector of the S74th Masonic District. And his mother was active in
Eastern Star, having served as Worthy Matron with his father as Worthy
Patron. When Steve was fourteen, he joined Venice Triangle Chapter of the
Order of DeMolay which he served as Master Councilor in 1967. He also
served as Jurisdictional Master Councilor of Southern California in 1970. He
was honored with the Degree of Chevalier, awarded for active DeMolay
service. He was further honored in later years with the DeMolay Legion of
Honor. and in 1992 was elected a Deputy member of the International
Supreme Council.
He served Triangle Lodge No. 548, now Triangle - Palms Lodge No.
512, in 1975 as Master. He has served Grand Lodge as chainnan or a member
of eleven committees and boards. including the Committee on Policy and
General Purposes and the Committee on Finance. He chaired the Grand Lodge
Conference of Yo.unger Members in 1990. He wa~ Grand Rib le Bearer in
1979 and Grand Orator in 1985.
Professionally, Most Worshipful Bro. Doan is a partner in the Los
Angeles finn of Adams. Duque & Hazeltine, where he specializes in business
law, estate planning and tax Jaw. He graduated in 1971 from the University
of California, Los Angeles, Summa Cum Laude. and was elected to Phi Beta
Kappa. He also graduated from the UCLA School of Law in 1974, where he
earned his Doctorate in Laws. He is the author of several works on tax and
estate law, and has taught professionally in his field.
He is married to Donna Doan. and they have two children, Stephanie
and Robert. They reside both in Rancho Palos Verdes and at Lake Gregory,
where they maintain a second home. He is a licensed Lay Reader in the
Episcopal Church, and served St. Francis Parish in Palos Verdes Estates as a
member of the Vestry.

R. STEPHEN DOAN

Our Grand Master has served his community in a number of ways,
particularly as President of the Boys and Girls Club of Venice and as a
member of the Board of Oirectors of the Midnight Mission in Los Angeles.

INFORM AL OPENING OF GRAND LODGE

The 1993 Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and
Accepted Masons of California began with an lnfonnal Opening at J:OO p.m.
on Sunday, October IO, 1993. The wives, families and friends ofthe brethren
as well as the public were invited. The lnforrnal Opening was held in the
Ma<>onic Auditorium of the California Masonic Memorial Temple in San
Francisco. At the conclusion of the program, the audience was invited to join
the Grand Master in a Vesper Service to be held at Grace Cathedral across the
stre-et.
The Informal Opening commenced with the entrance of the l 993
Grand Lodge Officers in their full Regalia. The special Sunday session was
raised by Worshipful Richard D. Watson, Master of Los Angeles Harbor
Lodge No. 332 in San Pedro who is also the Associate Bethel Guardian of
Bethel No. 24 in San Pedro. Brother Watson used the gavel which was
presented to the Grand Master by the Grand Master's parents when he was
installed as Master Councilor of his DeMolay Chapter on April 15, 1967.
An invocation was offered by the Grand Chaplain, the Very Reverend
Alexander H. Swan.
Grand Master R. Stephen Doan instructed the Grand Mmhal to retire
and present the nag of our country after which the Grand Master invited all
of those in attendahce to join him in the Pledge of Allegiance.
Grand Master Doan then welcomed the brethren, ladies and friends to
the lnfonnal Opening of the 144th Annual Communication of the Most
Worshipful Grand Lodge of free and Accepted Masons of the State of
California and hoped that all would enjoy the program to honor the Family of
Freemasonry.
Upon instruction of the Grand Master. the Grand Marshal retired and
conducted the leaders of the California Masonic Organi7.ations to a place west
of the Altar. The Grand Marshal introduced each individual dignitary, giving
name and Masonic title.
The Grand Master gave a very warm and appropriate welcome to the
leaders of our concordant and appendant bodies. The dignitaries were then
escorted 10 scats reserved for them. Those present and introduced were as
follows:

GRAND LODGE VESPER SERVICE

We should likewise journey through this world in our
pilgrimage of life ending in the Heavenly Jerusalem in the
same spirit of brotherly love celebrated by the Psalmist.

The Vesper Service for the 144th Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge of California was held on Sunday, October 10th in Grace
Cathedral. The service began at 4:30 p.m. with an organ prelude by the
Cathedral Organist. When all had assembled, they were welcomed by the
Grand Master. after which those present joined in singing verses one through
three of the hymn, "Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken". The Grand
Chaplain offered the invocation .
The Grand Secretary presented the first reading with the following
remarks:
Our first scripture reading is the 133rd Psalm.
Psalms were written as hymns to accompany acts or worship.

. ~e. hymn, "The Holy City", was then sung by Worshipful David
Francis Ph1hps, a Pa-.t Master of Arabic Lodge No. 763, Los Angeles.
The Grand Master presented the second reading and his message as
follows:
How many times does the familiar become so
common place that we forget the meaning? What about t.he
Pledge of Allegiance lo the flag of our country? Because we
have recited it so many times, do we really remember what
it means? The Pledge of Allegiance is concisely written.
Every word has significance. Yet, how often do we think of

Psalm 133 is a song of ascent or a song to be sung on a
pilgrimage to the Holy City of Jerusalem. Psalm 133

the significance of those words?

celebrates the joy of a scanered people coming together upon
the occasion of some special Jewish holiday, such as Yorn
Kippur. It celebrates the joy of fraternal hannony.

Everyday, you probably say "I love you" to a spouse
or another loved one. You certainly know what the words
mean. but how often do you say " I love you" with the
nonchalance or "hello, how are you", without caring really
what the response might be? Just as we sometimes say the
Pledge of Allegiance without thinking of the mean ing of the
words, oftc;n times we express ourselves to others with words
of great signifi cance without really th in king about them nor
saying them with the feeling which should accompany them.

Joy is symboli7..ed by two metaphors: first, by the
oil of j oy in the beard of Aaron, the first chief priest, and
second, by the dew of refreshment falling both on Mount
Hennon in the north and Zion in the south, symbolizing
God's great pleasure when all of his people dwell together in
fellowship .
Our conclusion? Fellowship or brotherly love is a
blessing of life forever more. It is a miracle of divine grace
wherein individual blessings are shared with mutual profit.
PSALM 133
Behold. how good and how pleasant it is when brothers
dwell in unity! It is like the precious oil upon the head,
running down upon the beard, upon the beard of Aaron,
running down on the collar of his robes! It is like the dew
of Hennon. which falls on the mountains or Zion! For there
the Lord has commanded the blessing, life for evcnnore.
This scripture passage has a second significance.
Jerusalem is a metaphor for Heaven. that state of perfection
to which we all aspire after our Earthly toils are completed.

7

There is a fami liar passage of Scripture which we
frequent ly fail to appreciate at its recitation just as we do
when we by rote repeat the Pledge of Allegiance or say "I
love you" without much passion. As 'With the Pledge, our
nonchalance results in part from repetition. Because of the
number of times that we have heard it. we sometimes find
ourselves not listening. Our lack of appreciation for it may
also result from our failure to understand fully what the
writer intended. That passage?
Though I speak with the tongues of men and of
angel~, and have not charity, I am become as sounding brass,

or a tinkling cymbal.
And though I have the gift of prophecy, and
understand all mysteries. and all knowledge; and though f
have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have
not charity, I am nothing.

8

PROC'EEDl~GS OF HIE

GRANO LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor.
and though I give my body to be burned, and have not
charity, it profiteth me nothing.

allusions which we have forgotten or perhaps not taken the
time to learn. The passage cannot be understood with the
meaning and passion intended without understanding these
words and symbols.

Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth
not; charity vaunteth not itself. is not puffed up, doth not
behave itself unseemly, sceketh not her own. is not easily
provoked, thinkcth no evil; rejoiceth not in iniquity, but
rejoiceth in the truth; bcareth all things, bclieveth all things.
hopeth all things, endureth all things.
And now abideth faith. hope, charity, these three:
but the greatest of these is charity.
Many Masons can probably recite from memory this
passage in the King James' version of the Bible. The
passage is an excerpt from a letter which Paul sent to the
church at Corinth, Greece. The passage is familiar but have
you ever thought what Paul meant when he wrote it? In
Lodge and in the King James· version, we say "charity".
although some more contemporary Bible translations use the
word "love". In the Greek Bible used by the early church.
this word, variously translated into English as charity or love,
was the Greek word agape. meaning "love of the
undeserving", love which gives, the effon to be kind to all
people at all times.
Charity in this sense is not therefore our Masonic
teaching of relief but our teaching of brotherly love. It is our
regard of the whole human species as one family, the high
and the low, the rich and the poor, who, as created by one
Almighty Parent, are to aid, support and protect each other.
Jews, Christians and Moslems believe that God loves each
one of us. Agape. love of the undeserving, is like this love
which God has for each one of us. If the Great Architect,
the Ma.<;ter of all that is, can love each one of us, regardless
of our imperfections, regardless of our human failings,
regardless of our irritating habits, regardless of our
controversial views, can we do no less than God does'? If
God loves my enemy, why cannot I make the effon to seek
to resolve our differences so that I may feel love also?
If we have misunderstood the meaning of charity or
love, what about our understanding of the other symbols in
this pas.sage of scripture'> V.'hat do the sounding brass and
tinkling cymbal mean? The passage is tilled with other

Read with a deeper understanding of charity and
with a knowledge of the allusions employed by Paul, this
passage could be recited as:
If I have human eloquence, however angelic, but
have no love for my brother, my words have no more
meaning than a noisy gong, a clanging cymbal or any other
loud instrument used in worship by Corinthian pagans. And
if I have the ability to foresee the future. and if I am well
versed in theology, and if I have such faith in God that I
believe that anything is possible with His aid, yet lack love
for my fellow man. I am nothing. If I give away every
possession which I own, including the supreme sacrifice, my
own life, but have not love for my fellow man, I remain
nothing io God's eyes.
Brotherly love means being long-tempered with
people, being generous and helpful. \\.'hen motivated by
brotherly love. I am not jealous of the success or gifts of
others. I. do not try to make my brotherly love ostentatious,
a show merely for applause. My brotherly love should not
be inflated with self-righteousness.
When actuated by
brotherly love. I should not be thinking of myself hut of
others. I should not be ready to take offense. I should
harbor no resentments for the perceived slights of others. I
should not take joy in the misdeeds of others. I should
celebrate right and truth whenever and by whomever
discovered.
Brotherly love causes me to withstaod the hostility
of others yet all the time attempting to credit them with good
intentions. seeking to find good in what others mav do even
when I may perceive it as hostility. When ac~uatcd by
brotherly love, I believe the best when I have no evidence to
the contrary. When evidence is to the contrary. I hope for
the best. And when hopes are repeatedly disappointed. I still
courageously wait.
Faith, truthful acceptance of God as lie is, hope,
perseverance in faith , and brotherly love, these three graces
fonn our unity with God, but the greatest grace is our honest

LEGISLATI ON
Grand Master Doan announced that the legislation to be presented at
the 144th Annual Communication would now be considered.
The Grand Master reiterated rules of order that would be used during
on the different pieces of legislation. Any Mason was allowed
discussion
the
to speak on any matter before the vote was taken. In order to do so, he would
approach the microphone, give the appropriate sign. and state his name and
lodge. The authorized representative of the legislation would have the option
of speaking first or last. Each authorized representative should have advised
the Assistant Grand Secretary before his resolution or legislation was
announced for discussion whether he will speak first or last. The proponent
of the legislation would identify himself as the proponent, in which case he
would be allowed 5 minutes in which to speak. All other speakers from the
floor would be aJlotted 3 minutes each. If the authoril-ed representative spoke
first, a speaker opposed to the matter would speak next, and the pro and con
speakers would alternate thereafter. Only 3 speakers on each side of any issue
including the proponent would be permitted on each item under discussion.

Ma~ter Doan began his presentation of his Decisions and Recommendations.

his written message reproduced in Appendix B, commencing at page 177. All
of the Grand Master's Decisions and the first five of his Recommendations

APPENDIX A

All committee reports must be in the hands of the Grand Secretary by
4:00 p.m. on Monday, October I Ith. Legislation shall be heard at the Tuesday
sessions. Each chainnan of a committee to which legislat ion has been referred
should be present at aJI times during the Tuesday sessions until all reports
from his committee have been given. If a committeeman is not present and
prepared to report when called for, the Grand Secretary shall read the
committee' s report . If the Grand Secretary does not then have a copy of the
report to read1 the vote will be taken without that report.
The Jurisprudence Committee shal l report only once, unless there is
a special matter before the Grand Lodge which the committee and presiding
officer believe warrant individual aucntion. The presiding officer shall
announce the vote required for passage of each item before di!>cussion begins.
Any legislation to be considered which has not been mailed to the
Lodges shall be printed in advance and distributed at or before the session at
which the matter shall be considered. No legislation may be modified at any
time without the consent of the proponent or his authorized representative
written on the face of the modified proposal. If any proposal is modified after
it has been made available to the delegates, any changes must be clearly
brought to the atteqtion of the delegates at the Grand Lodge session.
The Grand Secretary shall not read the minutes of any session during
the Communication. The minutes will be printed instead in the proceedings
of the Annual Communication.
When discussion of each resolution or other item of business is called
for by the presiding officer. the proponent, or his authorized representati ve.
shall have the option of speaking first or last. The proponent shall be allorted
five minutes. All other speakers from the floor shall be allotted three minutes
each .
If the proponent speaks first, a speaker opposed to the matter shall
speak next, and the pro and con speakers shall alternate thereafter. If the
proponent chooses to speak last, a speaker in opposition shall begin the
discussion, and the speakers shall alternate thereafter. Only three speakers on
each side of an issue, including the proponent, shall be pcrrnittcd on each item
under discussion. Speakers in favor shall speak from the microphone on the
Gr.ind Master' s left. Speakers opposed shall speak from the microphone on
the Grand Master's right.

GRAND MASTER'S MESSAGE
ORAL REMARKS

Brethren of the Grand Lodge:

APPENDIX B

The California Masonic Code requires the Grand Master to present at
each Annual Communication a written message setting forth all his official
acts during the year, the general condition of Masonry within the Jurisdiction
and bis recommendations of such legislation as he deems necessary or
expedient for the welfare of the Craft. The Proceedings for this Annual
Communication will contain a complete report on my stewardship of the
responsibilities and powers with which you invested me last October as your
Grand Master. Later today, I will separately present for your consideration the
decisions and recommendations which l have made. This morning, I report on
tbe highlights of other portions of my written report.

Grand Master's Special Project Fund
It ha-; been a custom for many years to make a presentation to the
Grand Master and his wife at events in their honor. This year, Donna and I
asked you to consider something other than a personal gift to us. fostead, we
established the Grand Master's Special Project Fund to which you could make
a donation in our henor.

Some of the proceeds from this fund will be used to award a
scholarship from the California Masonic Foundation. These scholarships arc
givea to deserving young people, regardless of their affiliation with our
fraternity. Masons are dedicated to self-improvement: that is what we came
here to do.
These scholarships help deserving students pursue selfimprovement through college or trade school study.
Some of the donations to the Grand Master's Special Project Fund
were restricted as to use. $300 of the receipts were designated by the donor
for the Homes Endowment Fund. Another $800 was designated by the donors
for the Youth Fund of Southern California which provides a home for the
DeMolay Jurisdiction of Southern California.
The balance of the donations were unrestricted, and most of those will
support the Grand Lodge charity of special significance to Donna and me: the
new PAL Program, a very special fund of our Masonic Homes established
through the generosity of a now deceased brother. The income from this fund
may be used to admit deserving children without known Masonic affiliation
to our Masonic Home at Covina. We ask only that they be sponsored by a

38

PRCJ<.:EEOI NGS OF ·n IE

Masonic Lodge.
Our children at Covina are no longer orphans, although sometimes
you need a genealogist to fin d a Mason on the fam ily tree! These children
have parents, although sometimes they do not know ·who thei r fat hers are.
Their parents are often times physical abusers, alcohol abusers or drug abusers.
During the time that I served on the Uoard of Trustees of the Masonic
Homes of California, we admitted two little boys to our Home. These linle
boys did not have a home. Their mother is a prost itute. They slept on the
Ooor of the motel room of their mother's trick for the night. These little boys
came to us without any underwear. These little boys now have underwear,
1bey now have a home, they now have a life, thanks to the generosity of lhe
Masons of California.
Through this new PAL or P rov ide A L ife Program, other young
people regardless of 1beir affiliation with our fraternity can have a life too.
Tltis fund, as supplemented by your contributions to it, will enable deserving

thanks to you.
From the donations which you have made to the Grand Master's
Special Project Fund as Donna and I have travelled this year, we will designate
for the PAL Program the sum of SI0,000.
Grand Lodge Operations

"Ibe Grand Master is the chief executive officer of Grand Lodge. A s
such, he is responsible for the supervision of all of its activities. Over the past
three years. the Grand Master with the counsel of the Deputy Grand Master
and Grand Wardens has focused on impro.,,ing the performance and cost
effectiveness of the Grand Lodge operations.
We have worked with the Grand Secretary to improve the operations
of the Grand Lodge office. We have asked the question: Is all we do in the·
Grand Secretary's office really necessary? A new Code Revision Committee
was appointed during the year to study the Grand Secretary's office and
consider streamlin ing the paper work which our law requires, such as with
dispensations. If we eliminate the needless paperwork, we can devote the
same resources to helping the Lodges do a better job, reall y the only reason
for the existence of the Grand Lodge in the first place! One of my
recommendations and three resolutions to be considered at this Annual
Communication address several provisions of our California Masonic Code
which currently hinder greater efficiency in the Grand Secretary's office.

GRAND I ODGE OF C'/\l.IFORNI/\

39

Grand Lodge and the related Grand Lodge entities are a multi-million
dollar operation. We need the best qualified people to manage the accounting
and Jong term financial planning of our organization. We have therefore hired
8 chief finan cial officer for the Grand Lodge and related entities to supervise
this very important area of Grand Lodge operations.
Another important area receiving attention has been the finan cial
health of our Grand Lodge. At last year's Annual Communication. I reported
my commitment to a balanced Grand Lodge budget, elimination of unnecessary
Grand Lodge expend itures ancl a li mit on per capita tax increases to the cost
of living. I am pleased to report that the estimated Urand Lodge expenditures
for the current fiscal year ending October 31, 1993 are under budget. Special
appreciation is extended to 1he Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors and
Committeemen for their help in keeping the Gran d Lodge within budget this

year.
We are under-budget this year because we have reduced Grand Lodge
expenses. In the last two years, the travel and meeting expenses reimbursed
for the Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors and Committeemen during the Grand
Lodge year have been reduced by more than one·half, for a savings of
approximately S2.00 per assessable member. Over the last three years, the cost
of the Annual Communication has been reduced from $295,000 to $235,000.
for a savings of approximately $ .50 per member. Over the last two years, the
expenses of the Grand Secretary's office have been reduced by $50,000, for
a savings of $ .40 per member.
Earlier this year, the Lodge assignments to District Inspectors were
changed, allowing us to eliminate thirty districts. Because of the reduction in
the number of Inspectors, we could also reduce the number of Assistant Grand
Lecture.rs, the men in Grand Lodge who are the Inspectors' immediate
supervisors. We now have four instead of six A.G.L.'s. Because of these new
assignments, Grand Lodge will save $25,000. the travel expenses associated
with thirty Inspectors and two A.G.L. 's.
All progrnms of the Grand Lodge are on a "zero-budget'' basis: they
receive no money unless they can justify their wonh each year. The Grand
Master, Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens interview periodically the
chainneo of all major committees. We have eliminated those committees
whose work does not justify the expense, such as Commercialism whose duties
have been assigned to Jurisprudence. We have changed the duties of others
to make them more relevant, such lL'> the assignment of consolidations to the
Chaners Comminee.
Because of these savings, Grand Lodge this year will have a surplus
(or profit, if you will) of slightly more than $300,000 or approximately $2.50
per asessable member. This surplus will be used to replenish the Grand

Lodge reserves. Over an eight year period ending in 1991. the Grand Lodge
spent approximately $600,000 more than it collected. The surplus from this
year and the surplus projected for Warren's year will replenish the Grand
Lodge reserves to approximately the same level that they were in 1983.

What can Grand Lodge do to help? We have the Wardens ' Retreats,
which in my opinion is the number one program of our Grand Lodge today.
Why arc these retreats so succ.essful? Each Warden learns ideas for successful
programs, programs which have made the difference in other Lodges and can
be imitated. Each Warden learns that others share his concerns and arc willing
to help resolve them: from the man who will be Grand Master when he is
Master to the men from his home area who will be Masters when he is. His
wife is included too. She learns what she can do to help and !hat she too has
a support system from the Grand Master's wife to the wives of the prospective
Masters of the neighboring Lodges. Most imponantly, each Warden leaves
with a renewed sense of enthusiasm for anticipated responsibi Iitics itnd
commitment to build Masonry. And the value of these retreats is not limited
to tbe new Mason. Past Masters who have attcn<lcJ as Wardens (even those
Past Masters who are fonner Inspectors who have anended the retreats as
Wardens) report renewed enthusiasm and commitment for their future
responsibilities.

These current surpluses do not mean that the financial future of Grand
Lodge is without worries. If our membership continues to decline by 5,000
a year. we lose the per capita income on those members, approximately
$70.000 a year. Grand Lodge expenditures must be reduced by $70,000
annually, or the future per capita assessments will increase by more than the
change in the cost of living. once the current surplus is gone.
Continuity
I am pleased to report another important development in Grand Lodge:
continuity. The programs of the Grand Lodge are now a team effort of the
Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens: every one of us has
had a role in their development and implementation. Every important decision
maJe this year has been discussed among the four of us before it has been
implemented.
What you see from the Grand Lodge will not be a one-shot approach.
It will not be an annual flip-flop as different philosophies rotate year to year.

You will see programs that are designed to huild on what has come before and
to provide a foundation for what will come afterward. This fraternity will
grow and prosper only with a long term approach to our concerns. an approach
that is designed to address our problems. an approach that is pursued with
vigor and improved with experience.
And, these programs to address our future cannot be successful
without the commitment of more than your future Grand Masters. It takes the
commitment of you and every member of the fraternity to address honestly
what lies ahead and how besl we can answer the needs of our present and
prospective members. It is only with the commitment of our fraternity. of all
members in all positions in all craft, concordant and appendant bodies, that we
can meet the challenges ahead and build Masonry for the Twenty-first Century.
Lodge Leadership

freemasonry will not be rebuilt by the effons of a Grand Master, by
the effons of the Inspectors or by the efforts of Committeemen. It will be
rebuilt because one leader in one Lodge wants to make a difference. His
enthusiasm and commitment will spark another Mason and another and still
another until that Lodge is a leader in its community and the Fraternity. When
enough Lodges are thus energized, our fraternity will be the force for good in
this country which we know that it can be.

My brothers, we do not have a membership problem in this fraternity.
We have a leadership problem. Better leaders planning better. more interesting
Lodge programs will attract more members! The Wardens' Retreats are
critical to rebuilding leadership in this fraternity. It is frankly more important
for a Warden to attend a Wardens· Retreat as both a Junior and a Senior
Warden than to attend Grand Lodge that year. if finances or vacation planning
require that choice. Let the Master represent that Lodge at the Annual
Communication. 9et the Wardens to the retreats to build for the future.
The training in our Wardens' Retreats has been supplemented by our
new Grand Lodge Master' s Notebook, a three-ring binder filled with practical
information on leadership, Lodge programs and administration and. most
importantly, what it means to be a Mason. The notebook material has been
supplemented by eighty-six letters which I have mailed weekly to the current
Lodge Masters.

Brethren of the Grand Lodge :
Section I 0608 of the California Masonic Code requires the Grand
Master to present at each Annual Communication a written message setting
forth all his official acts during the year. the general condition of Masonry
within the Jurisdiction and his recommendations of such legislation as he
deems necessary or expedient for the welfare of the Craft. I therefore present
the following report on my stewardship of the responsibilities and powers with
which you invested me last October as your Grand Master.
THEME FOR YEAR AND ITS APPLICATI ON

The first ponion of my message will discuss the theme selected for
this Grand Lodge year and how 1 auemptC(j to implement it. lmplementa1ion
was encouraged through the programs which the Lodges were asked to
undcnakc during the year. Implementation was also encouraged through the
remarks which I made during the year, encouraging the Mason~ of this
jurisdiction to consider why we arc Masons. If Masonry has existed for
.i;cnturics. then it must preserve some timeless truths regarding the human
condition which will permit it to grow and prosper in the future, if only those
timeless qualities are applied by every Mason to address the concerns faced by
society today.

Theme for Urand Lodge Year:
Masonry for the Twenty-First Century
Masons are builders Legendarily, we built King Solomon's Temple.
Historically, we built the great Gothic cathedrals in Europe during the Middle
Ages. We built our fraternity from a guild, or a labor union, if you will, of
operative stonemasons to a speculative society of nonoperati vc Masons
accepted to study and put into practice the philosophical prindples of the
ancient stonemasons' craft. the moral and philosophical lessons associated with
the working tools and practices of our operative forbearers.
Because Masons ha"e always been builders. some of us are uncenain

as to ho''' we can reverse the recent decline in the number of men joining our

fraternity. W e can find comfort in one overriding principle of civili7.ation:
institutions with a message or a truth on chc concerns of Man never die. They
adapt to changing times but the truths taught remain the same because the
concerns addressed remain the same: what is my relationship to God, Nature
and my neighbor? These truths make sense of an often senseless world. They
explain the mysteries of life and allow Man to live at peace with his God and
neighbor.

All great insti!utions have survived because they address an enduring
concern about life with a timeless message. Masonry possesses a timeless
message. It distinguished Masonry as an operative guild during the Middle
Ages and allowed. it to transfonn itself into a speculative society in the
Seventeenth and Eighteenth Centuries and grow in the Nineteenth and first half
of the Twentieth Centuries. Freemasonry will grow if we focus those universal
truths about Mankind which Masonry teaches to answer Man's concerns in the
Twenty-First Century.
What are the universal truths of Masonry that survive all ages? The
answer is so self-evident that we might otherwise overlook it. The truths are
so fundamental to Masonry that they are explained to e.ach man on the night
that he bt...-comcs a Mason; they are the principal tenets of Masonry; they arc:
brotherly love, relief and trUth.
Society today is often charncteri1..ed by disregard for the needs of
others. Brotherly love and charity or relief for one's neighbor arc infrequently
found. Masons must show che way by our own example! Wt: must involve
our members, their families and non-Masonic friends in activities outside the
tiled Lodge meeting. Let everyone sec how Masons can wnrk with brotherly
regard for one another. As a general rule. when an event is planned for your
Lodge other than a tiled meeting, we shou ld not ask: "Should we invite wives,
families and non-Masonic friends?" The question should be: "Is there any
reason not to invite wives. families and non-Masonic friends?" And make
what we do enjoyable! Lodges should offer a broad choice of activities. The

Applied Masonry

Lynn OumeniL from her doctoral thesis at Berkeley, wrote
Freemasonry and American Culture, 1880 - 1930. In it, she concludes that the
Golden Age of Freemasonry was not during the I 920's. It was not during the
J950's. In her view. Masonry's Golden Age was during the I 890's when
Masonry was much smaller, when the operat ions of our crafi were different
too. She believes that we Jost the essences of what it meant to be a Mason,
the essences which made Masonry great during this Golden Age, when we
became degree mills during the 1920' s and 1950's, when we became more
concerned with making men members than with making men Masons, when
many men joined Masonry for the perceived business, social and other
advantages to be obtained from their Masonic membership, rather than for
Masonry's philosophical, spiritual and ethical benefits.

Masonry for the Twenty-First Century is also an acknowledgment that
the threshold of a new century and mi llennium. This theme
at
are
we
to pause and reflect on both the past and the future . To what in

challenges
the past should we attribute our present condition? \\'hat do we foresee
occurring in the future') If that future is less than bright, what can we do now
to change it?
The next thirty years promise more advances in medicine, electronics
and other technologies than will have been seen in any prior thirty year period.
Yet, as great as these projected scientific advances may seem, the period yet
to come will not be the most significant in terms of recent human history. The
combined scientific, social. political and economic change was probably the
greatest in the thirty year period which began one hundred years ago.
Imagine that we arc in a Masonic Lodge in 1893 and are told that the
Grand Master's theme is Masonry for the Twentieth Century. What could we
foresee happening in the next thirty years: 1893 through 1923? The changes
that were then to follow were so fu ndamental that few people could have
predicted them. Women went from servant to an equal with the right to vote
and participate in the work place. Motion pictures, radios. automobiles and
airplanes were invented. Medicine and life expectancies advanced. But. the
period also saw the birth of modem warfare. communism and fascism.
Masonry also changed and expanded during that thirty year period.
In 1893, there were 17,000 California Masons. lo 1923. there were 100.000
California Masons, a five fold increase. The number of Lodges went from 255
to 445.
Our country and our craft saw tremendous progress from 1893 to
1923, or did they? Much has changed since 1893 . But, is the human
condition that much heller? Are we really happier now than people were in
1893? We have more creature comforts . We fear less the possibility of de.ath
because of advancements in health care and medical science. But what of the
human spirit? Are we truly better people? Have we really progressed in the
last one hundred years if progress is measured by the degree of human
kindness found today?
What about Freemasonry? While the number of Masons has declined
in the last thirty years, there are more Masons today than there were in 1893.
But is this progress? Is Masonry better today than it was in I 893, simply
because it is now larger? Some believe that the Golden Age of Freemasonry
was during the I 920's or the l 950"s when our membership expanded
dramatically. But, was membership expansion really progress?

53

What made the 1890"s the Golden Age? In the I 890's, Lodges were
smaller. Most every Mason attended Lodge. If a man did not attend,
somebody called on him at his home to find out why not, true brotherly love
in action. When was the last time that anyone here contacted a brother who
did not come to Lodge to find out why? Lodge activities were different also
in the 1890's. A friend of mine who is currently the Grand Master of Masons
in Washington belongs to a Lodge on the Olympic peninsula, most of whose
members were lumberjacks during the l 890's. Their Lodge was small but
most men came to every meeting. What did those lumberjacks do at their
meetings? They conferred few degrees because most every worthy man in the
area was already a Mason. Was their trestleboard filled with practice nights?
No way! At each 01eeting, a brother would talk about what Masonry meant
to him, why he had become a Mason, how Masonry had changed his life.
These were not men of tremendous fonnnl education nor were they recognized
philosophers of their day. Their deeds and words were recorded nowhere other
than in that Lodge's minutes. Out, Masonry meant something to them. At
Lodge, they could meet with other like-minded men and study those timeless
Masonic truths of human existence which are common to all centuries nnd
circumstances. They studied the timeless truths of our fraternity which make
our craft timeless.
I would suggest that here may be found a clue to what we must do for
the future. The practice of those same timeless truths is the key to the future,
but only if we can demonstrate to the people of this century and circumstance
how those timeless truths respond to the concerns of people today. We cannot
create another golde.o age for Masonry simply by duplicating things exactly as
lltcy were in 1893. Masonic truths are timeless but the craft will die if the
'l'Plication of those truths is unchanged, if what we do as Masons is
unchanged, as if chiseled in granite. never to be modified. Masonic truths
never change but their application docs. We must apply those truths to answer
tbe needs of the impending century and circumstance.

The stan of our work for the future is easy: we know what Masonry's
timeless truths are. They are the first lessons taught a man on joining a
Lodge. They are the brotherly regard which we show for one another and the
extension of that regard to those less fortunate than we through our Masonic
relief or charity. It is the search for truth, not just the search for that which
is true but the search to make ourselves true: true to our God and those things
that our God wishes us to be in this life. We pursue truth by perfecting our
own conduct in accordance with these ethical standards. A Mason's search for
truth is his search for self-improvement.

The next step is harder. We must apply those timeless truths to the
problems of today. How Jo we do that? History again provides a clue. When
our craft began, the Master Masons were men well-skilled in the technical and
artistic skills used by the operative stonemasons to build the great European
cathedrals. They went into the fields to find laborers for their building
projects, unskilled fam1en. who would become their apprentices. Their
apprentices undertook self-improvement to learn the operative skills necessary
to build buildings. They also learned those timeless truths regarding the
ethical conduct, the right conduct, which we owe to our creator and our fellow
creatures. as taught through the symbolism of the tools and techniques
employed by the Masons in the construction process. As the demand for
monumental stone churches diminished. the timeless truths did not die with the
decline in construction. The truths did not change, but the application of them
did. We passed from Operative lo Speculative Masonry. when men joined, not
to build buildings as Operative Masons did. but to speculate on, or study, as
we would say, the philosophical content of our craft.
As Operative Masonry was at its height during the middle of the
Thineenth Century during the construction of the great Gothic cathedrals of
France, Speculative Masonry was at its height one hundred years ago when a
man truly joined our fraternity for no other reason than to speculate on its
timeless truths, to consider and learn from them, to improve his conduct
cowards God and Man. That is why chose lumberjacks on the Olympic
peninsula talked so much about what Masonry meant to them at their Lodge
meetings. They were true Speculative Masons. The clue from our craft's past
regarding its future? When the need for Masonry changed. Masonry changed.
It passed from operative to speculative. Masonic truths did not change. only
their application, to fit the needs of the day.
Today's needs are different than they were in the J950's, the 1920's
and the J890's, and therefore Masonry must be different. People today are no
longer content to sit back and be told what to do. People today wan! control
over their own lives and destinies. People today are not passive as they were
in the 1890's, willing to let others tell them what to do and think. Mason~ can
no longer sit by passively either, separate and apart from everything that is.
happening around us in the world. We cannot allow what we do as Masons

speculative Masonry. People of ac~ion toda) do not. want JUSt a ph1losoph1cal

to put what they know into action. They want to apply to the_ ~orld's

Applied Masonry is action. It is treating every person with whom we
come in contact as an equal. If we believe that people are so special that God
loves each one of us, regardless of controversial beliefs or irritating habits.
how can we do any less than God docs? How can we do any less than love
one another? And we express that Jove by the regard which \lie extend to all
with whom we come in contact, regardless of their affiliation with our

And Applied Masonry is something more . People today want control

Mason should search for truth, all people must strive to improve themselves,
sometimes in material terms, but always in spiritual tenns. in the dc;pth of our
faith for our God and our brotherly love and relief for our fellow creatures, our
spiritual self-improvement. Masons must lead by example, by lives dedicated
to improving the human condition of all God's creatures.
The medieval cathedrals built by our operative forbearers would have
been destroyed by the elements centuries ago had not each stone been perfectly
hewn, laid and bound with the requisite mortar. The Operative Masons built
well. And now is the hoor for Applied Masons to build well. to lead by

Masonic Informa1ion Program (January):

What is a Mason ic Information Program? It is an opportunity to
invite your non-Masonic friends to visit your Lodge and tell them what
Masons do. Let them see where we meet and learn about our activities. Let
them witness the fun we have when we go to Lodge. Tell them that we are
the world 's oldest and largest fraternity and heirs to the philosophical teachings
associated with the working tools of the Medieval stonemasons. Tell them that
we are dedicated to the principles of brotherly love or regard for our fellows.
Tell them that we show our care for others by Mason ic relief or charity. Tell
them that we strive for truth by our Masonic journey through life seeking to
perfect ourselves on earth by our faith in God and practice of Masonic
teachings.
Let them know that our families are an important part of Masonry.
Explain our social and civic activities that involve the Masons and their
fam ilies. Explain Eastern Star, Amaranth and the other organizations involving
our wives and explain the youth groups. Explain how these other groups teach
the same lessons ~ are taught in our Lodges.
Let them know about the prominent persons who have been Masons.
know about the California public schools week program, Shriners
them
Let
Hospitals for Crippled Children and other benefits to the community sponsored
by Masons.
Dispel the myths about Masonry. Explain that we are not a religion
or a substitute for it. We do not promise salvation to those who are members.
We work to improve the human condition on earth . Our Masonic lessons do
not promise life everlasting by being a good Mason a lone. Let the nonMasons know that people of all religious beliefs who believe in a Supreme
Being can and do become Masons. Let them know that people of all ethnic
backgrounds can and do become Masons. Explain that we are not a secret
organization but an organization with certain signs, words and other methods
of making ourselves known to one another. There is nothing secret about who
we are, where we meet or what we stand for.
Most importantly, tell them how to become a Mason. To be one, you
must ask one. No one will ask you!

Widows Program (February):

Our Masonic obligations bind us to aid and assist our widows. What
can we do? We can start with an event during the month of February when
every Lodge in California is asked to honor our Masonic widows.
Plan an event that all of the ladies of the Lodge members would
enjoy. Don't cry something like a dance that requires couples but an activity
that singles would enjoy too. It can be a good dinner and entertainment. It
can be something different yet special: a theater party, a mystery trip, a
Valentine's Party or a Sunday brunch. Naturally, include all of your members
and their wives in the activity.
Make sure that all widows of your Lodge's members li ving in the area
are informed of this special event. Mail a special flyer. Follow up the mailing
with a personal telephone call. Make sure that each widow who needs
transportation receives it.
Present the Grand Lodge widow's pin at the event. if convenient
These pins are available through the supply room at the Grand Lodge office
and can be ordered by your Lodge's secretary. Order them in plenty of time
to avoid disappointments. If it is not convenient to present the pins at the
special February event, present them at a Lodge Stated Meeting dinner or al
any other time during the year when the program is appropriate.
A special February program is important to demonstrate our care and
affection for our widows on a special occasion. But, don't limit your Lodge's
Widow's Program to this single event. Whenever your Lodge has an eveat
when the members' wives are included. invite your Masonic widows too!

Try the Grand Lodge Sisters of Hiram program available through the
Grand Lodge Committee on Masonic Widows Program. The Sisters of Hiram
is a social group composed of the widows of members of a Lodge. There is
no ritual. There is no state-wide organization or rules of operation prescribed
by the Grand Lodge. Its members meet informally for companionship and
mutual support. lls members are often a support group for the Lodge too,
providing volunteer assistance for Lodge programs, such as dinners and other
social events.

In my own Lodge, we involve wives and families in almost all of our
ICtiviues other than our tiled meetings. When a brother dies, his widow
continues to attend just as she did before, and some of our Lodge's best
supporters are these widows who continue to give of their time and talent for
the betterment of Freemasonry.
Plan now for your special February event to honor our widows but
lllO plan your year to involve these widows in all of your Lodge' s social
ldivities. You will not only thereby fulfill your Masonic obligation but you
will also tap a potential new source of enthusiastic supporters for your Lodge.

Public Schools (April):

Why do Masons support public schools? Why did Masons sponsor
the first Public Schools observance in 1920? Why should Masons be active
in today's Public Schools Week observances and events 10 demonstrate the
concern of all right-thinking people for the continued high standards of our
public schools'?
Beginning with the stonemasons of medieval Europe who built the
great. Gothic cathedrals. Masons have been dedicated to self-improvement,
learning to better oneself. just as the medieval stonemasons taught themselves
and their successors the building a.rrs which allowed them to erect the massive
stone edifices which survive to this day. Beginning with the stonemasons of
medieval Europe, Masons have been dedicated to freedom, the medieval
Mason so that he might travel to whatever jurisdiction might have work for
him and today's Mason so that every person may by self-improvement achieve
what.ever success hard work and dedication might bring. Masons support free
public schools because only an educated citizenry can, through elections and
pub Ii c service, guarantee that our constitutional svstem of Ii be rt ies w iII be
preserved and, therefore, that we and future g~nerations will have our
Constitution in a democratic society available to preserve our search for
personal truth.
Masons arc commined to our public schools, because no society can
re~ain free without an educated citizenry, and the largest part of our citizenry

VI.

Sojourners (June):

Over the years. t have met a number of Masons who have moved but
who have never been sufficiently motivated to visit a local Lodge. Some
estimate that there are as many Masons living in California who belong to outof-state Lodges as there arc members of California Lodges. Many California
Masons have moved to new areas in the state and no longer attend their home
Lodges, but have never attended a Lodge near their new home either. What
a potential source of new members for your Lodge, new members who are
already Master Masons and potential officers and committeemen for you!
Perhaps . if you contacted some of these sojourners in your local area and
invited them to a Lodge event. they would become active aga in .
A number of Masonic groups have used the following program to lind
sojourning Masons. They obtain from Grand Lodge its mailing list for Master
Masons known to the Grand Lodge who live in zip codes near the Lodge. The
Lodge Secretary then eliminates those on the list who already belong to the
Lodge, and the members of the sojourners committee contact those who do
not. They look for telephone numbers in the local directory and call the
sojourners on the list. Alternatively, an active member who lives near cbe
sojourner makes a personal visit. A number of Lodges have successfully
recruited new members from this program.

GRANO l.OIXiE OF CALll'ORNIA

69

An important part of any successful sojourners program is the
impression which you make on the first time visitor to your Lodge. An
important part of that first impression is the examination which you conduct
for first time visitors to your tiled Lodge meeting. How do you satisfy
yourself that a visitor is a Master Mason and eligible to visit your Lodge?
First, check his dues card. ls the dues card for the current year? Has
it been signed by the Lodge Secretary and the member? Verify the visitor's
name and signature on the dues card against his driver' s license. Does the
dues card have the Lodge seal on it? ls it issued by a recognized Lodge?
Your Lodge Secretary has a list of all Masonic Lodges in the world under the
jurisdiction of a Grand Lodge recognized by our Grand Lodge. Look at the
book in case of doubts. When checking a visitor' s dues card, remember that
a visitor has the right to check your dues card also and the Lodge ·s charter!
With this preliminary behind you, can a member of your Lodge
present before the meeting begins vouch from personal knowledge that the
visitor is a Master Mason? Normally, this is done when one of your members
has sat in another Lodge with the visitor. If no one can vouch for this visitor,
then your examination committee members must satisfy themselves that your
visitor is a Master Mason.
The examination committee should be composed of three members.

Why not start this program in your Lodge? The Grand Secrl!tary has
organized the Grand Lodge mailing list by zip codes. Make a list of those zip
codes within five miles of your Lodge. Ask the Grand Secretary's office for
the list of those Masons known to the Grand Lodge who live in the zjp codes
on your list. When you receive your list, have your Lodge Secretary eliminate
the names of those Masons who already belong to your Lodge or who are
known to be active in another Lodge. Appoint a committee to contact those
remaining on the list. Invite them to a Lodge event.
Sponsor a Rusty Trowel program in June. Information with respect
to this program is available from the Grand Lodge Sojourners Committee.
Invite the sojourners whom you have identified from the Grand Lodge list.
Mention in your Lodge bulletin the importance of each member inviting a
sojourner known to him to attend also. Have your member bring his guest to
the event. Each of us probably knows at work, church or elsewhere a Mason
who is no longer active but who might become interested in the craft again by
attending a Rusty Trowel program at your Lodge.
Make the Rusty Trowel event interesting. lnclude entertainment, a
meal or anything that will make the event something that everyone will enjoy.
Within a few days after the program. contact the sojourners again and invile
them to something else. Get them bad, in the habit of attending Lodge.

It is best to have a standing committee responsible for examining first time
visitors, the mem~ers of which are known to your Tiler. Your Tiler then
knows whom to ask to conduct the examination when a visitor attends your
tiled Lodge meeting.
The members of this standing committee should read this letter and
discuss with you the responsibiliti es of such a committee. Once so trained, it
would also be helpful to have the committee members practice an examination
on you to see how well they understand their duties. If you go to a lot of
work to encourage sojourners to visit your Lodge, you do not 'llrant to scare
them away with the examination.
The examination committee should use the following procedure. The
ex1111ination committee members should invite the visitor to a quiet place, such
•the preparation room. The Test Oath is given first. The Test Oath should
be given by one of the examination committee members from memory,
lltbough it may be read from the Monitor if no one present has memorized it.
The Test Oath should be recited in shon sections so that the visitor can repeat
It in Ill understandable manner. The visitor and committee members all hold
Ille Holy Bible while the visitor repeats the Test Oath. The person reciting the
T• Oath should ask the visitor to kiss the Holy Bible on the completion of

Ille Test Oath.

George Washington was a Mason and the Master of his Lodge. The
French General Lafayette was a Mason. Paul Revere was a Mason. John Paul
Jones was a Mason.
Of the fifty-six. signers of the Declaration of
Independence. eight can be proven to have been Masons, including Benjamin
franklin and John Hancock. Another twenty-four signers may have been
Masons, based upon fragmentary evidence which has survived until today.
These early American, patriotic Masons demonstrated the noblest support of
established civil authority: they temporarily set aside their loyalty when that
authority was clearly and oppressively wrong to replace it with one dedicated
to freedom and liberty.
Since the founding of our nation, men preeminent in American
political life have been Masons, in(;luding Presidents Andrew Jackson, a Past
Grand Master, James Polk, James Buchanan . a Past Master, Andrew Johnson.
James Garfield, William McKinley, Theodore Roosevelt. William Howard
Taft, Warren Harding, Franklin Roosevelt, Harry Truman, a Past Grand
Master, and Gerald Ford. Our fonner Governor of California and funner Chief
Justice of the United States Supreme Coun, Earl Warren, was a Past Master
of a Lodge in Oakland and Grand Master of Masons in California during the

1930's.
Dedication to active service as a c1t1zen is the special charge of all
Masons. Today, when a man is initiated into a California Masonic Lodge, he
is enjoined to be exemplary in the discharge of his civil responsibilities, by
never suggesting or supporting any act which might subven the peace and
good order of society. He is further enjoined to pay due obedience to the laws
under whose protection he lives and never to lose sight of the allegiance due
by every citizen to his or her country. We expect the individual Mason to
work at the duties of citizenship, making himself available for service to his
community, state and nation . Only through this service can the privileges
which we enjoy as Masons and as Americans be saved for posterity.
We commemorate the signing of the United States Constitution to
make our Constitution more immediate in our lives, to prevent it from
becoming "ancient history." We bring it into our contemporary understanding.
We emphasize the need for civic education, wisdom and vinue; for the
willingness to sacrifice immediate personal gain for the greater Jong-term
benefit of all; for commitment to our constitutional system of ordered liberty;
for the ingenuity to solve complicated new problems. as we have done so
many times in the past. What better way for any of us to direct our active
support for the system of government we cherish than to emphasize these

qualities which will sustain the cornucopia of
benefits engendered by the
personal creativity and vitality of the American peopl
e and encouraged by our
constitutional syscem of government.

How Can We Interest More People in the Craft?
Is your membership aging? Do you have fewer candidates for the
degrees than you would like? What can you do about it? If we are to build
Masonry for the Twenty-First Century, then we must find the answers to these
questions. Here are some thoughts.

How Can We Encourage More Men to Become Masons? Many men
have limited amounts of additional time available for fraternal activities
because of work and other family commitments. Many wives work. It is
difficult to interest many men, particularly younger men, in fraternal organizations unless families are involved and time devoted to the organization's
activities is used in the most effective manner possible.
What can you do? All Lodge activities other than tiled meetings
should include families. The programs should be designed to interest not only
Masons but their wives, children and non-Masonic friends and families. Child
care should be provided by the Lodge for younger people attending Lodge
activities with small children. Activities of interest to younger people, such
as sports teams, should be encouraged. We should be more active with the
Mason ic youth groups.

Masonry and Religion

Some religious groups criticize us because Masons who are Christians
allow Muslims, Buddhists, Jews and other non-Christians to become Masons.
we are criticized because Masons respect a Muslim's right, a Buddhist's right,
a Jew's right to believe in a divine word other than the New and Old
Testaments. We are criticized because Masons who arc Christians do not deny
that non-Christian Masons can be saved . Do Christians have a monopoly on
ethical behavior? Why should a consideration of ethics be limited to the
members of one religious group? Because Masonry docs not deal with
salvation. what is the relevance of its members' various views on that subject?

A troublesome development this year has been a rise in the number
of religious critics of our fraternity. A number of religious groups and some
members of the news media have questioned whether Freemasonrv is
compatible with Christianity. As a committed Mason and a licensed. Lay
Reader in the Episcopal Church, I would like to share some thoughts on the
subject.
Masonry has been criticized over the centuries by various religious
groups. Some of these cri tics allege that Masonry is a religion. These cri tics
argue that Masonry offers a plan of salvati on based upon good works of its
members. They therefore claim that members of their faith cannot be Masons
because one cannot have two religions. This criticism is often heard from
some members of those Christian groups which emphasize that faith alone and
not good works is necessary for salvation.
Masonry is not a religion. Religion deals with salvation, the
preparation of our spirit for its return to the God who gave it. Masonry, on
the other hand, is about ethics: right and wrong conduct in the here and now.
How should we deal with our fellow creatures. Confusion sometimes arises
because religion talks about ethics too but its focus is different. Salvation, not
ethics, distinguishes religion. Masonry deals exclusively with ethics.
Nowhere in our Masonic ritual is there a promise to our members that
they will go to heaven if they are good Masons. Recognized Masonry in this
country has never sought to be the means for salvation. It is self-improvement
in th is world for which we strive as Masons. We strive for admission to
heaven through our religious preparation.
Some of these criticisms are based on a misunderstanding of our
Masonic ceremonies. For example, some religious critics misconstrue that
portion of the Masonic funeral service when the Master declares that the
lambskin apron is representative of that purity of life and conduct so
essentially necessary to gaining admission into the Celestial Lodge above.
Does this mean that we get to heaven by good works as a Mason? No! It
means that we are unblemished in our record of what our God wants us to be.
regardless of our individual religious belief, the nature of that God and that
God' s expectations of us. For a Christian, "that purity of life and conduct''
mentioned in the foneral ritual means a lite of faith and righteousness.
Some religious critics allege that Masons swear oaths on the Bible
with penalties which they do not intend to enforce and therefore commit
blasphemy. Any thoughtful Mason knows that these penalties are symbolic
only. Religions are rich with symbolism also.

Rotary, like religion and Masonry, also deals with ethics. Rotarians
consider ethical conduct in their business dealings with others. Does this make
Rotary a religion? Are Christians therefore prohibited from becoming
Rotarians? Some religions have dietary rules that prescribe proper food
preparation. So does Betty Crocker's cookboo~! . Does that n:ake her
cookbook a. religious volume? Of course not! Religion overlaps with many
other ideas. including those of Masonry and Rotary. But, religion deals with
something that no other group does: salvation, and it is the search for
salvation that makes religion.
Why the criticisms of Masonry? Some religious critics fear the
unknown. It is easy to ascribe evil intentions to something which we do not
understand. Members of our Masonic family must do a better job at our
Masonic Information Programs and whenever the subject arises in discussions
with non-Masons to. explain why Masonry is not a religion.
Some religious critics fear competition, competition for the time, talent
and treasure of their members. Should any group with an important and
worthwhile message fear competition? Doe~ not the strength of the idea stand
oo its own? And some religious critics, regretfully. show a Jack of toleration
of any views that may differ from their own, an intolerance which wi ll destroy
this countrv if allowed to grow unchecked. One prominent Masonic critic,
John Anke;berg, in his anti-Masonic text, The Secret Teachings of the Masonic
Lodge, attacks not just Masons. lie attacks Jews. Mormons and Jehovah's
Witnesses too.
Sume Masonic cnt1cs criticize every group, Masonic or religious,
whose views do not exactly match their own. It reminds me of Lenin, Stalin
and every other demagogue of history. What would Jesus say about such
people? Jesus said: "Love one another." He also taught his followers to.
"love thine enemy". How can one be a good Christian yet be as intolerant of
the views of others as are people like Mr. Ankerberg.,
It is the beauty of Masonry that good people regardless of religious
beliefs may gather and share those timeless truths about human nature,. a.bout
ethics, about right and wrong conduct, that are common to all great re11g1ons.

For me. one o f the enjoyments which I derive from Masonry is the opportunity
to share with Jews, Muslims and others those timeless truths regarding ethical
conduct. common to all right thinking people. to deepen m> own personal faith
and understanding of God with the added perspective of others who believe
with possibly differing inlefllreLations.

increase in violence in society today is not limited just to schools but ~ay be
found among both school age children and young adults . .The pubh~ cuts
support for welfare and other social service ~rograrns. as consistently as 1t cuts
ublic education. Non-English-speaking children, violence and tax cuts ha~e
~urt public education . But, I believe that Californians would once .again
support adequate funding for public education if they h.ad confidence in the
results. There are problems within the public schools which must be corrected
before student performance can improve and public confidence return.

82

Masonry is important in this age. as it has been in those before us and
will be in those 10 come, because it unites; it does not divide. It respects all
people and does not seek to replace the religious beliefs of any of them, nor
to claim that some are superior to others . It practices toleration. Our
membership requirements are simple: we require only a belief in God.
Peoples of any faith who have this one simple belief may belong.
Masonry is unique because it is the only place where all people of
God may share in their search for the ethical approach to all that we do. It is
the only place where people from different religious backgrounds can share
each's perspective with respect to ethical behavior. It is the only place where
a Christian, a Jew, a Muslim or any other believer in God may share his
approach to that same ethical conduct to which we all strive and which is
common to every major religion: doing to others as we would want them 10
do to us.
Is not this what the world needs today? We need more unity. not
more division. We need more places where like-minded people can. gather and
share thoughts with respect to the improvement of the human condition.
Masonry is good because it allows good people of all religious views to unite
for the improvement of people in this world. Such has been Masonry's
greatness in the past. So may it ever be in the future.

Education at the Crossroads
The education of our young people and therefore the future of our
society is at the crossroads. The results of slandardized tests suggest tha1
public school students today are not learning as much as they did even twenty
or thirty years ago. It is reported chat 135,000 children bring guns to school
every day in America. In some of the larger metropolitan school districts, the
high school drop out rate is thirty percent. Violence on campus is common
place. The American public does not reward such poor performance and
therefore ballot measures to increase spending on schools are consistently
defeated. Parents with school age children often vote "no" on the performance
of public schools by enrolling their children in private schools.
Many reasons. or rather excuses, are given for poor public school
performance. The population of recent immigrants in California from nonEnglish-speaking countries is at its highest level in modem limes. The

A performance crisis is often preceded by a leadership crisis. What
bout the leadership in today 's public schools? We have school boards.
~mposed not of community or parent representatives. but .of teacher
representatives more concerned with teache'. ben~fi~s than with s.tude~t
education. We have school districts top heavy in administrators. In. C~hforn1a
school districts. there arc one or more paid administrators at the dist.net lev~l
whose sole responsibility is curriculum selection. In Minnesota. cum~ulum ts
selected on a state-wide basis. Minnesota does not waste mo~e~ with extra
administrators at the district level who duplicate the same decisions in each
district throughout the state.
What about the teachers? There are many dedicated teachers in public
education. But what about those teachers who should be removed fro m the
classroom but are protected by tenure? \\'hat about those teachers w ho do not
have the temperament to deal with young people? What about those teachers
who were once goC>d but lost their enthusiasm for teaching y~ars ago, whose
cynicism results from years of coping with undisciplined children, a lack .of
discipline encouraged by couns and school boards more . concerned with
individual student rights than with a quality educatton environment for the
students who want to learn?
There are California school districts with excellent student test sco.re
records. tittle violence and few students who drop out of school. But, despite
many such successes, Californians are frustrated with the poor perf~rmance of
public schools in those districts which have poor student scores, v1ol~nce and
high drop out rates. What is the answer? School l~der~ respo.nd wit~ pleas
for more money but. until they see some results. Californ.1ans w11l .contmue to
register their displeasure by reducing funding for pu~lic ~duca11~n and by
removing their children from the public sc~ool~. Cahfom1ans will have an
opportunity to register their displeasure again this November 2nd when there

Without quality free public education available to all citizens, what
would our society be like today? How could the German immigrants or the
immigrants from Southern Europe, or the immigrants from Eastern Europe
have improved themselves, without public education? How could many of
their descendants have risen to prominence in Amencan life without public
education?
What will our country be like in twenty years if today's
immigrants cannot get .a quality education? Thirty percent of California
students are from homes where English is not spoken or spoken only haltingly
as a second language. Sixty percent of California students are from broken
homes. Twenty percent of California students have at least one parent on
welfare. These are the students today most in need of the quality, free
education that America promised and provided to generations past.
What can Masons do to bring quality back to California education?
First, we must educate. We must study again the important contribution to the
development of our society that free public education has perfonned. We must
srudy how free public education has made more Americans productive
members of our country than most any other nation has done with its citizens.
We must study how free public education has heretofore prevented class

di visions from rearing al the fabric of our counrry as has occurred abroad.
When we have learned these important lessons once again, we must educate
those outside of the Masonic family on them also. Just as Masons in 1920
pioneered public schools observances to focus the attention of California
citizens on the then pitiful state of public education, we must again educate
those outside of the Masonic family on the importance of public education.

And, more important than study and talk, we must act. We must
work. We cannot complain about failures which we have all seen in public
education without trying to rectify those failures. We complain that students
do not learn. Most of us cannot become teachers but we can volunteer in
libraries and read to young students. Studies consistently report that students
read better when they have been read to as young people. We can vol unteer
as math tutors. Do you know something about computers? Today and
tomorrow, young people are at competitive disadvantage if they cannot use a
computer. If you have the skills, volunteer to rutor students in the computer
laboratory at the local school. If the local school does not have a computer
laboratory, make it a Lodge project to buy the computers to start one. Can
you volunteer in the school library or in the computer laboratory? Of course
you can, and my wife has been doing it since our children started school.
There are oppommities to serve outside the classroom. Sponsor an
outstanding teacher award to recognize those teachers in your local schools
who are enthusiastic. who have the temperament for teaching and who have
not been defeated by cynicism. Give them a reward but not with cash or a
fancy plaque. Ask them what they need in their classrooms and then buy it.
Sponsor an essay contest and ask the s1udents to write about the importance
of public education . Get our young people to understand why public education
is important. Have both the teacher and student winners to the Lodge to
rece ive their awards. When they come, tell those in attendance what the
teacher did to get the award. Have the students read their essays. Ask the
local newspapers for publicity. Local papers love human interest stories.
What could be more news-worthy than a teacher who teaches well or a student
who writes well ! The cost? Use money from your Lodge's refreshment fund!
Run for a seat on the local school board. This past year, I met a
majority member of Rainbow for Girls who is on one of our California school
boards. She is discouraged and has contemplated serving one term only. She
wants better schools for studenLo; but every other school board member wants
a platform to launch a campaign for higher office. We need more school
board members like that former Rainbow Girl who want to help students and
not their personal political careers.

California is at the crossroads. Do we choose the easy road? We
could abandon public sch ools whose current failures obscure for many citi:t..ens
publ ic education's past successes. We could choose school vouchers this
November and dual school systems. This is the easy road, but, by choosing
it, we also abandon those young people must in need of education . Or do we
choose the rough and rugged road? Do we fight to refonn public schools?
The fight will not be easy. The road is beset with ruffians: an apathetic and
at times hostile public, religious groups that want government subsidies for
their own brand of education and school personnel more concerned with selfpreservation or self-promotion than student self-improvement. We must fight
first by preparing uurselves and others on the issues. We must work as
volunteers to help with the education of our young people. We must run for
schoo l boards and vote for school board candidates who put America's youth
first.
Am¢rica is great because its people are. great. That greatness will be
lost if we abandon our young people by denying them a quality education. We
can no longer criticize past. poor performance and do no more. We must work
to improve public education, not abandon it. We must remedy its past
problems and rebuild it. At the crossroads, we must choose the road whi~h
history proves produced our present greatness. We must choose public
education. our hope for the Twenty-First Century.
