Even more important than the American Constitution itself. our system
of government has survived because there have been succeeding generations
of Americans willing to implement that framework in the spirit of our nation's
founders, whether by Congress passing laws, the President enforcing laws or
the Courts implementing Jaws. In 1821, New York abolished property
ownership as a qua] i ti cation for voting. In 1841, Rhode Island ex!ended the
right to vote to all iidult males. In 1870, Congress removed race as a voting
barrier. In 1920, women were guaranteed the vote, which had already been
won in many states in the prior 60 years.

What then is the true source of our liberties? It is the Constitution
which guarantees those liberties and provides the framework of the government
which protects them. It is public education which equips us to rule ourselves.
And, most importantly, it is our vigilance in preserving the Constitution, never
countenancing an y person who would, by force or ill advised legislation,
abridge its liberties for any person, regardless of station or belief. Preserve
your freedoms by your personal commin:i1ent to e~tend to every man, woman
and child: justice, liberty and the pursuit of happiness.

Nowhere does our Constitution mention the social security program.
But, the Preamble establishes the Constitution to, in part, "promote the general
welfare." The Constitution further provides Congress with the power to make
laws necessary and proper to execute the purposes for which the Constitution
was established. Thus, the authority for social se~urity, enacted in the I930's,
can be found in a document written almost 150 years before when the concept
of social security had not yet been thought.

Freemasonrv and Good Government

90

The original liberties for all people in the Constitution and Bill of
Rights have endured because Americans were ~ducated in the duties and
privileges inherent in political power and a free society, Americans were
granted the right to vote and otherwise participate in the political process as
they became traioed to participate and Americans passed that knowledge on
to their descendants.
How can we preserve what has survived for almost 200 years but
which is increasingly challenged from within and from without? Experience
is the application of past successes and fa ilures to current problems. The
example and experience of the Americans who preceded us should be our
beacon. We must remain dedicated to the ideas which have made our system
of government a success in the past.
First, our Constitution must remain a foundation, a framework, an out·
line. It must remain unc luttered by restrictions of only passing importance,
distrustful of those who follow us tu administer it properly. Second, in
completing that foundation and framework to house current generations, we
must enact laws required by today's society which are mindful of the rights
and liberties of all persons and of the sacrific.e s which we must make to future
generations through public education to repay our heritage by guaranteeing it
for future inhabitants of our land. Finally, we must guarantee a free education
to all willing to learn, nut in private schools with narrow aims supported by

91

Why do Masons place special importance on celebrating the American
Constitution? Why do Masons set aside a special day in September each year
to observe the anniversary of the adoption of our Constitution?
We celebrate our Constitution because it symbolizes the guarantee of
our personal freedom and liberties. Masons have always supported personal
As a necessary corollary, Masons support good
freedom and liberty.
government as the Qn!y guarantee of freedom and liberty. Our dedica~ion to
personal freedom can be traced to the founding of our order. Legendan ly, we
trace the origins of Freemasonry to the building of King Solomon's !:mple
in approximately 950 B.C. Historically, however, some trace the on gms ?f
freemasonry to the building of the Gothic Cathedral of Strasbourg, now m
France, in the year 1275 A.O.
The stonemasons who erected the great, stone Gothic cathedrals of
Europe were unlike most peoples of the Middle Ages. The secrets of
architecture employed in the construction of those edifices were known only
to the stonemasons. They were few in number. Because of the demand for
their services, the stonemasons were free to travel from one political
jurisdiction to another in order to work on whatever stone cath~dr~I th~n
required laborers. To assure hannony among the workers at the bu1khng site
and confidence among employers that the workers would perfonn their duties
with honesty and dedication, the medieval stonemasons developed a system of
morality which paralleled their architectural and construction techniques.
Each became a symbol for the other. For example, the respective
jewels of the Master and Wardens of this Lodge are a square, a level and a
plumb. each used to test the com erston~ and each additio~al sto~e
subsequently added to the edifice. To the medieval stonemason, and m today s

93

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

URAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Masonic Lodge, the square is a symbol of virtue and teaches us to square our
actions by the square of virtue; the level is a symbol of equality and teaches
equality among all peoples, regardless of station; and the plumb is a symbol
of morality and teaches us to walk uprightly in our several stations before God
and man.

Masons have been and remain dedicated to freedom and champions
of liberty. Yet, dedication to freedom and liberty and therefore the good
government which can bring it is of little value unless one is willing to commit
action to support it. George Washington, our most distinguished American
statesman and Mason, observed that ". .. The United States, which gives to
bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance, requires only that ... We
who live under its protection should ... [conduct ourselves] as good citizens
... [by] giving it on all occasions . .. [our] effectual support." Put more
succinctly by another American Mason, President Theodore Roosevelt, "The
first requisite of a good citizen in this republic of ours is that he should be
able and willing to pull his weight."

92

The medieval stonemasons began to realize that, as physical freedom
allowed them to travel to wherever work might be found, intellectual freedom
from the self-interested views of a political or religious tyrant allowed them
to pursue the moral truths symboliz.ed by their building trade. Physical
freedom, therefore, led naturally to a high regard for freedom of thought and
therefore the ability to pursue truth wherever they might find it.
By the Seventeenth Century, the building of the great European stone
cathedrals was on the decline. Consequently, the medieval stonemasons'
guilds declined also. Although the exact date is unclear, sometime around
1600, Lodges began to admit members who did not actually work for their
livelihood as stonemasons. These men joined not to learn the actual
techniques of architecture and construction but to learn their moral symbolism,
the moral science associated with the building science. Because the Masons
continued to reject any blind reliance on any narrow political or religious
doctrine, Freemasonry continued to attract freedom-loving people. Many of
the progressive philosophical and political leaders of Europe joined. The great
French philosopher Voltaire was a Mason.
When Freemasonry came to America in 1731, it continued to attract
like-thinking people. Many leaders of the American Revolutionary War who
fought for our freedom from British colonial rule were Masons: Paul Revere,
George Washington, Benjamin Franklin, John Hancock, General Lafayette and
John Paul Jones. When the war ended, Masons continued in the peace time
struggle for good government as the best guarantee of their newly-won
personal freedom. Fourteen presidents, from President Washington through
Presidents Roosevelt, Truman and Ford, have been Masons, as well as eighteen
Vice-Presidents of the United States. Five Chief Justices of the United States
Supreme Court were Masons and two were Grand Masters. Eighteen
governors of California have been Masons, including Earl Warren, both
Governor and Chief Justice of the United States Supreme Court, and a Grand
Master of Masons in California during the l 930's.
Masons have been active in the fight for freedom and its preservation
in other countries as well. Giuseppe Garibaldi, the Nineteenth Century
military leader in the movement for unification and independence of Italy, was
a Mason. Simon Bolivar, the South American soldier-statesman who freed
Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Colombia and Panama from Spanish rule,
was a Mason.

Our society does not now face the challenges that it did during the
American Revolution when George Washington was a leader or even during
the Great Depression when another Mason, Franklin Roosevelt, was president.
Yet, every day there are those who would work against our freedom and
liberty. How can we pull our weight? We can demonstrate publicly our
support for good government as the best guarantee of personal liberty and
freedom . We can educate ourselves on the issues facing us and work to
educate others. We can vote for leaders who support good government. In
general, we can put our ideals into practice by our vigorous support for those
leaders and programs which encourage freedom and liberty for all, which
respond to the needs of our citizens and which encourage our citizens to
participate actively in the fonnation of policy.
Our nation 'was conceived in freedom and liberty and dedicated to the
proposition that all its citizens are created equal. Yet, these blessings will not
long remain unless we are able and willing to pull our own weight and to
work for the good government needed to preserve them. We must be
dedicated to this unfinished work which will never end, which those who have
preceded us have thus far so nobly advanced. We must be dedicated to the
great task always remaining before us, to guarantee freedom and liberty for all
our citizens, that this nation of the people, by the people and for the people
shall not perish from the earth.

Diversity
There is a beautiful and powerful, yet often misunderstood, passage
of scripture which has significance for the Masonic Family at the brink of the
Twenty-First Century. It is the plea of the heroine of the Book of Ruth :
"Entreat me not to leave you or to return from following you; for where you
go I will go, and where you lodge I will lodge; your people shall be my people
and your God my God; ... "
For those who do not belong to Eastern Star, this passage is most

94

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

commonly heard during the marriage ceremony, ostensibly as an expression of
devotion which the bride and groom thenceforth pledge to one another as
husband and wife. While a beautiful expression of the sentiment, such was not
the intention of the passage. Ruth , as we know, made this pledge to her
widowed mother-in-law , Naomi, and not to her husband! In Eastern Star, this
story is told as an illustration of constancy as evidenced in Ruth's devotion to
Naomi, despite Naomi 's entreaties that Ruth remain with her people and not
return with Naomi to Israel.

among those who might otherwise have remained at a perpetual d istance."
Despite this noble intention e xpressed in the ritual of our order, despite the
example of Solomon and his great-grandfather Boaz, we as California Masons
do not have a particularly exemplary record of practicing what we preach, of
imitating the example of Solomon and Boaz, when it comes to welcoming
those outside our normal circle of friends into Freemasonry .

The significance of Ruth 's story intensifies when one considers its
historical context. There have been periods in Jewish history when a person
could not become a Jew unless his or her mother were a Jew. How could
Ruth expect to return with Naomi to Israel and become a Jew when Ruth 's
mother was not Jewish? Also, the Book of Ruth was probably written at a
time after the exile when the prophets Ezra and Nehemiah required Hebrew
men to divorce their foreign wives and marry only within the covenant
community. Ezra and Nehemiah sought to preserve the identity of the Hebrew
people by eliminating foreign influences. Despite these traditions which would
discourage foreigners fro m Israel, Ruth entreats Naomi to be welcomed as a
part of the Hebrew nation, to which entreaty Naomi accedes when she returns
with Ruth to Israel.
In my view, the story of Ruth is not about spousal devotion, as
implied in the marriage ceremony, nor about constancy, as taught in Eastern
Star, as much as it is about diversity: welcoming into our group those
outsiders who desire to join regardless of their background, just as the elderly
Naomi brought Ruth, the damsel from Moab, back to Israel. We also learn
from scripture that Ruth later marries Boaz and thus becomes one of King
Solomon 's great-grandm others.
We know that Solomon, King of Israel, whom Masons have adopted
as their legendary founder, himself welcomed diversity during his reign. He
married the Queen of Sheba. More importantly for Masons, Solomon invited
participation of Hiram, King of Tyre, and the artificer in bronze, Huram-Abi,
the widow 's son from the tribe of Naphtali, to participate in the most glorious
activity of Solomon' s reign : the building of Solomon's Temple to God. If
Solomon welcomed outsiders to so great, glorious and sacred an undertaking
as the building of the temple, how can we do any less than our royal founder?
If outsiders, men of different nations and religions, could play such an
important role in the legendary founding of our Masonic order, how can we
do any less than welcome into the Masonic Fraternity all good men and true,
regardless of faith or race, to join us as we build Masonry for the Twenty-First
Century?
In our Entered Apprentice Degree, we learn that "... Masonry unites
men of every country, sect and opinion; and causes true friendship to exist

Over t he decades, Jews have become Masons but have been largely

The theme for this Grand Lodge Year, Masonry for the Twenty-First
Century, challenges us to rebuild our Fraternity by first identifying those
timeless teach ings .of our order which transcend the ages, which answer
people's problems regardless of the century and circumstance in which they
live, and then by demonstrating that Masonry can answer th e problems of the
Twenty-First Century by apply ing those t imeless truths to everyday actions.
By addressing the problems which we face by Masonry's answers, our actions
will provide a powerful example to encourage others to follow us.
In the press everyday, we learn that hatred among ethnic and relig ious
groups is tearing apart South Africa and the peoples in what was once
Yugoslavia. C loser to home, we are informed of black and Hispanic gangs
assassinating one another in drive by shootings. We hear of white supremacist
skin head gan gs plotting to blow up black churches. Masonry 's timeless
answer?
Masons are taught to "... regard t he whole human species as one
famil y, the high and the low, the rich and the poor, who, as created by one
Almighty Parent, and inhabitants of the same planet, are to aid, support and
protect each other." A Mason is t hus charged to practice brotherly love.
Brotherly love has been a standard o f Masonic ethics since the historical
founding of our fraternity in the operati ve stonemasons guild of medieval
Europe when Masons made a sacred covenant to provide for one another in the
event of a d isabling or mortal accident at the building site. Masons were also

96

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

there charged to practice brotherly love so that the entire community at the
building site could live in peace and harmony with one another while there
employed. It is by the practice of this teaching, by the practice of brotherly
love, that Masonry today should unite men of every country, sect and opinion.
Thus united, regardless of race or religion, our actions as Masons will
demonstrate to those in our community and in the world the regard which all
people should hold for one another. If we have all been created by God, and
if God believes that each one of us is so special that we may each by faith and
by keeping God's commandments attain salvation, if God has such love for
each one of us, then how can we do any less than God does? How can we do
any less than love one another?
A part of Masonry for the Twenty-First Century therefore is
demonstrating to the world through our own actions that every person must
extend brotherly love to all peoples, not adversarial hatred. And, if our duty
is to demonstrate to the non-Mason that brotherly love and regard, how can we
teach it if we do not practice it within our own Lodge halls? How can we
demonstrate to California skin heads or Bosnian Serbs that we must love one
another, when Hispanics and blacks do not feel welcomed in every California
Lodge?
It is the most natural of human inclinations to seek our own kind. It
stems from the most basic of human instincts, the need to propagate the race
by mating with persons most like ourselves. We are conditioned through
family and friends for solidarity with our own kind. But what is our own
kind? People of just our own race and religion? Our Masonic ritual directs
otherwise. It is the whole human species who as created by one Almighty
Parent are to aid, support and protect each other.
What can we do to welcome diversity in our Masonic family, just as
Naomi and then Boaz welcomed diversity in their families? At Grand Lodge
this October, there will be several items of legislation on this issue. In my
recommendations, I will ask you to recognize the right of a Jew, a Moslem and
any other non-Christian to be obligated on the Holy Writings of his faith. In
California, we now require all candidates for the degrees of Masonry to be
obligated on the Christian Bible. The Christian Bible contains teachings which
Jews and Moslems do not accept. How welcomed do we make a Jew and a
Moslem to California Masonry when we do not permit him to be obligated on
the Holy Writings of his faith? My Recommendation No. 5 for Grand Lodge
this year asks you to give him that right, a right which many other
jurisdictions outside the United States have already granted to our Jewish,
Moslem and other non-Christian friends who have asked to become Masons.
Also at Grand Lodge this year, I will submit for your consideration a decision
and a recommendation with respect to our future dealings with Prince Hall and
other unrecognized Masons in California. These will be important first steps
as we continue to refine our relationship with Prince Hall and other Masons

whom we do not now recognize.
While we can collectively through Grand Lodge take steps to make
all men welcomed in Masonry regardless of skin color or religious belief,
Grand Lodge does not initiate, pass and raise good men and true. You do. A
Grand Master can inspire you, and you as delegates to Grand Lodge can
provide the legal foundation. However, only you can make the difference.
Only you can make men from Latin America, men from the Philippines,
blacks, Jews, Moslems, all men welcomed in Freemasonry. At work or in
community groups, I am confident that each one of you knows a man of good
moral character who may be Hispanic, black, Jewish or Moslem. Invite him
and his family to a Masonic lnfonnation Program. Encourage the other

intended each one of us to be. If he asks to join us, welcome him and his
family. Get him active in the work of your Lodge. Include him and his
family in social gatherings in your own home. In short, make him and his
family as welcomed a part of our Masonic family as you would any brother
Mason and his family.
Only when we welcome men regardless of ethnic or religious
background, in all aspects of Freemasonry, at all levels of Freemasonry, only
then will we be true to the practice of brotherly love. Only then will we be
truly prepared to lead Masonry as the force for change to rebuild our
fraternity, our society, our world to meet the challenges of the Twenty-First
Century.

Faith, Fear and Freemasonry
What do you do when you are afraid of something? Some people run
away, some people are frozen in inaction by their fears, some fight back.
These are uncertain times. The economy is not good, particularly in the
defense and real estate industries which are important to California. There are
many managers, white-collar workers, in the traditional vernacular, who are
without work and may be without work for some time to come. There is
uncertainty and therefore fear about our country's future.
With the demise of communism, the world has indeed been made safe
for democracy: Woodrow Wi lson's dream only took seventy-five years to
achieve. But, despite wealth, technology, freedom and peace, a majority of
Americans believe that our country is on the wrong course. More properly
put, they do not know what course our country is now on and therefore fear
where that unknown course may lead.
The theme for this Grand Lodge year is Masonry for the Twenty-First
Century. It is a personal search wh ich each one of us must undertake for the

accordance with them. If we do, our example will be an inspiration for others
to follow. We will attract to our cause others of like view who will take

What does Masonry say about the fear of the future? What answer
does Masonry provide to this fear of the future? Masonry has an answer. It
is symbolically represented when a man undertakes the unknown course when
he first enters a Lodge of Masons: he puts his trust in God.
We are taught as Masons that no important undertaking should begin
without asking God for assistance. Masonry is not a religion because it does
not promise salvation to its adherents. It is not concerned with the hereafter
but with the here and now. It is a system of ethics, the consideration of that
right conduct in which each person must engage. And, that right conduct is
all based on one premise and one premise alone: all right conduct ultimately
is in fulfillment of the commands of our creator. Fear of the future is
answered by God through faith which is the right conduct in these times of
uncertainty.
From the beginning, concerns about the unknown course of human life
have been answered through faith. In Genesis, we learn that Abram had no
legitimate children and an elderly, barren wife. He, like us, feared the future,
the course which he must have foreseen as an unhappy journey of loneliness
with no one to care for him and his wife Sarai or to carry their righteousness
to future generations. Then, God appeared and entered into a covenant with
him: if you remain faithful to me as your one God, I will bless you with
many descendants for whom I will faithfully provide. When confronted with
fear, Abram turned to God in faith. God changed Abram's name to Abraham
who became the spiritual forbearer of every Jew, Christian and Muslim.
In the Book of Job, we are told that no man's faith was as great as
that of Job. Yet, the devil went to God and challenged Job's faith. Take away
Job's family, wealth and health, the devil said. Deny him all creature
comforts, and Job would deny God. Job's response? His faith deepened.
We learn from scripture that faith is the assurance of things hoped for,
the conviction of things not seen. What do we hope for? We hope for the
blessings of God on this earth and also the ultimate blessing, to be reunited
with God in the life to come. If we put our trust in God and are faithful to
God's requirements, God will provide, perhaps not in the way that we might
plan, but as will be best for us.

journey.

Keeping Promises

the opinion that corruption and deception are vital if you want to get ahead.
What will be the future of our civilization if the members of it are of the
opinion that promises are to be kept only when convenient? Why will we
want to make promises in the future if we do not think others will keep their
promises to us? How can we be secure in our own rights if we do not trust
others to keep their promise to respect our rights as we do theirs?

Promises are fundamental to the maintenance of our way of life. In
civilized society, each of us implicitly promises to respect the rights of others
in exchange for their implied promise to respect ours. Without such promises
made and kept, we are no more than barbarians. Without such promises made
and kept, we would have no security in our person or property. How could
we take time to educate ourselves, contemplate our spirituality or improve our
physical welt-being if we were constantly fearful of what our neighbor might
do to us when we were not vigilant of our personal defense?
Another important promise is also at the foundation of human
existence: the promise which God has made to all human beings, first with
Abraham. If we are strictly faithful to God and demonstrate our faith by
keeping His law, then He will protect us. We know the result when we break
this promise. From time to time over the centuries, as frequently evidenced
in the Old Testament, humans have not been faithful to God and have broken
His law. And, we know of God's reaction when His people's promise with
Him is not kept: God punishes His people for their faithlessness and their
unrighteousness.
Important promises are made not just with God and with society at
large. We make them with one another. When we marry, we promise to be
faithful to our spouse, agreeing not to undertake a husband and wife
relationship with any other person. We promise to care and provide support
for that person for so long as that mutual promise is undertaken by both
parties. Masons make an important promise upon joining our fraternity. Each
of us promises to aid and assist alt who ever have been or ever will become
a Mason in return for that same promise from all who ever have or ever will
join our fraternity.
Whether formally undertaken as in marriage or implied from our
relationship with God, promises are essential to our relationship with God,
with society at large, with those in our families and with those in our close
circle of friends. Civilized society could not exist without promises made and
kept. Promises made and kept build our personal sense of security, they foster
confidence that our rights will be respected when we respect the rights of
others. Keeping promises is the foundation for expectations: promises kept
are the only reliable foundation for making and accepting further promises.
If a politician does not keep a promise, if a salesman does not keep a promise,
you should be less likely to vote again for that politician or buy again from
that salesman.

If promises are so important, why then does it seem in today's society
that promises are readily broken? A recent Roper poll for Shearson Lehman
Brothers found that thirty-eight percent of those under the age of thirty are of

10 1

There is a general feeling today that people cannot be trusted. Our
trust in others is shaken because too many of us do not keep our promises.
Our trust in others is shaken when those in public life, those with whom we
deal in business and those with whom we have personal relationships do not
do what they have promised us they will do. What of the prominent politician
who makes promises in order to get elected and then follows the lobbyist' s
lead and does something else? What of the salesman who makes a promise
to get a sale and then forgets you when the product needs servicing? What of
the man who promises fidelity to a woman to get married and then sees other
women?
There are of course circumstances under which promises need not be
kept. By mutual consent, a promise may be terminated. You may enter into
an agreement for the lease of an apartment. However, with the consent of the
landlord, that agreement may be terminated before the end of its term. There
are also circumstances under which the termination of a promise is justified
even though the other party has not consented. When there has been a
significant change in circumstances and with advance notice, the terminat ion
of a promise could be justified. But, these are the exceptions and broken
promises seem increasingly to be the rule.
Why are promises broken? It is sometimes hard to keep a promise,
and more often it is easier to break one. Regrettably, promises are often kept
only when the promiser fears that some penalty will be exacted if he does
otherwise. If laws are broken, the lawbreaker faces a fine or jail depending
upon the severity of the infraction. If a contract is broken, a court can award
damages. However, people have increasingly seen these penalties as illusory.
Criminal courts are clogged : plea bargaining effectively eliminates many fines
and jail time. C ivil courts are clogged: litigants can spend more money on
And these are the broken
attorneys than can be recovered in damages.
promises which are caught! What about those who are dishonest on their
taxes, those who assume that they will never be audited and caught? For
many, a broken promise is alright if you do not get caught, because then there
can be no penalty. If society provides no effective penalty for a broken
promise, what then is the deterrent? Why should we keep promises?
When we see people of prominence who do not keep their promises,
when we deal with people on a daily basis who do not keep their promises, it
is natural for us to feel foolish or even stupid when we attempt to keep ours.

What answers does Masonry provide to our concerns, answers to society's

Masonry' s answer? It is expressed in each one of our Masonic organizations

There is also another teaching, a teaching characteristic of all of our
Masonic organizations. Masonry teaches that there is a standard of ethical
conduct, a standard of right conduct, which each of us owes to our creator and
our fellow creatures. The ethical conduct, the right conduct, is our faith in
God. The ethical conduct, the right conduct, is the brotherly love and relief
or charity which we extend to our fellow creatures. The ethical conduct, the
right conduct, is our personal search for truth or self improvement, a search by
which we continually endeavor to improve our conduct toward God and our
fellow creatures. In all Masonic organizations, it is also something more. The
ethical conduct, the right conduct, is our fidelity to promises, the commitment
to keep promises when made.
And while this fidelity to promises is expressed during the ceremonies

do any less in the promises which we make outside a Masonic hall? The

elected, he or she should keep that promise. When a member of our Masonic
family makes a promise to a spouse to be faithful, he or she should keep that
promise.

If we do not keep the promises which we make everyday regardless

Each of the three, major western religions has taught that it provides

Likewise, Masonry has timeless truths which addressed the concerns
of the medieval stonemasons and address our concerns today. Our medieval
stonemason ancestors lived at the building site. They were together twentyfour hours a day. They worked together, they worshiped together, they rested

his death? There was no worker's compensation insurance or welfare. It was
a Mason's relief or charity which provided for those distressed worthy
brothers, their widows and orphans.
Most significantly, these early
stonem asons were often the uneducated sons of farmers. They had no formal
education. They had no training in the operative skills of a stonemason w~en
they apprenticed. Many were unfamiliar with the social skills needed to hve
in a closely confined building site. They could not become skilled craftsmen
or brothers to their fellow workers without self-improvement, a Mason's search
for truth.

These requisites for medieval stonemasons to live together in
harmony; brotherly love, relief and truth; found expression in the ideas of the
craft. I believe that these and other philosophical lessons regarding ethical
behavior, the right conduct wh ich each of us must demonstrate to our creator
and fellow creatures, were associated by the master workmen symbolically
with the tools and techniques of the stonemason's craft. As master workmen
taught the use of these tools and techniques to the apprentices and fellows of
the craft, I believe that they also taught the ethical standards associated with
them . Each of the working tools of the craft acquired a symbolic meaning,
among them: the square, morality; the level, equality; and the plumb, rectitude
of action. Each too l symbolized a standard of action which the user owed to
God or Man. Once an apprentice had learned the physical and symbolic use
of each of the tools in the stonemason's box, he would be skilled not only in
the building trade but in standards of conduct by which we measure a person's
brotherly regard for his creator and fellow creature.
That brotherly regard meant more than restraining an apprentice's
temptation to interfere with the rights of others. A young Mason was charged
to demonstrate that brotherly regard by helping those less fortunate than he,
by extending Masonic relief or charity for the disab led, widowed and
fatherless, symbolically represented by the twenty-four inch gauge or ru ler
which symbolized the Mason's obligation to spend at least a third of his time
in the service of God and his less fortunate, fellow creatures. Masonic truth
is more than the standard of ethical conduct which requires us to be truthful
in all that we do. lt has become also the search for truth , the undertaking of
self-improvement. Just as the apprentice improved himself in the skills of
chiseling a stone to remove its imperfections and prepare it for addition to the
structure being erected, so he learned to improve his conduct toward his God
and fellow creatures by chiseling away at his own personal imperfections: his
personal vices and superfluities which inhibited his proper relation with God
and Man. He thereby fitted himself as a living ston e for the superstructure
which is human society.
Those ancient stonemason lessons of ethical conduct; brotherly love,
relief and truth; are as important today as they were in the Thirteenth Century.
Why is there crime today? Why are there people suffering at the hands of
others today? The causes are not hard to find. Many people th ink only of
themselves. What can I get for me? Let my neighbor be damned! A Mason's
brotherly regard for his fellow creatures, our concern for their well-being, is
just as important for the preservation of harmony in society today as it was
necessary for the preservation of harmony at the medieval cathedral building
sites of Europe. Today people suffer. In every civilized society, there will be
those at the lowest spoke of life's wheel whom life has passed by. Our
brotherly regard must be more than an expression of our concern. It must be
manifested in action by the relief or charity which we extend to the less
fortunate. We must do more than say we care. We must demonstrate our care

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

by what we do, by alleviating in some small part the distresses of others.
Most importantly, the Masonic search for truth calls us more strongly today
than ever before. We have schools which warehouse children for twelve years
and then tum them loose unprepared to meet the challenges of society. We
have families which consider children as perhaps cute play things at first and
then burdens to be endured for the shortest time possible until they can be
pushed out into the world unprepared for its challenges. It should not be a
wonder that many today believe government or society as a whole owes them
something when they have not a clue as to how they can earn it for
themselves.

Why Are People Active in Masonry?

!06

Masonry aga in provides the answer. It is not what another can do for
you, but what you can do for yourself. It is the personal responsibility which
each one of us has to be better than we were before. Just as a medieval
stonemason chiseled away and made the rough boulder a perfectly smooth and
square stone to be laid during the erection of the building, so should we, each
one of us, chisel away at ourselves. Chisel away at our own personal
ignorance by reading and studying, perfecting the skills necessary for us to
earn our living, the skills necessary for us to be informed voters. C hisel away
at the imperfections of our spirits: those imperfections which prevent us often
from demonstrating brotherly regard and relief for the needs of others; those
imperfections which prevent us from acting in an ethical manner toward our
fellow creatures; those imperfections which prevent us from doing unto others
as we would wish that they would do unto us; those imperfections which
prevent us from loving God with the same fervency with which God loves
each one of us.
Our nation has been great because it provides individual freedom, free
public education and freedom of speech. Each of Judaism, Christianity and
Islam has been great because each teaches an answer for human salvation
through faith in God and love for our fellow creatures. Masonry has been
great because its ideas are brotherly love, relief and truth. But, the greatness
of each is more than its ideas. Their greatness rests also with the people
dedicated to their preservation and propagation. Our country is great because
its people have defended their freedoms, their right to free public education
and their right to be informed. The message of the great western religions
remains powerful today because each has believers who have and will live by
faith in God and love for their fellow creatures . Masonry has been and will
remain great because all members of our Masonic family have and will
practice brotherly love, relief and truth.
What makes an institution successful, century after century ? It is both
ideas and people. It is timeless truths and tireless people, our commitment to
practice the truths we teach. Those who have preceded us have passed to our
stewardship our nation, our faith, our Fraternity. Defend them all by your
lives led true to their dictates.

In the Senior Wardens' Retreats last year, I asked every man present
to consider the answer which he might give to the following question: "Why
aro I a Mason?" Why is it important that each of us should consider this
question and develop a concise answer to it? I can answer this question with
another. How can we interest others in joining us if we cannot concisely say
why we ourselves devote the time that we do to Masonic activities?
I suppose that many might be tempted to answer this question, why
am I a Mason, with the reasons why they originally joined Masonry. You
might say: my father was a Mason. A good friend was a Mason. I liked the
Masonic regalia and the public Masonic ceremonies. These may be the
reasons why you joined, but are they the reason why you are an active Mason
today?
The Reverend Randy Phillips, a former Grand Chaplain of the Grand
Lodge and a Methodist Minister, suggests that there is a hierarchy of reasons
why people are active in churches: ceremonial, social and mystical. He
suggests that people are first attracted to active church participation by the
ceremonial aspects of religious activities: the liturgy or church service, the
vestments worn and the music played. As a person 's religious needs mature,
so do the reasons why a person remains active in church . The needs fulfilled
go beyond the ceremonial: they become the social, the social interaction with
other members of the church. The most mature needs fulfilled, the needs of
those whose religious concerns have matured beyond the ceremonial and
social, are the mystical: one's personal exploration of his or her faith, his or
her relationship with God and fellow creatures . It is Randy's view that a
church will grow and prosper only if it satisfies the ceremonial, social and
mystical needs of its members. The church must excel in each to be
successful. Could not the same be said of Freemasonry?
I would suggest that a similar hierarchy of needs explains our Masonic
involvement. And, this thought provides a clue as to what each Lodge should
now do to strengthen itself for the future. If we are to keep people interested
in our craft, we must satisfy our members' ceremonial, social and mystical
needs, or better stated, their ceremonial, fraternal and philosophical needs. We
must excel in each of these areas to keep our members' interests alive. A
Lodge will grow and prosper only if it satisfies the ceremonial, fraternal and
philosophical needs of its members. The Lodge must excel in each to be
successful.
In Masonry, the ceremonial is our ritual. It is also our protocols, not
just how we introduce people, but the way in which we do all things when we
meet as Masons: how we structure our meetings, the specific courtesies and
titles which we extend to those who have excelled in their service to our craft,

108

our regalia and our facilities. If the newest member's needs are satisfied by
the ceremonial, how attractive is Freemasonry today?

Is your Lodge actively involved in its community? Does your Lodge
each month have a civic or a community event in which it participates? Does
it actively support local community charities with its donations of time and the
services of its members? The members of my Lodge staff the parking lot for
the most important charitable event in our community: an art exhibition for
the benefit of a local clinic offering medical care to the indigent. They wear
identification to inform even the casual observer that the staffing of the
parking lot is the project of the local Masonic Lodge. What does your Lodge
do for the community?

A candidate's first exposure to the ceremonial aspects of our craft
often occurs on the occasion of the conferral of his Entered Apprentice Degree.
How attractive is that first degree? Is each station filled by a brother who is
proficient in the work? Or, on the man's first admission into a Lodge of
Masons, is he greeted by ritual which he cannot hear or, if he can hear it,
ritual recited without expression, haltingly with much prompting? How will
the ceremonial aspects of our fraternity keep this new Mason's interest when
the ritual work is poor? When the man first beholds the interior of the Lodge
with his own eyes during the ceremony of his initiation, does he see a room
filled with Masons on his right and on his left? Or, are only the officers and
one or two sideliners present? Often times, the first thing which a new Mason
hears upon joining our fraternity is poor ritual and the first thing which he sees
is poor attendance. How impressive are the ceremonial aspects of our craft to
the new Mason when we show so little regard for it ourselves?
Our facilities are part of the ceremonial aspects of our fraternity. How
impressive is your Masonic hall? Is it a place where you would be pleased to
bring a guest? Or, is it in need of painting, new furniture, new glass for
broken windows? And what about the most commonly understood aspects of
our Masonic protocols? How well organized are your Lodge activities? Are
your Lodge's programs fast moving and entertaining? Or, are they dull, long
and repetitious?
What about the fraternal or the second level of needs of your
members? Unfortunately, too many Lodges perform only the ceremonial,
holding Stated Meetings and an occasional degree. Such a Lodge is nothing
more than a degree factory and at that, not surprisingly, a factory that does not
work very often because it has so few candidates for the degrees. What does
your Lodge do to satisfy the fraternal or social needs of your members? Does
your Lodge have a social event every month to which the members, their
wives, families and friends are invited? Do you have a dinner before your
Stated Meeting at which wives, families and friends are invited? Does your
Lodge take trips with wives, families and friends?
The fraternal needs of your members extend beyond what your
members do with one another. Their fraternal needs are also fulfilled by what
they do for others. Some accuse young people today of being part of the "me"
generation, concerned only with themselves. Out 1 would suggest to you that
there are many young people today who are concerned with more than just
themselves. There are young people today who are concerned about doing for
others. Look at the service clubs in your community or those churches which
have grown because they have an active program to involve their members,
particularly their younger members, in the community.

Ceremonial and fraternal , these are important, but one more plateau
must be reached. The ceremonial and fraternal needs must be complemented
by Lodge programs to satisfy the philosophical needs of your members: their
need to deepen their understanding of the philosophy of Masonry, the
philosophy which distinguishes Masonry from every other secular..group in
society today. That philosophy is the source of strength and res1!1ency by
which our fraternity has lasted more than seven hundred years and transformed
itself from a medieval guild, a forerunner of today's labor union, into the
world's largest fraternity, into a fraternity composed of people who obviously
no tonger join us to chisel stones for great Gothic cathedrals.
Masonry today is the world's oldest and largest fraternity because it
is unique. It is unique because it is the only organization where people of all
religious backgrounds, all people who believe in God and the immortality of
the soul, may join 39d consider those timeless truths of human existence, those
timeless truths which answer the concerns of people regardless of the
circumstance or century in which they live. It is the one place where people
of God, regardless of their religious views, may study not the means to the
hereafter, the study of salvation which is the exclusive preserve of religion, but
study the here and now. We are unique because of the philosophy of our craft,
the search for the standard of right or ethical conduct which each one of us
owes in the here and now to our God and fellow creatures.
What is that standard of ethical conduct? It is brotherly love and
relief, the regard which we show for our fellow creatures. It is also our search
for truth, the search not just for that which is true but the search to perfect
ourselves, to divest ourselves of those vices and superfluities which otherwise
cause our passions and our prejudices to control our conduct. It is selfimprovement by our study of the symbolic meanings of the working tools and
techniques of the medieval stonemasons' craft. The philosophical needs of our
members are identical to those of all other good people who strive to be better.
It is our constant effort to regulate our conduct by the ethical standards of all
good men and women, despite temptations to the contrary.
If the most important part of our fraternity, if the reason why our
fraternity has lasted for seven hundred years and transformed itself into what

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

it is today, is the philosophy of our craft, where do we teach it, other than in
a rote and often times boring recitation of our ritual? When else is the
timeless philosophy of our craft considered by the members of your Lodge?
Once a month, preferably at your Stated Meeting dinner, when wives, family
and friends are present, have someone talk about some aspect of why we are
Masons. Have someone talk about Masonry's teachings on ethics. What are
ethics? Ethics is the consideration of how we should act toward our creator
and fellow creatures. What does Masonry say about a business man who does
not honor his promise to service a product which he has sold? What does
Masonry say about drug and alcohol abuse? What does Masonry say about
people who physically abuse others?

Freemasonry Needs a Bogey-Man

110

The consideration of our Masonic philosophy should begin when a
man first petitions our Lodge. He and his family should meet with the officers
and their families. They should talk infonnally about what it means to be a
Mason . The discussion should not be just about the history of our craft but
about our unique philosophy, a philosophy that is unique, not because it is
exclusive to us, but unique because we are one of the few secular groups in
society which has preserved that philosophy for centuries. rt is a philosophy
dictating the ethical or right conduct of people for the last seven and for the
next seven centuries. Answer the petitioner's and his family's questions about
the craft. You may find another salutary result from such a session, a result
which I experience whenever I teach a class. The teacher in explaining the
lesson often gains new insights too and thereby often times learns more than
the student!
these three needs of our
Ceremonial, fraternal, philosophical:
members must be satisfied by you and your Lodge or your Lodge fails our
craft. Our fraternity will grow in the future not by what I do as your Grand
Master nor by what your Inspector does in your District. Freemasonry will
grow and prosper only if one man in every Lodge takes the initiative, only if
that one man demonstrates commitment and enthusiasm in leading the Lodge
to excellence in all its activities, only if that one man then so inspires one
more man and then another and then another and then another.
Freemasonry will succeed only if a nucleus of enthusiastic and

possible those ceremonial, fraternal and philosophical needs of their brothers.
Then, and only then, will Masonry surpass past glories. Then, and only then,
will we build Masonry for the Twenty-First Century.

When I was Junior Grand Warden, I was invited to San Diego to
resent the keynote address for the annual flag day program of the local
~asonic Officers Association. After the program, a brother approached me to
advise that he had the answer for all of Masonry's problems today. Naturally,
I was a bit skeptical. He also told me that the answer to Masonry's problems
was written on the inside o f this folded piece of index card which he then gave
to me. My skepticism deepened! I thanked him politely and put this c'.11'd in
my pocket without looking at it. When I returned home that evening, I
unfolded the card and found written these words: "Freemasonry Needs a
Bogey-Man". I chuckled, but the simplicity of the thought intrigued me. I
saved the card, and I have thought about this simple passage many times in the
years since.
Freemasonry needs a bogey-man. We need an opponent whose
challenge can mobilize Masons to rally around our craft. In the history of
modem Masonry, we have faced these challenges before and have recovered
from them, recovered stronger than ever. Consider the vitality of Masonry
over the centuries. Our historical beginnings can be traced to the construction
of the great European Gothic cathedrals in the late Thirteenth Century.
Operative Masonry thrived and expanded as every population center wit~ a
bishop sought to build a cathedral more impressive than the other. Operative
Masonry faced extinction in the Seventeenth Century when cathedral building
slowed. It was then.that men in increasing numbers were admitted to Masonry
to study or speculate on the moral and philosophical lessons associated with
the working tools and techniques of the operative stonemasons, and our
Fraternity expanded once again. Masonry responded to the challenge by
transforming itself into the speculative society which we know today.
Masonry expanded to this country, arriving with the Colonists.
However, in the 1820' s, many blamed the Masons for the disappearance of a
William Morgan who had published an alleged expose regarding the secrets
of Freemasonry. The public's reaction was so severe against Masonry that in
New York alone over a four year period the number of Lodges dropped from
five hundred to eighty-two and the number of members from over twenty
thousand to fewer than three thousand. Masonry again faced extinction but
responded to the challenge. After the Civil War, the growth of Freemasonry
in America was rapid and permanent w ith only a temporary set back during
the Great Depression and the hopefully temporary set back which commenced
about twenty years ago.
Jn Europe, Freemasonry was forced underground by the Fascists and
The Nazis and Communists
Communists in the Thirties and Forties.
systematically arrested all Masons simply because they were Masons. Yet, so
dedicated were these men to their craft that those who escaped arrest kept it

underground, faithfully preserving the seeds to replant and nourish after the
fall of Communism. Today, we see the rebirth of Freemasonry in Russia and
other countries formerly behind the Iron Curtain, thanks to the perseverance
of those Masons who preserved their craft in secret until more favorable times.
Masonry faced extinction but survived because its principles were so important
to the faithful underground that they risked arrest by their practice of its rituals
hidden from totalitarian view.
We face challengers to our craft in America today. These challengers
do not se~k us out for arrest as the European Fascists and Communists sought
to extennmate our European brethren, but their intent is the same. America's
Masonic c~allengers seek nothing less than the elimination of our fratemity.
We face this challenge from the Doctor Hollys, John Ankerbergs and similar
religious critics who attempt to discredit us by claiming that we offer a
substitute for religion. We know that to be false because nowhere in our
Masonic ritual do we promise salvation by a faithful practice of our teachings.
Masonry promotes ethical conduct in the here and now. It is only through the
practice of our religious beliefs that we find hope for salvation in the hereafter.
The real reason for challenge from the religious right is not its
fabricated argument that we replace religion. These religious critics seek also
to discredit the beliefs of Roman Catholics, Mainline Protestants, Mormons,
Seventh Day Adventists, Jews and anyone else who disagrees with them.
They are most vocal about Freemasons because we represent what our
religious critics hate the most: toleration for the views of others. Our
religious critics do not tolerate any views which differ from their own.
And, these religious reactionaries do not stand alone as challengers of
modem Masonry.
We face challengers that are more pernicious, more
threatening, because these challengers are harder to identify. The opponent,
the bogeyman, is not as visible as a Hitler, Stalin or a John Ankerberg. We
live in a society today with fundamental antipathy toward the ethical standards
for which Masonry stands. We live in a hedonistic society with people
concerned about me; damn my neighbor. Brotherly love for our fellow
creatures is ignored when white supremacist skin heads plot to destroy black
churches and when black and Hispanic gangs engage in drive-by shootings.
Relief, helping those less fortunate than we, seems a lost cause to those
yuppies more concerned about the material self aggrandizement of putting me
first. And Masonic truth, not only being truthful, but seeking that which is
true, the perfection denied us at birth, the perfection which we hope for in the
hereafter through God's grace and love for His faithful children who practice
His commandments, what role does truth play in society today, when
politicians shave principles for votes and business people shave principles for
profits? Who in America stands for truthfulness? When people are me
centered, convinced that happiness is a function of human achievement not
divine grace, what place is there for God or for faith in His mercy?

GRAND LODGE OPERATIONS

The next portion of my message will discuss the operations of the
Grand Lodge for the year.
Appointments
A Grand Master makes over five hundred appointments during his
tenure in office. In making these appointments, I have attempted to select the
best qualified people whom I could find. I have also attempted to give
consideration to as many different areas as possible.
I attempted to appoint Grand Lodge Officers so that each of the major
geographic areas within the state would be represented. Of the twenty-eight
Grand Lodge Officers installed on October 14, 1992, three were from Division
I, three from Division II , four from Division III, two from Division IV, eight
from Division V and seven from Division VI. This dispersion approximates
the dispersion of Masons among the Lodges of the then six Divisions. Of
these twenty-eight officers, two were born in the 19 IO's, eleven were born in
the 1920's, seven were born in the l 930's, four were born in the 1940's and

As a general rule, the California Masonic Code provides that a
member who has served for nine consecutive years as an Inspector or on a
specific committee is ineligible for reappointment until the lapse of one year,
although an exception is provided for an Inspector if the Grand Master
determines that such Inspector's reappointment is appropriate for the good of
the craft. I am pleased to report there was only one Inspector in office at the
end of my term for whom this exception was granted. He is Worshipful
Jacques C. Bourguignon, the Inspector of the 330th District to which is
assigned Vallee de France Lodge No. 329 only. No other qualified brother
was available in Southern California to supervise the ritual of this Lodge
which is authorized to confer the Entered Apprentice Degree in the French
tradition.

Expense Reimbursement Policy

Accordingly, the following organization was used for each of these
committees during the Grand Lodge year. The chairman of each of these
committees was asked to recommend a coordinator from his committee's
membership for each of the Inspectoral Divisions in California. These people
and the chairman then formed the Steering Committee for the committee. This
was the group responsible for planning the long range strategies for the
committee as well as refining new programs. These coordinators were also the
persons responsible for taking new programs to the entire committee and
supervising their implementation by each individual member.

The Grand Lodge provides a limited amount of reimbursement for the
out-of-pocket expenses of the Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors and Committee
members which are incurred while on Grand Lodge business. We should
preserve this program for as long as we can possibly afford it. Without it,
many men of talent will be denied the opportunity to share their talents with
the fraternity when they cannot afford to assume personally the out-of-pocket
expense involved.
The Grand Lodge has had an expense reimbursement policy which
was updated and issued last October. It was prepared by the Executive
Committee with many useful suggestions from the members of the Ritual
Committee. The policy describes the rules with respect to reimbursements for
travel, lodging, meals, telephone and postage expenses only. From time to
time, other expenses are contemplated by committee members and others
which are not described in the policy. These would include printing costs and
the purchase of supplies. These costs and expenses are not reimbursable by
the Grand Lodge unless the responsible person has first secured from the
Grand Secretary a purchase order. It is hoped that we can control our Grand
Lodge budget better if such costs and expenses can be reviewed before they
are incurred.
The other members of the elective Grand Lodge line and I appreciate
the continued efforts of the Grand Lodge Officers, Inspectors and Committee
members to minimize the expenses of the Grand Lodge. We recognize and
applaud the sacrifices that many of you make in Grand Lodge service for
which you request no reimbursement. It is only by your dedicated service that
we can hope to strengthen "Masonry for the Twenty-first Century."

Committee Operations
A number of changes were made in the operations of the Grand Lodge
Committees during the year.
Steering Committees
The Grand Lodge has seven large committees: the Masonic Homes
Endowment Board, the Masonic Widows Program Committee, the Public
Relations Committee, the Public Schools Committee, the Sojourners
Committee, the U . S. Constitution Observance Committee and the Youth
Orders Committee. Because these committees are so large, organization is
important. Large committees cannot be effective without an appropriate chain
of command and accountability of its members.

117

Because we are an organization of volunteers, more delegation is
important. However, large committees tend not to work as a planning group.
Tue chairman was asked to recommend his committee's best member in each
Division as the Coordinator to assist in planning as well as the implementation
of that committee's programs. State-wide meetings were discouraged. the
chairman was asked to meet periodically with the Steering Committee of
Division Coordinators, but meetings of the entire membership of the committee
were suggested on a Division rather than a larger area basis. There were
exceptions in certain cases, such as the Endowment Board for which a meeting
at each of the Homes is helpfu l for the members.
Each lnspectoral District in the state was assigned to one of the
committee members. The identification of the Divisional Coordinators and the
district assignments were included in the Grand Lodge Roster. The roster also
included for the fir?t time a telephone number for each committee member.
Support for Featured Monthly Programs
The Grand Lodge Committees responsible for the Masonic
Information program, the Widows program, our Masonic Youth Orders, Public
Schools, Homes Endowment, Sojourners and Constitution Observances were
asked to provide the Lodges with support for these programs. Four months
before the scheduled month of each activity, the committee chairman was
asked to write the 1993 Worshipful Masters reminding them of the need to
plan this program. In the letter, the chairman was asked to offer the
committee's members' assistance in planning and executing the program. The
cbainnan was also asked to suggest proven program ideas of which he may be
aware that are in addition to those in the enclosed material. The offer of
assistance was to include the offer of committee members as speakers at such
programs.

GRANO LODGE OF CALIFORN IA

A special project of the CMMT Board will be the Old Masonic
Temple in Los Angeles. This temple is situated in a state park in Los Angeles
which includes the original Plaz.a, the original Plaza church and Olvera Street.
The Lodge room is located on the second story o f one of the buildings in the
park. The downstairs housed a furniture store in 1858 but is now vacant and
controlled by the state.

therefore sent a letter to all the Lodges and Inspectors last October advising
them that consolidations generally will not be approved unless the Lodges have
met with a member of the Committee on Charters during the process of
negotiating the consolidation.

120

The Old Masonic Temple in Los Angeles, as the only Southern
California site other than the Fallbrook Cemetery, offers the Fraternity a
unique opportunity to preserve the history of Masonry's involvement in the
development of Southern California. Because it is located in an area that
many tourist visit, it should be preserved in a manner as will reflect well on
our fraternity. The second floor Lodge room area and the vacant first floor
area would be ideal for the establishment of a museum featuring Masonry's
role in the development of Southern California. In the early history of
Southern California, most of the English speaking settlers of prominence who
did not marry into the Spanish land grant families were Masons. Many of the
early leaders in the City of Los Angeles were Masons. No place is this history
preserved. CMMT is now considering this very project.
The preservation of our Masonic historic sites and buildings in
California is important. Because several are located in areas frequented by
many non-Masons, it is important that the sites and buildings be maintained
at the highest possible level and that they tell the story of Freemasonry's
involvement in that historic site in the most effective manner possible.
Charters
The assignments for the Charters Committee were greatly expanded
this year. The Committee's charge in our California Masonic Code is to assist
In recent years, the committee' s
Lodges in the process of formation.
responsibilities have diminished as fewer and fewer Masons seek to organize
new Lodges. Indeed, there have been some recent suggestions that we could
eliminate the committee entirely. At the same time, the number of Lodge
consolidations continues to increase with very little fonnal help offered the
Lodges as they consolidate. We have all seen consolidations that have been
very successful and those which have only perpetuated the problems of the
consolidating Lodges.
It was my view that our Grand Lodge could be of great service to
consolidating Lodges by sharing with them the successes of other
consolidations to prevent mistakes from being repeated. Therefore, the
members of the Charters Committee were asked to become actively involved
in advising Lodges desiring to consolidate. The committee served as the
liaison between the Grand Master and the consolidating Lodges. Most all
consolidations require the consent of the Grand Master to be completed. I

Once the Grand Secretary's office was notified of a contemplated
consolidation, the committee and the Inspector or Inspectors of the Lodges
involved were notified. The Chairman of the Charters Committee, Worshipful
Loyal Stark, then assigned a member of the committee to meet with the
Lodges and the Inspector. The committee member then helped the Lodge
through the checklist included in the consolidation manual, discussed
subsequently, and in completing the requi site forms.
The assigned committee member was also asked to offer constructive
suggestions when appropriate to resolve problems as they arise during the
consolidation process, as well as perhaps suggest some ways that others have
made consolidations more successful. For example, has the right local Lodge
been chosen for the consolidation? Are the members and their interests
compatible or would a different Lodge make a better consolidation partner?
What name, meeting night and meeting place will be used? Some of the more
successful consolidations in the past have abandoned all of the predecessors'
names and chosen a new nan1e and a meeting night on which none of the
consolidating Lodges met before. Some have even chosen to move to a
different building when none of the Lodges owned a building. By choosing
a new name differept from those of the consolidating Lodges, a new meeting
night and sometimes even a new meeting place, no Lodge feels like it is the
"junior" partner to the consolidation. The members of each consolidating
Lodge should feel that each has been treated equitably not only with respect
to the continuance of prior traditions but also with respect to officer and
If consolidations can be accomplished with a
committee appointments.
minimum of problems and with as many members as possible feeling that they
had been treated equitably, consolidations stand a better chance of success.
Charters was also asked to be more proactive with the Inspectors in
identifying weak Lodges that should consolidate. I anticipate that the Grand
Lodge will become more aggressive in the years to come in encouraging weak
Lodges to consolidate. Many of us have noted a decline in the quality of ritual
in areas with weak Lodges. If we are to preserve the strength of our ritual
system in California, we need stronger Lodges and, therefore, we must be
more aggressive in seeking consolidations.
During the consolidation process, Charters was encouraged to involve
the Grand Lodge Committee on Lodge Resources Development and the local
Inspector to assist the consolidating Lodges in re-building after the
consolidation. I have separately written the anticipated chainnan of that
committee asking him to involve his committee in these activities.

Code Revision
This is a new special committee of the Grand Lodge. With the
advance approval from the Grand Master and other members of the Executive
Committee with respect to areas selected, this new committee was asked to
study and recommend proposed revisions to the California Masonic Code to
improve the operations of the Grand Lodge and local Lodges. Three initial
areas of assignment were made.
First, the committee was asked to study the Trials and Restoration
portion of the California Masonic Code. The committee studied how to
improve the procedures and forms. The procedures and forms should be
understandable and usable by non-lawyers. The procedures and forms should
be designed to maintain appropriate due process for the accused. Resolutions
No. 93-4 and 93-5 were introduced as a result of this portion of the
committee ' s work .

123

The third area studied involved Temple Properties. The committee
was asked to consider adding the words "and Taxation" to the title of the
committee, as that responsibility was assumed in the Temple Properties charter
during Most Worshipful Ron Sherod's year. At present, the Temple Properties
Committee's approval is required for many activities of Masonic Temple
Associations but not sales of their properties. It would seem that the sale of
all or substantially all the assets of a Masonic Temple Association should be
subject to the approval of Temple Properties just as the purchase of assets is
subject to that approval. The committee was also asked to consider the $7,500
threshold after which activities of Temple Associations require approval of the
Committee. That threshold should be considered for increase. At present,
Temple Associations may only own real property used or contemplated to be
used in connection with a Masonic meeting place. Lodges may wish to invest
in other types of real property which only should be done through Masonic
Temple Associations. Perhaps it is appropriate to expand the types of real
property that may be owned by a Temple Association, subject of course to
Temple Properties ·prior approval. Resolutions No. 93-6 and 93-7 were
introduced as a result of this portion of the committee's work.
This committee worked with the Grand Lodge Committee on Trial
Review (on recommended legislation affecting the Trials and Restoration
portion of the Code), with the Grand Secretary (on recommended legislation
affecting his office) and the Grand Lodge Committee on Temple Properties (on
recommended legislation affecting Masonic Temple Associations).

lnsQectors' Orientation
The Inspectors' Orientation Committee conducted three Inspectors
Seminars in October and November of 1992. Each Seminar began at I 0:00
a.m . and was completed by 4:00 p.rn . Lunch was served. Attendance by each
Inspector in California at one of these Seminars was mandatory, just as it is
at the Divisional Inspectors conferences with respect to ritual.
Each Semiaar opened with appropriate introductory remarks from Paul
Hodiak, the Chairman of the Committee on Inspectors' Orientation, and from
me. Our Junior Grand Warden then discussed the role of the Inspector as the
representative of the Grand Master. After the morning break, our Senior
Grand Warden discussed proper planning for cornerstone laying ceremonies,
Lodge dedications, mortgage burning ceremonies and Grand Master visitations.
During the lunch program, our Deputy Grand Master discussed his
anticipated year as Grand Master. After lunch, our Deputy Grand Master
discussed Grand Lodge resources available to Inspectors who need help with
specific problems. He discussed how various Grand Lodge committees could
help with specific Lodge and Masonic Temple Association problems and how
these committees could help Lodges plan successful programs. Warren also
discussed how the Grand Secretary's office can assist the Inspectors in the
discharge of their duties. Warren discussed the kinds of problems which might
arise and what specifically each Grand Lodge resource can do to help. Of
course, one of the first places for an Inspector to seek help with a problem is
his mentor (for the newer Inspectors) and to the Assistant Grand Lecturer of
the Division (for all Inspectors).

You should have comprehensive public liability coverage to protect

by the Grand Lodge or any tenant which you may have in the building. Such

.
The insu_rance should also include coverage for the Masonic property
and its contents, m the event that they are destroyed by fire or other calamity.
The coverage should be for the replacement cost of the building and its
contents. It should be based upon the actual cost to replace your building and
its contents, not the price paid for them many years ago. Without replacement
cost coverage, if the Masonic hall is destroyed in a fire, you may find that you
get significantly less than you need to rebuild. If you would not rebuild on the
same site, be certain that the policy's replacement cost coverage permits
rebuilding on an alternate site. The policy should also include coverage to
bring a damaged building into compliance with more stringent building code
requirements enacted since the building was completed. The Board of
Directors of the Temple Association should obtain a periodic appraisal of the
Masonic building and contents to verify that adequate coverage has been
secured.
The Temple Association must also have workers compensation
coverage for its employees. It should have fidelity coverage for those Temple
Association personnel who handle large amounts of money. Its officers and
directors should also consider directors and officers insurance to protect from
personal liability the members of the Board of Directors of the Temple
Association.
The Temple Association should not just rely on its own coverage if
1t 1s renting its facilities to third parties, whether the tenant is there every
month (such as an Eastern Star Chapter) or it is only a one time rental (such
as for a wedding reception). Such Temple Associations should always obtain
certificates of insurance from tenants who rent Masonic facilities. For outside
rentals to private parties, a certificate of insurance with respect to the renter's
personal homeowners policy should be adequate. Temple Associations should
also obtain certificates of insurance from independent contractors who perform
work on Masonic properties. Certificates of insurance should include workers
compensation coverage, owned and non-owned automobile liability coverage
and comprehensive general liability coverage.

Jurisprudence
There has been confusion in recent years as to the proper role of the
Jurisprudence Committee. I believe that it would be helpful to reduce to
writing what that role should be, so as to minimize confusion in the future.
Three roles are possible: judge, advocate or counselor. When a
question as to the interpretation of a law arises, a judg~ chooses an answer.
The advocate argues for the selection of the answer which he wants chosen.
The counselor advises his client of the legal effect of the alternative results of
choosing between the competing answers. As reasonable men _often differ as
to the interpretatiol'} of law, it is rare when there are not competing answers to
questions of interpretation.
I find no provision of the California Masonic Code which authorizes
the Jurisprudence Committee to serve as the judge of disputes arising ~s to
interpretations of law. While an advocate's role is possible, it is in~ppropnate.
It compromises the independence and credibility of the Committee. The
Committee's advice on an issue would be suspect if the Committee were
known to be advocating a position on that or any other issue. If the
Committee were to take the view that only one interpretation of the law can
be correct, it has thereby given the appearance that it is advocating a position.
Such should be avoided.
When advising the Grand Master or others at his request between
Annual or Special Communications, or when advising the. craft during sue~ a
Communication, the Committee should carefully explain each altema~1ve
interpretation available, the legal support for selectin~ each and the po~s1ble
legal ramifications from selecting each. The Committee may ~ppropnately
give its views as to the relative strengths o~ the legal arguments i_n support of
each alternative.
However, its presentation must be made m the most
circumspect manner possible, so as to avoid the slightest appearance t~at only
one view can or should be selected. This care should be taken particularly

134

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

when dealing with those who are not experienc ed in dealing with lawyers.
Many who are not experienc ed in dealing with lawyers at times find it difficult
to distinguis h between a lawyer's explanati on of several, competin g
alternativ es and a lawyer's advocacy of the one alternativ e among several
which the lawyer wants the listener to adopt.
When differenc es as to the interpreta tion of law arise, the Grand
Lodge resolves these difference s when in session. Between sessions, the
Grand Master resolves them, although his decisions may be reversed by the
craft at an Annual or Special Commun ication and do not bind his successor
unless incorpora ted into our law at that time.
This discussio n has been reviewed by the current members of the
Jurisprud ence Committe e who have expressed their concurren ce in it.

Today, a ~idow 's needs may not be financial. Her husband through

but emotional. She may need your love. She may need your companionship.

Jn my own Lodge, we involve wives and families in al~ost al~ of ~ur

continues to attend just as she did before. Some of my Lodge's best
supporters are these widows who continue to give of their time and talent for
the betterment of Freemasonry.
Masonry' s strength is not its money in the bank, not its buildi~gs , not

truths taught by it which respond to people's needs regai:dless of the century

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

past, when Policy recommended a "no" vote on an item of legislation, its
report would discuss why the proposed action was not consistent with the
general purposes and policies of the Grand Lodge. When Policy recommended
a "yes" vote on an item of legislation, its report would discuss why the
proposed action was consistent with our general purposes and policies or why
those policies should now be changed to accommodate the proposed action.

Its leaders share many of the same concerns which trouble us. They have a
declining membership. They have difficulty in attracting men for leadership
roles, particularly younger men, although I was impressed with the number of
younger men who are Prince Hall Grand Lodge Officers and Lodge Masters

140

To expand the information available to the delegates who ultimately
must decide both the outcome of proposed legislation and changes to the
general purposes and policies of the Grand Lodge, Policy will not recommend
either a "yes" or a "no" vote when the proposed action is inconsistent with our
general purposes and policies. It will report why a "no" vote is consistent with
our general purposes and policies. It will also report how and why those
purposes and policies might be changed to support a "yes" vote on the matter.
Based on the relative merit of the arguments both for and against, you must
decide whether to follow or change our purposes and policies by your vote on
the matter.
