Public Relations

In response to requests from our committee, I have made a
recommendation and a decision, reported on elsewhere in this message, on
matters of interest in the Prince Hall study. Can a Grand Lodge recognize a
Prince Hall Grand Lodge within its jurisdiction without violating the American
Doctrine of exclusive territorial jurisdiction? In my view, it can, and my
Recommendation No. I would clarify our law on this issue. Our law also does
not provide sufficient guidelines on what recognition means nor the activities
which we may undertake with members of Masonic jurisdictions which we do
not now recogn ize. My Decision No. 6 provides guidance on this issue also.

successful in recruiting new members because of this program .

These new duties required a committee that is more geographically
disbursed through the state than we previously had so that they are closer to
local media. Before last October, thirteen of the committee's fifteen members
lived in Southern California. Of those, nine of the fifteen lived in Division VI.
The "rule of fifteen" described earlier was used in making new appointments
to this committee. A dynamic, new chainnan was appointed also, Worshipful
Ray Rosenbaum, who has done a fine job this year.
Public Schools
This committee had many challenges this year, and it was ably guided
in meeting those challenges by its new chainnan, Worshipful Darel Reynolds.
The Public Schools Month program for 1993 is discussed elsewhere in this
message. Also, Proposition 174, the school voucher initiative, was addressed
by the Grand Lodge. O ur Grand Lodge position on the subject is explained
earlier in this message under the heading: "Education at the Crossroads".
Excerpts from this portion of my message were published in the Autumn 1993
edition of the California Freemason.
Some complaints were received regarding Grand Lodge's position on
school vouchers . Some brothers felt that this proposition was a political matter
which should not be discussed in Lodge nor in an official Grand Lodge
publication. However, Section 15060 of our California Masonic Code clearly
authorizes discussion in Lodge of statewide public school welfare and
solicitation of support for any statewide purpose concerning the protection or
improvement of the public schools system. While the discussion of politics
is prohibited in our Lodges, public education, being the cornerstone of our
freedoms, is not a matter of politics; it is a matter of our survival as a
democracy.
Recognition of Foreign Grand Lodges
At the suggestion of Most Worshipful William H. Price, the chairman
of this committee last year, the responsibilities of this committee were
transferred to the Grand Secretary, and this special committee was disbanded.

Special Insurance Study
I appointed this special committee to undertake a comprehensive study
of our Grand Lodge insurance program. This included the insu rance of the
Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes, the Memorial Temple and the local Lodges.
Do we have the best coverage available? Do we get the least expensive
premiums available for the coverage received? Do we have the proper
structure in place to monitor properly the adequacy of insurance coverage and
premiums in the future? What type of procedures should be implemented on
an ongoing basis to assure best coverage at the lowest premium? The report
of this special study may be found elsewhere in these proceedings.

before they become serious problems.

Index to the 1991 Code
With almost two years experience in using the 1991 Code, a more
complete index was suggested. Such has been prepared by Most Worshipful
Stanley L. Channon and sent by the Grand Secretary's office with the current
year's changes to the 1991 Code. Brother Channon' s work is very much
appreciated.
Placement of Nonbinding Decisions in the Code
Over the years, there has been some confusion as to the distinction
between a Grand Master's decisions and his recommendations. A Grand
Master may only interpret law. He may not make law. Therefore, when a
Grand Master reports his decisions for review by Grand Lodge, the vote to
sustain them should never be more than a simple majority. A five-sixths vote
is required only when there is a change to the Grand Lodge Constitution and
Ordinances, which a Grand Master cannot do by his decision.
If the Constitution and Ordinances should be changed to reflect the
"decision" (for example, a Grand Master wants to mandate that his successor
always follow what was for him a discretionary act), then such a "decision" is
more like a recommendation. On such a matter, the required vote to approve
the Grand Master 's request will be governed by the vote required for such a
change.
Confusion has arisen in the past because Grand Masters have at times
styled an item of legislation as a decision because the matter originally arose
as an interpretation of the law. When Grand Masters have asked you to bind
future Grand Masters with respect to any such interpretation, such was done
by an amendment to the Code which required a five-sixths vote. It was really
a recommendation, thus causing the confusion.
I would suggest the following procedure to minimize such confusion
in the future. When the Grand Master does not intend to bind his successors
with an interpretation of the law which he has made, it should be styled a
decision and a simple majority vote only is required to sustain the Grand
Master's actions. When the Grand Master does intend to bind his successors
with an interpretation of the law which he has made, it should be styled a
recommendation and the law should be amended which would require a fivesixths vote.
If a Grand Master does not intend to bind his successor by a decision
which is approved by a simple majority vote only, that decision should not be
recorded in that portion of the California Masonic Code containing the Grand
Lodge Constitution and Ordinances. Only matters approved by a five-sixths
vote and carryover matters approved by a two-thirds vote should be recorded

GRAND LODGE OF CA LIFORNIA

15 l

in the Constitution and Ordinances. An interpretative but nonbinding Grand
Master' s decision should be listed in an appendix to the Code for reference as
a permissible interpretation of the law only.

Inclusion of 1991 Carryover Resolutions in the Code
Last October I was asked what changes were required to the 1991
edition of the Califo~ia Masonic Code because of the adoption of carryover
resolutions at the 1992 Annual Communication.
At the 1991 Annual Communication, Resolutions No. 91- 1I, 91-22,
91-33 91-39 91-40 and 91-41 were presented for consideration. These

resol~tions when mailed to all Lodge Masters and Secretaries _in J~ly of 19~1
contained proposed changes to the red 1975 edition of the Cahfom1a Masom.c
Code. These resolutions were approved by more than a fifty percent vote m
1991 and were carried over until 1992. In July of 1992, these carryover
resolutions were again mailed by the Grand Secretary to all Lodge Masters and
Secretaries. At the 1992 Annual Communication, they were adopted by the
requisite two-thirds vote.
For the 1992 Annual Communication, the members of last ye~'s
Jurisprudence Committee proposed its own set of resolutions _on the su~Ject
tt
f the 199 I carryover resolutions. These new resolutions contained
ma er o
t'f; . M
. Code
proposed changes to the blue 1991 edition of the ~a 1 om1a asomc . .
It was the view of last year's Jurisprudence Committee that new resolut'.ons
should be introduced on the subject matter of the 1991 carryove.r resolutions
because the carryover legislation made changes to 1975 Code which would be
repealed as of the close of the 1992 Annual Communication. However, the
Jurisprudence resolutions were not properly submitted to th~ Grand Secretary
180 days prior to the 1992 Annual Communication as required by the Code.
They therefore were not legally before the Grand Lodge in 1992 and were not
adopted.
This result raised another question: How should the adoption _of these
carryover resolutions be reflected in the blue 1991 California Maso~1c Code
when they contain changes to the repealed 1975 Californ ia Masonic Code?
Our law provides no guidance, yet Grand Lodge's de~ision to adopt these
resolutions must be respected. Accordingly, the following steps were taken.
The Grand Secretary and I located those sections of the blue Code
corresponding to the provisions of the red Code whic~. were amended by the
1992 carryover resolutions. The corresponding prov1s1ons of the ~lue _Code
were changed to incorporate the exact language proposed for adoption ·~ the
1991 carryover legislation. These changes to the blue Code are shown m an
appendix to this message. The supplements to the blue Code sent to the
Lodges earlier this year reflect these changes.

I have also reviewed the text of the Jurispruden ce Committee 's 1991
report on Ron's Recommen dation No. 2 as well as Jurisprudence's suggested
changes to the Code to implement this recommend ation. It is clear from the
Jurispruden ce report that other Masonic organizatio ns would be limited under
the same rules applicable to Masonic Lodges with respect to advertising. I
have also read the report of the Policy and General Purposes Committee in the
1991 proceeding s. It is clear to me from reading both the Jurispruden ce and
the Policy reports that these two committees were working with a draft of a
recommend ation which would continue the advertising restrictions of the Code
for other Masonic organizatio ns.
The question therefore was:
what version of Ron Sherod's
Recommen dation No. 2 was carried over to and adopted at the 1992 Annual
Communic ation? Was it a version which did not extend the craft Lodge
restrictions on advertising to other Masonic organizatio ns or was it the
Jurispruden ce version which did extend those restrictions to other Masonic
organizatio ns?
In arriving at an answer to this question, l have analyzed the
following. The Grand Lodge' s present method of proposing and adopting
legislation dates from the adoption of Resolution No. 7 at the 198 1 Annual
Communic ation. Resolution No. 7 was presented by the Special Commission
to Study the Organizati onal Structure of the Grand Lodge. In its report, the
Commissio n recommend ed that "the exact proposal to be voted upon at the
Annual Communic ation, subject of course to emergent amendments made by
the Grand Lodge itself," be sent to the membershi p by the Grand Secretary at
least sixty days before the Annual Communic ation.
The adoption of Resolution No. 7 established the current Grand Lodge
rule with respect to legislation which modifies our California Masonic Code:
the exact proposal upon which the membership will vote must be sent to all
California Lodges at least sixty days before the Annual Communication. There
are only two exceptions to this rule. The exact proposal upon which the
membershi p will vote need not be sent to all California Lodges before the
Annual Communic ation if five-sixths of those present and voting at Grand
Lodge agree to suspend the rules and consider the proposal as an emergent
measure. Also, the exact proposal upon which the membership will vote need
not be sent to all California Lodges if it is included in the Grand Master's
written message. (At the 1980 Annual Communic ation, the Grand Lodge
voted to make all Grand Master's recommend ations and decisions emergent
automatically when included in his written message.)
Thus, a Grand Master's recommend ations are treated differently from
any other Code changes proposed to Grand Lodge. The Grand Master's
recommend ations, as well as those decisions which he reports in his written
message, need not be submitted to the Grand Secretary 180 days prior to the

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Annual Communic ation and need not be mailed to the Lodges before the
Annual Communic ation. See Sections 160, 500 and 4000 of the Code.

or committee may propose, unless such has been (1) included in the Grand
Master's written message, (2) properly submitted more than 180 days before
the Communic ation and mailed as required to the Lodges by the Grand
Secretary or (3) presented as an emergent resolution. For the Code changes
drafted by the Jurispruden ce Committee pursuant to Section 1204 to be the
binding modificatio ns to the Code, they must be contained in the Grand
Master's recommend ation in his written message. Otherwise, they are

154

Our law is clear as to what constitutes the Grand Master's
recommend ation. Pursuant to Section 1052 of the Code, a Grand Master' s
recommend ation is the matter contained in the Grand Master's written
me~sage. Only the recommend ation in the written message is afforded a
waiver from the nonnal deadline for submission of changes to the Constitutio n
and Ordinances and from the requiremen t that the exact language of such
proposed changes be sent to the Lodges before the Annual Communic ation.
When the members of Grand Lodge vote on a Grand Master's
recommend ation, therefore, they are voting on what is contained in his written
If it is not in the written message, it is not part of the
message.
recommend ation.
The recommend ation on which the membershi p votes is not what the
Grand Master may have mailed to the jurisdiction before he delivers his
written message, unless that prior mailing has been included in the written
message. The recommend ation on which the membershi p votes is not what a
co1:'1mittee might present at the Annual Communic ation with respect to that
written message, unless that committee 's thoughts are contained in the written
message. The written message is the recommend ation and nothing else is.
Grand Master Sherod's written message did not include the required
Code changes to implement his Recommendation No. 2. Where then do we
look to find the language to codify his proposal? On those occasions in the
past when the Grand Master's message did not give the specific modificatio ns
to the Code required to implement his intent, the required language to codify
a Grand Master' s recommend ations and decisions in the Code was written after
Grand Lodge. For example, see Grand Master Smith's Recommendation No.
I, a~ . codified in Section 192a of the 1956 Code, Grand Master Crigler's
Dec1s1on No. I, as codified in Section 3 I 9f of the 1956 Code Grand Master
Crigler's Decision No. 2, as codified in Section 405k of the J956 Code and
Grand Master Roberts' Recommen dation No. I, as codified in Section 2'J I 8c
of the 1975 Code.
. In .m?re recent years, a custom developed for the Jurispruden ce
Committee m Its report on the Grand Master' s decisions and recommend ations
to recommend implement ing language. (This custom is authorized in Section
1204 :'hich was added to the 1975 Code to pennit the Jurispruden ce
Committee to prepare the changes to the Code required to accomplish the
Gran.d Mast~r' s recommend ations.) This suggested implementi ng language
pro~1des guidance to the membershi p as to what language will be used to
codify the Gr~nd Master's decisions and recommendations, if approved.
However, Section I 052 of the Code is clear. It is the written message that is
the matter before the Grand Lodge and not something that some other group

guidelines only.
In my view, Grand Master Sherod's written message proposing
Recommen dation No. 2 intends a different regime or regulation for Masonic
organizatio ns than for craft Lodges. Through some failure of communica tion
or mistake, the language suggested for implementation by Jurisprudence
Section 1204 of the Code authorizes the
provides a different result.
Jurispruden ce Committee to prepare the changes to the Code required to
accomplish the Grand Master' s recommendation, which in this instance it did
not do. Therefore, its language cannot be used.
One member of the Jurisprudence Committee has suggested that we
should consider the suggested language in the Jurisprudence Committee 's
report as binding because we have considered Jurispruden ce's suggested

Such, however, is not the case.
language binding in the past.
Jurispruden ce Committee itself has considered the proposed implementi ng
language in its report as only a guideline for the Code changes to be drafted
after Grand Lodge.. For example, in its report on Grand Master Sherod's
Recommen dation No. 3, the report of the Jurispruden ce Committee suggested
implement ing changes to Sections 1108 and 1218 of the Code. However,
when Jurispruden ce produced the 1991 Pocket Supplemen t to the 1975 Code,
changes were made to Section 1218 only! And, even if we had considered
Jurisprudence's suggested language binding in the past, a tradition is not law
in this jurisdiction . While in some legal systems, over time, a tradition can
have the force of law, such is not the case in the Grand Lodge of California.
As decided by Grand Master McCaw in his Decision No. 5, if it is not in the
California Masonic Code, it is not the law .
It is troublesom e that this altered result was presented in the
Jurispruden ce report in a fashion such that the average listener would not
recognize that a fundamental change had been made from what the Grand
Master had written in his message and orally deli vered j ust hours before the
Jurispruden ce Committee made its report. At the very least. the Jurisprudence
Committee should have clearly stated that the suggested implementing
language was a change from what the Grand Master had just rep~rted, . that
such change had been authorized by the Grand Master and that his written
message would be thereafter modified to confonn to the change indicated by
the Jurispruden ce Committee 's language. It is also troublesome that a member
of last year's Jurispruden ce Committee acknowled ges hearing this di screpancy

156

Based upon the foregoing analysis, the enabling legislation suggested
by the Jurisprudence Committee cannot be used to implement
Recommendation No. 2. The suggested implementing language is inconsistent
with the fundamentals of the Grand Master' s recommendation in his written
message, the matter on which the membership voted.
Because the
Jurisprudence language was not delivered to the Grand Secretary 180 days
before the 1991 Annual Communication and was not sent to the jurisdiction
in accordance with Sections 160, 500 and 4000 of the Code, that language
does not qualify as a resolution properly before the membership in 1991.
There was no emergent resolution adopted by a five-sixths vote authorizing
this alternative proposal on advertising as contained in the Jurisprudence
Committee' s report. r can find no legal basis for the language in the
Jurisprudence Committee's report being effectively before the Grand Lodge for
its consideration. It therefore had no force and effect. It is only one
committee's suggestion as to the language to place in the Code to implement
Recommendation No. 2. However, because it ignores a fundamental provision
of Recommendation No. 2, it cannot be used as a guide for drafting the Code
changes required to implement the recommendation.
What language should then be used as the carryover language from
1991? I believe that we must return to the procedures used in the past when
no suggested language was presented to the delegates at the Annual
Communication. The language must be written after the Communication.
Fortunately, such language has already been written. Grand Master Sherod
mailed to all California Lodges in July of 1991 language to implement his
Resolution No. 2. That language is consistent with and sufficient to implement
his Recommendation No. 2 as contained in his written message to the Grand
Lodge.
Fortunately also, that very same language was given by the
Jurisprudence Committee to the Grand Secretary to mail in July of 1992 as the
language which had been approved at the 1991 Annual Communication!
In Grand Master Sherod's Recommendation No. 2, as reported in his
July 1991 mailing, he asked Grand Lodge to amend the first paragraph of
Section 2072 of the red 1975 edition of the Code. The first paragraph of
Section 2072 of the red Code became Section 15110 in the blue 1991 Code.
Therefore, in accordance with the adoption of Ron's Recommendation No. 2,
the Grand Secretary amended Section 151 I 0 in the blue Code supplements sent
to the Lodges earlier this year to read as proposed in Ron's July 1991 mailing.
Section 15110 as so amended now reads as follows:

To minimize the risk that such a disagreement will arise in the future,
several changes have been implemented this year. First, as set forth. in _the
Rules of Order for Proceedings at the 1993 Grand Lodge Commumcat1on
published elsewhere in these proceedings, no legislation may be modifie~ at
any time without the consent of the proponent or ~i~ authorized representativ,e
written on the face of the modified proposal. This includes a Grand Master s
recommendation. Second, if any proposal is modified after it has been made
available to the delegates, any changes must be clearly brought to the attenti~n
of the delegates at the Grand Lodge session. Third, my written message will
include the exact changes to the Code necessary to implement my
recommendations and decisions.

Presentation of 50-Year Golden Veteran Awards

Jn addition to the procedures set forth in Section 510 of the Code, the
following procedures were observed by the committee. Each member of the
committee was asked to submit to me the name of one or more members of
the Grand Lodge whom th e member wished considered for selection as the
recommendee. Pursuant to Section 510, we could only consider members of
Masonic Lodges assigned to Masonic Districts in one of what was then
Divisions V or VI. If a brother's name was submitted by three or more
members of the committee, he was considered by the committee during its
January 30th deliberations.

It is a great privilege for a member of Grand Lodge to present a 50Year Golden Veteran Award to a deserving Brother Master Mason. This
recognition of ~ h~lf-century of service to Freemasonry is highly valued by
those who receive 1t, and the opportunity to present it is an honor.

Until now, the presentation of these pins has been the prerogative of
the Inspector of each Masonic District. They have done an admirable job, and
I could not be more pleased with their service as a representative of the Grand
Lodge of California in these presentations. However, our Grand Lodge must
present almost seven thousand Golden Veteran Awards through the end of
1994, and there will be more in 1995 and later years! The number of
members who will achieve this half-century mark in our Fraternity will make
~ur current system of presentation unworkable. Our Inspectors do not have the
t1m~ to m~age these additional pin presentations without sacrificing some of
their other important responsibilities.
l therefore concluded that it would be appropriate for each Master to
present the Golden Veteran Awards to those eligible in his Lodge. The new
system became effective on July I, 1993. The Grand Secretary's office
pro.v!ded. instructions how this process will work. The Grand Secretary's
ma1lmg rncluded a copy of the ceremony used for the presentation. There are
three participants in the ceremony: the Master, the Chaplain and the Marshal.
The ceremony is most effective when memorized. However, if the Master
would be more comfortable reading it, then he should have read it a sufficient
number of times before the presentation to enable him to read it well. As with
any of our ceremonies, the Master, the Chaplain and the Marshal should
practice the presentation before the ceremony is actually held.

Selection of Recommendee for Election as Junior Grand Warden
P.ursuant to Section 510 of the California Masonic Code, a meeting of
the committee to recommend to Grand Lodge a member for election as Junior
Grand Warden was held on Saturday, January 30, 1993 at I 0:00 a.m. at the
Ontario Airport Hilton. In addition to the Grand Master and Past Grand
Master.s who are members of this committee by reason of position, I appointed
Worshipful John F. Lowe, the Inspector of the 5 I 2th Masonic District and a
Past Master of Oxnard Lodge No. 341, Brother Auri Spigelman, the Senior
~arden of Composite Lodge No. 595 in West Los Angeles, and Worshipful
Dixon J. Webb, Jr., the Inspector of the 633rd Masonic District and a Past
Master of Seafaring Lodge No. 708 in Newport Beach. The other members
of the ~xecutiv~ Committee were invited to attend the meeting as observers
only, with the r~ght to participate in the discussions but without the right to
vote or to submit names for consideration.

After the initial discussions were completed with respect to those
brothers whose names were submitted by three or more members of the
committee, a ballot was taken on all of those men who have been discussed
during the meeting. A 5/6th majority vote of those present and eligible to vote
was necessary to select the recommendee. We had further ballots and
discussion until such a 5/6th vote was reached. A recommendee and two
alternates were thus selected.
At the meeting, Worshipful Allen B. Gresham, a Past Master of San
Bernardino Lodge No. 348, was selected as the recommendee. Allen accepted
the recommendation, and his name was communicated to the District
Inspectors on February 4th. As required by our Code, each Inspector was
asked to communicate this information promptly and as often as is necessary
to the Masters and Wardens of the Lodges in each' s District and through them
to other members qf the Grand Lodge.

surplus during the Grand Lodge year beginning on November l, 1993.
Together, these two years' surplus will replenish the Grand Lodge reserves to
approximately the same level that they were in 1983.
These surpluses do not mean that the future is without worries. Your
Grand Lodge leadership has promised to limit future increases in the per capita
assessment to the cost of living adjustment. To limit the per capita increase
to the cost of living adjustment, expenditures must be reduced annually by the
per capita revenue loss from the membership decline. For example, if
membership declines by 5,000 a year with a $14.00 per capita assessment,
Grand Lodge expenditures must be reduced by $70,000 annually. Otherwise,
the current annual surplus will disappear after 1997, and the per capita will
thereafter increase by more than the change in the cost of living.

If our membership continues to decline at the present rate, then each
incoming Grand Master must reduce Grand Lodge expenditures from the prior
year. This will require annual reductions of $70,000 to $100,000, depending
upon the number of members lost and the rate of inflation. Where can future
reductions be made? Here are some suggestions:
A.

Travel and Meeting Expenditures. Grand Lodge reimburses expenses
for those on Grand Lodge business. This includes mileage, airfare,
meals and lodging. While Inspectors and Committeemen participate,
approximately forty percent of these expenditures are incurred by the
Grand Lodge Officers. In the current year, Grand Lodge reimbursed
travel and meeting expenses totaled $375,100 or $3 .00 per assessable
member. (This total includes both expenses during the Grand Lodge
year and expenses for attending the Annual Communication.) Grand
Lodge is the only Masonic group in California with an expense
reimbursement program of this magnitude. Not all of these expenses
can be eliminated without an amendment to the California Masonic
Code because the Code permits the Inspectors to request
reimbursement of their expenses for attending the Annual
Communication.
Grand Lodge also gives a mileage allowance to one representative
from each Lodge for attending the Annual Communication.
Elimination of this expenditure would require a change to our
California Masonic Code but would have saved $24, I 00 this year.

B.

California Freemason. The magazine will cost more than $140,000
this year to publish. This expense could be reduced in several ways.
The magazine could be published less frequently. The number of
pages could be reduced. We could publish a newspaper instead of a
magazine. We could accept advertising.

We have other important programs under way. We are striving for
increased professionalism in the Grand Secretary's office. Our Grand
Secretary and his staff seek more timely delivery. Examples: Roster,
proceedings and current information of importance to Lodge Secretaries,
Masters and Inspectors.
Our Grand Secretary and his staff seek better quality. They have
implemented the P.R.I.D.E. program : personal responsibility in developin g
excellence! Each staff member is committed to producing the best work
possible, a work product that will be of assistance not a hindrance to the
Lodges.
We are asking the question: ls all we do in the Grand Secretary's
office really necessary? A new Code Revision Committee was appointed
during the year as outlined before to study the Grand Secretary ' s office and
consider streamlining the paper work which our law requires, such as with
dispensat ions. If we eliminate the needless paperwork, we can devote the
same resources to helping the Lodges do a better job, really the only reason
for the existence of the Grand Lodge in the first place!
Grand Lodge and the related Grand Lodge entities have hired a Chief
Financial Officer. He is Douglas A. Scott. We are a multi-million dollar
operation . We need the best qualified people to manage the accountin g and
long term financial planning of our organiz.ation.
Another important area receiving attention this year is fiscal
responsibility. The Deputy Grand Master now prepares the Grand Lodge
budget with help from the Finance and Executive Committees. The Grand
Lodge fiscal year has been changed to coincide more closely with the Grand
Master' s term so that you can measure the Grand Master's success in meeting
his budget. The Grand Master prepares his own budget, and you will know
if he does not meet it!
The commitment of your Executive Committee is to keep the
increases in the per capita tax for the foreseeable future to the cost-of-living
increase. But, with a declining membershiP., a cost-of-living keeps us about
even. We must therefore reduce expenses by $70,000 a year so that the per
capita tax even with a cost of living increase will cover the budget.
How are we doing it? The redistricting plan is just one example. All
programs of the Grand Lodge are on a "zero-budget" basis: they receive no
money unless they can j ustify their worth each year. The Executive

What you see from the Grand Lodge will not be a one-shot approach.
It will not be an annual flip-flop as different philosophies rotate year to year.
You will see programs that are designed to build on what has come before and
to provide a foundation for what will come afterward. This fraternity will
grow and prosper only with a long term approach to our concerns, an approach
that is designed to address our problems, an approach that is pursued with
vigor and improved with experience .
And, these programs to address our future cannot be successful
without the commitme nt of more than your future Grand Masters. It takes the
commitme nt of you and every member of the fraternity to address honestly
what lies ahead and how best we can answer the needs of our present and
prospective members. It is only with the commitment of our fraternity, of all
members in all positions in all craft, concordant and appendant bodies, that we
can meet the challenges ahead and build Masonry for the Twenty-first Century.

GENERA L CONDITI ON OF CALIFOR NIA MASONR Y
While our law requires me to report on the general condition of
Masonry within the Jurisdiction, I do not believe that a long statistical or other
detailed analysis is warranted. Many thoughts on this subject are expressed
elsewhere in this message. We read in the Grand Secretary's report each year
the continued declining trend in the number of members, the number of
raisings and the number of Lodges. The general quality of the ritual and the
administrative performance of our Lodge leaders is not what it was even
twenty years ago.
Your Grand Lodge leadership recognizes that these trends will
continue without strong, well-planned and consistent intervention . We do not
have a membership problem in this fraternity. We have a leadership problem.

OTHER ACTIONS AND ACTIVITI ES
AS GRAND MASTER
This portion of my message discusses other actions and activities as
Grand Master.
Grand Master' s Travels
This year, l encouraged the craft to plan for the Grand Master to visit
district events rather than individual Lodge events. In recent years, attend~ce
at such events has decl ined, due in part I believe to overexposur~. Sometimes
the Grand Master has been seen too often in an area. By the third, fourth and
fifth visit, fewer and fewer people are in attendance. Also, fe~er ~ut better
attended events during the year means that the Grand Master s reimbursed
travel expenses will be reduced even though he eventually will appear before
the same number of people.
Fewer but better attended events will also make it easier for younger
men to serve as Grand Master in the future. If we are to attract younger men
to Grand Lodge leadership roles, the time commitment for Grand Lodge m~st
be consistent with a man's work schedule. In that regard, I travelled outs~de
my home area on weekends only, much as Most Worshipful Myron E .. Smith,
Most Worshipful Donald B. McCaw and other Grand Masters did who
continued to work at their professions while serving as Grand Master.

Prayers at Cornerstones
A problem arose during Most Worshipful Stanley M. Cazneaux's term
which continued during the current year. Stan cancelled a cornerstone laying
ceremony scheduled for September 1992 because the school would not allow
the ceremony to be conducted if it included an invocation or a benediction.
Two recent and important court cases on the issue are Bennett v.
Livennore .Uni~ed School District ( 1987) 193 Cal.App.3d 1O12, 238 Cal. Rptr.
819 (a Cahforn1a Court of Appeals decision) and Lee v. Weisman (1992) 505
U.S. _ , 120 L.Ed.2d 467 (decided by the United States Supreme Court).
These cases h:ld that an invocation may not be included as part of a public
school graduation ceremony. Both courts held that such an inclusion would
violate the Establishment Clause of the United States Constitution. The
Establishment Clause guarantees that the government may not coerce anyone
to support or participate in religion . The courts held that the inclusion of the
invocation at the graduation ceremony was just such coercion. Tue fact that
the students had the option of not attending the ceremony did not excuse any
"coercion" because the ceremony was so important that the students were not
truly free to absent themselves from it.
While the Masonic cornerstone laying ceremony has not been litigated
. .
m h~ht of these recent decisions, to the best of my knowledge, we can
ant1C1pate how these decisions would be applied if it were. If the students are
required to attend the cornerstone laying ceremony, as they sometimes are
when it is conducted during school hours, our invocation and benediction
would be impermissible "coercion" based upon the Supreme Court test in Lee.

A middle ground is also available. Grand Lodge has participated in
cornerstone laying ceremonies where a local member o~ th~ cl~rgy has. been
asked to open the ceremony with appropriate words of msptratton. Tuts'. for
example, is the approach used at my children's school for P. T. A. meetings

Masons may sponsor programs to explain what Masonry is and invite
non-Masons to the program in an attempt to create a favorable impression
toward the fraternity. Our Masonic Information programs in California have
been used successfully by our Lodges to create such a favorable impression
without crossing the line separating information from solicitation.
A member may ask a man whom he believes to be a worthy
prospective Mason if he has considered membership in the Masonic fraternity
or if he would like to have information to enable him to make such a decision.
A member must inform the prospective member or inquirer that the fraternity
does not extend an invitation to become a member, that his application must
be made of his own free will and accord, and that he must pass a secret ballot
for admission.
After providing the information, the inquirer or prospect should be left
to make his own decision without persuasion. If the inquirer makes no
decision within a reasonable time, the member may make a s ingle follow-up
contact to see if additional information is needed.

DECISION NO. 3
Alcoholic Beverage Guidelines

Great care should be taken when a Mason approaches a non-Mason
under circumstances which might imply some coercion or intimidation. For
example, a supervisor at work should be very careful when approaching a
subordinate.
An older family member should be very careful when
approaching a younger family member. Under no circumstance should a
prospective member be led to believe that certain favors or benefits will result
from his membership, except that he may be made aware of the program of
care provided for elderly members and their spouses through our Masonic
Homes, if their conditions eventually warrant such care.
All communications with a prospective member should be courteous
and friendl y. Information about the fraternity should be factual. If questions
cannot be answered adequately, the member should seek assistance from other
members.
If you approve this decision, the text of it will be added to the
appendix of the C alifornia Masonic Code in which Grand Master's
interpretative decisions are recorded.

Report of the Commitlee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master seeks to clarify and include in an Appendix of the
California Masonic Code procedures and guidance with respect to boundaries
of propriety in discussing Masonry with the non-Mason.

At the I 989 Annual Communication, the Grand Lodge adopted more
liberal rules with respect to the use of alcoholic beverages at the activities ?f
Lodges and Masonic Organizations and by other groups when on Masonic
property. In 1990. the Grand Master promulgated Gu_idelines to help Lodges
and Masonic Organizations interpret the new rules. Smee those Grand Lodge
Guidelines for Use of Alcoholic Beverages were published in I 990, some
revised interpretations have been made. There is therefore a need to publish
a revised version of those Guidelines, a copy of which is set forth at the end
of this decision. These Guidelines are based on both the California Masonic
Code and the requirements of the laws of the State of California.
I ask you to approve the following Guidelines so that they may
provide guidance on this issue when required in the future:

182

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

GUIDELINES FOR USE OF ALCOHOLIC BEVERAGES
BY MASONIC LODGES AND MASONIC ORGANIZATIONS

Lodges and Temple Associations may not use funds
from the Lodge's or the Temple Association' s treasury to
purchase alcoholic beverages. However, funds collected by
a committee of the Lodge for social purposes are not Lodge
funds. Therefore, if a committee of the Lodge plans a Lodge
activity where alcoholic beverages are served, the committee
may use the money collected from ticket sales to purchase
alcohol ic beverages. The excess ticket sale proceeds may not
be given to the Lodge until after the reimbursement has been
made. No Lodge or Temple Association funds may be used
to reimburse anyone who has purchased alcoholic beverages.
These restrictions apply only to Lodges and Temple
Associations. The Scottish Rite, the York Rite bodies, the
Shrine, Eastern Star and other Masonic Organiz.ations may
reimburse the purchase of alcoholic beverages from their
treasuries, if their regulations so pennit.

Questions frequentl y arise with respect to
pennissible use of alcoholic beverages in Lodge halls, on
other property owned by or leased to a Masonic body and at
Masonic activities held elsewhere. These guidelines explain
the Grand Lodge rules applicable to such use. These
guidelines apply to Lodges, Temple Associations, the
Scottish Rite, the York Rite bodies, the Shrine, Eastern Star
and all other prerequisite organiz.ations and their Temple
Associations.
These guidelines address only the policy and
regulations of the Grand Lodge. Your use of alcoholic
beverages also must comply with the applicable laws of the
State of California and the rules established by your Masonic
Temple Association or other landlord.
A Masonic Lodge, Temple Association or other
Masonic Organiz.ation may allow alcoholic beverages to be
served on Masonic property to their members and invited
guests, with one exception. Alcoholic beverages are not
pennitted in the room where a Lodge or a Masonic
Organiz.ation meets unless that room is also the regular social
hall.
Members and guests may bring their own alcohol,
but alcoholic beverages may not be sold. You cannot have
a cash bar or sell drink tickets or tokens to be exchanged for
alcoholic beverages. You may charge for the meal or other
event at which alcoholic beverages are served, so long as
everyone pays the same price, regardless of whether they will
be served an alcoholic beverage.
Under no circumstances may the general public be
present when alcoholic beverages are served. You may not
advertise to the general public an event at which alcoholic
beverages will be served on Masonic property. Only
members of the sponsoring Masonic body and their invited
guests may be in attendance when alcoholic beverages are
served on Masonic property. The tenn "general public" does
not include the members of the organiz.ation, their families
or friends.

Lodges, Temple Associations and other Masonic
Organiz.ations may maintain a bar on Masonic property so
long as alcoholic beverages are not regularl y or permanently
stored in the bar. Alcohol should not be sto red elsewhere on
Masonic property either.
Lodges, Temple Associations and other Masonic
Organiz.ations may rent or lease their land or buildings to
business establishments which serve and sell alcoholic
beverages as an incidental part of their businesses. For
example, you may rent to a restaurant which has a bar or to
a grocery store that sells alcoholic beverages. However, you
may not rent to a bar business or a liq uor store, even those
bars and liquor stores with incidental sales of non-alcoholic
products.
Lodges, Temple Associations and other Masonic
Organiz.ations may rent or lease their land or buildings to
non-Masonic tenants other than business establishments who
serve alcoholic beverages, if alcoholic beverages are not sold.
For example, you may rent your building for a wedding
reception or similar activity where alcoholic beverages will
be served but may not be sold by the sponsor or caterer.
No Lodge or Temple Association may directly or
indirectly apply fo r, assume title to or operate under any
governmental license or pennit for the purpose of
consuming, serving or selling alcoholic beverages, whether
in, on or away from premises owned, leased or rented by a

Masonic Lodge or Temple Association. As a general rule
no license or pennit is required if alcoholic beverages are no~
sold and the premises are not open to the general public
when alcoholic beverages are being served or consumed.
These. ~estrictions apply only to Lodges and Temple
Associations. They do not apply to the Scottish Rite, the
York Rite bodies, the Shrine, Eastern Star and other Masonic
Organizations.

Such is not the law. There are only three ways in this Grand Lodge

Some also believe that the suggested language in the Jurisprudence
Committee's report as binding because we have considered Jurisprudence' s
suggested language binding in the past. Even the Jurisprudence Committee
has not considered its own language as binding! For example, in its 1991
report on Grand Master Sherod's Recommendation No. 3, Jurisprudence
suggested specific changes to two sections of the California Masonic Code if
Grand Lodge approved Ron's recommendation. Grand Lodge approved the
recommendation but Jurisprudence changed only one of those two sections and
then not with the exact language which had been in its report!
Because some members of Grand Lodge do not agree with this
decision, the matter is submitted to you for final resolution. You may decide
which Code changes are required to implement Ron Sherod' s advertising
recommendation. If you agree that it is Ron's version which was mailed in
July of 1991 and July of 1992, then you should vote "yes" on this decision.
If you agree that it is the version included in the Jurisprudence Committee's
report at Grand Lodge in 1991 and 1992 and also mailed in July of 1992, then
you should vote "no" on this decision. The majority rules. Whichever version
gets the most votes will be included in the next supplement to the California
Masonic Code.
While this is an unprecedented approach to resolve this matter,
Jurisprudence concurs that it may be used and that your decision shall be

DECISION NO. 5
Advertising Guidelines
At the 1992 Annual Communication, the Grand Lodge adopted more
liberal rules with respect to the solicitation of advertising by Lodges and
Masonic Organizations. As with the recently modified Guidelines regarding
alcoholic beverages, advertising guidelines would help Lodges and Masonic
Organizations interpret the new rules. Such guidelines have been prepared, a
copy of which is set forth at the end of this decision.
I ask you to approve the following Guidelines so that they may
provide guidance on this issue when required in the future:

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

GUIDELINES FOR ADVERTISING
IN MASONIC PUBLICATIONS
Guidelines Applicable to Masonic Lodges.
Our California Masonic Code pennits Masonic
Lodges to accept advertising in Lodge publications under
limited circumstances. These Guidelines answer many of the
questions which may arise in connection with that
advertising. If a question arises which is not adequately
answered by these Guidelines, Section 15110 of the
California Masonic Code should be consulted. If questions
remain, then the Grand Lodge Committee on Jurisprudence
should be contacted.
A Masonic Lodge may pennit advertising only in
Lodge publications. A Masonic Lodge may therefore accept
advertising for its monthly bulletin or trestleboard. It may
also accept advertising for its Lodge Roster and installation
programs. It may not accept advertising which will not be
printed in a Lodge publication. For example, commercial
advertising material cannot be posted in the Masonic hall.
Advertising may be accepted only from the Lodge's
members an~ from businesses or commercial establishments
owned or operated by its members. Advertising may not be
accepted from mem bers of another Lodge. Advertising may
not be accepted from the wife or other relatives of a member.
Advertising may be accepted from a business only if a
member of the Lodge has an equity or other ownership
interest in the business or holds an operating or managing
position in the business.
The advertising must be in good taste and within the
bounds of propriety. While "good taste" is difficult to
define, nothing should be accepted which would offend
accepted standards of behavior among Masons. If a matter
would be inappropriate for discussion at a Masonic social
gathering where wives, families and friends are present, it
should not be part of an advertisement in a Lodge
publication. This standard applies to the size and subject
matter of the advertisement as well as to its text, art work
and color. Sexual inferences and vulgarity would not be
acceptable.

189

190

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Neither the advertising itself nor the products or
services which it promotes may be unethical, fraudulent,
misleading or illegal under applicable state and federal laws.
Advertisements may not be accepted for prescription
drugs and other controlled substances. Advertisements may
not be accepted for alcoholic or tobacco products.
Advertisements for religious or political groups may not be
accepted.
Neither the Lodge's mailing list nor the Grand
Lodge Roster may be furnished to advertisers, either directly
or indirectly. Even if the advertiser offers to mail the
publication as a service to the Lodge, the Lodge's mailing
list may not be delivered to an advertiser for any purpose.
No one may tell a Mason that it is his duty to
advertise in the Lodge's publication. No pressure, either
directly or indirectly, may be applied to any member to
advertise in a Lodge publication. Keep in mind that pressure
can be applied by what we say as well as by the implications
of what we do.
Solicitation of advertisements may be made only by
a member in good standing of the Lodge for whose
publication advertising is solicited. The Lodge may not
employ anyone, either directly or indirectly, to solicit
advertising, unless the man is a Mason in good standing of
the Lodge for whose publication advertising is solicited. A
member of another Lodge may not solicit advertising.
The revenue from advertising may be used only to
offset the cost of publishing, printing and mailing the
publication in which the advertising appears. If the revenue
from advertising is greater than the expenses of publishing,
printing and mailing that publication, the profit must be
donated to a recognized Masonic charity, such as the
Masonic Homes Endowment Fund or the California Masonic
Foundation. Advertising has been pennitted to help Lodges
meet the cost of Lodge publications. It is not designed to
generate income for the Lodge's other activities. To prevent
any abuse of the advertising privilege, any funds over the
amount needed for the actual publication, printing and
mailing of the publication in which the advertising appears
must be given to a recognized Masonic charity.

Fraternal Dealings with Unrecognized Masons
During my tenure as Grand Master, I have been asked on several
occasions to decide whether certain dealings with unrecognized Masons are
legal under the California Masonic Code. For example, I was asked to attend
a luncheon with the leaders of Californi a Prince Hall Masonry on October
16th. I was asked to attend a devotional service at the Annual Communication
of the Prince Hall Grand Lodge on July 18th. I was asked by a California
Lodge whether it could allow a Prince Hall Masonic Club of military
personnel from the local base to meet in its Masonic hall. As we have seen
in other jurisdictions, contacts with Prince Hall Masons will increase in the
future. My decisions in these circumstances should therefore be considered by
you and, if you agree, published as a guide when similar questions are asked
in the future.
While the specific circumstances varied, one question was common
to each: To what extent are the members of a Californi a Lodge restricted in
their fraternal dealings with persons who are not members of an organization
to which the Grand Lodge of California has extended Masonic recognition?
While Grand Master Pavlovich added some guidelines on such dealings when
we are present in a sister Masonic jurisdicti on, there is much uncertainty as to
the appropriate conduct while we are in California.
Under Section 15040 of the Californi a Masonic Code, we may not
have Masonic intercourse with a person who is not a member of an
organization to which the Grand Lodge of California has extended Masonic
recognition. Under Section 18 of the Code, Masonic intercours e means any
communication involving the esoteric or secret portion of the ritual, that is, any
portion of the ritual which in this jurisdicti on is not monitorial. These Code
Sections establish a definite standard. We may not sit in a tiled meeting
within California with a person who is not a member of a Masonic jurisdicti on
to which the Grand Lodge of California has extended Masonic recognition.
We may not discuss our esoteric or secret work with any such person. We
may not answer with the appropriate Masonic response when greeted with one
of our modes of recog nition by any such person.
The only other prohibitio n on dealings with unrecognized Masons is
set forth in Section 15040 of the Code. A Lodge may not give Masonic
recognition to any body not chartered by the Grand Lodge in whose territorial
jurisdiction the body is located. What is recognition? In my view, recognition
means that we have agreed to have Masonic intercourse with such body and
its members.

RECOMMEND ATIONS

RECOMMEND ATION NO. 1
Interpretation of the American Doctrine
During the Grand Lodge year, the Prince Hall Recognition Study
Committee asked whether a Grand Lodge violates the American Doctrine of
exclusive territorial jurisdiction when it recognizes Prince Hall Masonry within
its jurisdiction.
California's current official statement on the American Doctrine is set
forth in Section 220 of the California Masonic Code. In short, the American
Doctrine has been interpreted by many to mean that there may be only one
Grand Lodge in any state or territory of the United States. If such were the
case, then how could the Grand Lodges of Connecticut, Washington and
several other states recognize the Prince Hall Grand Lodges within their
jurisdictions without violating the American Doctrine?
To answer this question, some background on the development of the
American Doctrine is helpful. The first official California authority which I
find regarding the American Doctrine is in the proceedings for the 1872
Annual Communication at page 552:
"We have established a rule, recognized throughout
the United States and British America, that only one Grand
Lodge shall be established in any State or Territory, and that,
whenever one is established, it has the absolute control and
government of all Masons and all Lodges of the first three
degrees; and that no other Grand Lodge can in any way
interfere with its jurisdiction, to establish new Lodges
therein, or even to maintain those already established. The
territory is absolutely, exclusively, and perpetually the
territory of the Grand Lodge established over it; and the
Grand Lodge of any State not only has exclusive jurisdiction
within the limits of the State, but it has full, original, and
exclusive legislative, judicial, and executive power within
that territory, subject only to the great landmarks of the
Order."

Contrary actions have been taken subsequently. Grand Master H

If the American Doctrine does not permit a jurisdiction to waive
exclusive jurisdiction in its own territory, then the actions in recognizing the
Grand Lodge of Alaska without withdrawing recognition of the Grand Lodge
of Washington violated that doctrine. Upon the formation of the Grand Lodge
of Alaska within a state of the United States with the approval of the Grand
Lodge which previously had jurisdiction over that territory, we should have
recognized the Grand Lodge of Alaska as the only Grand Lodge with authority
within Alaska.

interpretation is more consistent with the theory of Grand ~odge sov~~e1gnty:
if 8 Grand Lodge has the right to exclude .other '."fasomc au.thon.ues and

This interpretation is also consistent with the rules on territorial

This interpretation of the American Doctrine would harmonize our
decision to maintain recognition of the Grand Lodge of Washington when the
Grand Lodge of Alaska was formed and when Washington recognized Prince
Hall Masonry in its jurisdiction. If you approve this interpretation of .the
American Doctrine, it would also give California the right to recogmze
concurrent jurisdiction within its own territory without abandoning the
American Doctrine.

Our action in Alaska was consistent with the American Doctrine only
if Alaska could waive its right to exclusive territorial jurisdiction within its
boundaries and permit Washington to continue to govern some of the Lodges
within that state. Thus, our recognition of the Grand Lodge of Alaska without
withdrawing recognition of the Grand Lodge of Washington did not violate the
American Doctrine only if the American Doctrine permits a Grand Lodge to
waive the right to exclusive territorial jurisdiction within its state and pennit
concurrent jurisdiction.
At our 1990 Annual Communication, our Grand Lodge authorized
California Masons to sit in a tiled Washington Lodge at which there are
present Masons from Washington Prince Hall Lodges now afforded such rights
by the Grand Lodge of Washington. (Grand Master Pavlovich's Decision No.
3.) No suggestion was made that we withdraw recognition from Washington
or that Washington did not have the right to waive its right to exclusive
jurisdiction over its territory. In effect, our Grand Lodge has taken the exact
opposite stand that it took in response to similar actions of the Grand Lodge
of Washington in June of 1898!
It is therefore my view that the American Doctrine is more properly
recited as follows: there may be only one Grand Lodge in any state or
territory of the United States unless the Grand Lodge which we recognize with

of our law, I recommend that the last sentence of Section 220 of the California
Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
This Grand Lodge shall recognize only one Grand Lodge in any state
or territory of the United States unless the Grand Lodge which we
recognize with exclusive jurisdiction over that state or territory
chooses to waive its right to maintain exclusive jurisdiction and
pennit concurrent jurisdiction. In the event of such a waiver, th.is
Grand Lodge may also recognize such additional Grand Lodges m
that state or territory as have been granted such concurrent
jurisdiction.

RECOMMEND ATION NO. 2
Grand Lodge Investment Guidelines
Our present California Masonic Code contains guidelines for the
investment of the funds of the Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes and the other
Grand Lodge entities . These guidelines were enacted many years ago and
represented prudent investment practice at the time. In the years since their
original enactment, prudent investment practice has changed but our law has
not. Many financial instruments now widely held were unknown a few years

The adoption of this recommendation would pennit our Grand Lodge
and other Grand Lodge entities to earn the same prudent investment benefits
routinely secured by other major nonprofit organizations in this country.
If you adopt this recommendation, Section 7020 of the California
Masonic Code will be repealed and replaced with the following:

many years and have on numerous occasions broadene d to allow access to a
variety of different investmen t vehicles.

Our current law does not allow the flexibility to use many of the

would be removed and replaced with the same investmen t standards which
Californi a law requires of all trust fiduciaries.

Grand Lodge Fiscal Responsib ility
During the eight year period beginning on July 1, 1983, this Grand
Lodge lost over $200,000 , computed on a cash b~is. While no~ every year
during that eight year period showed a loss, most did. By the sprmg of 1991,
Grand Lodge had no money left. Grand Lodge was forced to borrow money
to make payroll and to pay its other necessary expenses. Our then Gr~d
Master Ronald Sherod declared a moratoriu m on all but the most essential
expenditu res until the per capita was collected the following July.
Our Junior Past Grand Master, Stanley C azneaux, initiated a number
of new procedures in response to the crisis. First, as Deputy Grand Mas~er,
Stan assumed responsib ility for the preparation of the budg~t for the followmg
Grand Lodge year. The Grand Master is ultimately responsib le to the craft for
the implemen tation of the budget once it has been approved by the Grand
Lodge. If it is the Grand Master who must guard against budget overruns,
then the Grand Master must be well informed about the sources of Grand
Lodge expenditu res to know what to change w~en a budget overrun ~eems
likely. Also, the preparation of a budget provides the best opportuni ty to
evaluate the effectiven ess of current and proposed programs of the Grand
Lodge. In the budgeting process, Stan eliminate d or .reduced many expense
categories, including many associated with our committe es.

RECOMMENDATION NO. 4

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Extension of the Pilot Program on Fund-Raising
Grand Master Doan has made this recommendation to set forth details
for the increase fiscal responsibility of Grand Lodge.
This recommendation attempts to amend or add to various sections of
the California Masonic Code (CMC) details of the preparation of an annual
budget for Grand Lodge and the responsibility for its preparation. Also, the
Grand Master includes a new section for the CMC to establish a Grand Lodge
Endowment Fund.

During his term as Grand Master, Most Worshipful Stanley M.
Cazneaux entered into a pilot program with the Shrine Temples of California.
Pursuant to the predecessor of Section 15100 of the California Masonic Code,
Grand Master Cazneaux authorized the Shrine Temples to solicit the general
public for fund-raising activities which support Shrine fraternal operations, but
·
only if the Shrine Temples observed the following guidelines:

I.

The square and compass, the words "Mason", "Masonic",
"Freemasonry", "Freemason" and any variation of any such
words could not be used in connection with the activity or
any publicity associated with it.

2.

The activi~ could not be unethical, fraudulent, misleading or
illegal under applicable state and federal laws.

3.

Finally, your committee believes that the attempt to create a new
Endowment Fund in the same recommendation as preparation of a budget is
improper. A new Endowment Fund and the budget should not be included in
the same recommendation, this, we believe, is contrary to our policy.

The sponsor disclosed that any profits from the activity
would be used for the sponsor's fraternal and not charitable
purposes, if such were the case. In the event that such
disclosure were not given, through inadvertence or otherwise,
all proceeds from the activity would be given to a recognized
Masonic charity.

4.

Solicitation of support would not occur on the premises of
any Masonic Lodge.

Your committee also has other concerns on the proposed Fund, such
as it does not detail the manner in which the fund will operate and who will
operate it.

A similar consent was given by me at the beginning of the current Grand
Lodge year.

Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes fiscal
responsibility is necessary for individuals as well as organii.ations, and Grand
Lodge is no exception. Also it is our opinion that the budget proposals have
merit. However, the new sections directed to a budget trouble your committee
because of some inconsistencies in sub-sections, such as consultation with the
Committee on Finance and then under proposed Section "D" giving them the
job of reporting to the Grand Lodge, yet the proposed Section "E" the Deputy
Grand Master presents the budget to Grand Lodge. In proposed Section "G"
there are two categories. It is the committee' s belief that the amendments
could confuse rather than clarify.

In my view, this pilot program has been a success. California Shrine
Temples have sponsored public fund-raising activities, such as their Shrine
Circuses to maintain the quality of Shrine programs without additional dues
increase;. No one has brought to my attention any abuses nor any violations
of the Memorandum of Understanding by which the consent was granted.

It now appears appropriate to expand this program. At present, the

success if they are assured that they may sponsor such fund-raising activities
two, three or five years hence. Because of the success of this program, I
believe also that its benefits should not be limited to the Shrine. Its benefits
should be extended to the other members of the Family of Freemasonry.
I therefore submit for your consideration the following. I recommend
that all Masonic Organizations in California be permitted to solicit the general
public for fund-raising activities which support fraternal operations, under the
same limited circumstances which governed Shrine fund-raising activities
during the last two years. Permitted fund-raising activities would include the
solicitation of advertising from any individual or business.

Initially, this special permission would only be available for Eastern Star, the
Masonic Youth groups, the York Rite, the Scottish Rite, the Shrine and all
other Masonic organizations in California, other than Blue Lodges.
I also recommend that this grant of authority be for more than just one
Grand Master's term but that it not be made permanent. I believe that the

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master seeks to extend the so-called Pilot Program on
Fund-Raising involving the Shrine Temples in California to most of the
members of the Family of Masonry in Californi a. This continued experiment
will not include the Blue Lodges and is proposed for a period of five years to

PROCEEDrNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

This pilot program is the result of a Memorandum of Understanding
during 1992 and 1993 between the Shrine Temples and the Grand Lodge of
California authorizing solicitation of the general public for fund raising
activities under certain prescribed guidelines to support the Shrine's fraternal
endeavors.

conform to California Grand Lodge regulations which differ and are more
restrictive than those in some of the other jurisdictions.

212

The initial implementation of this program was a unilateral action by
then Grand Master Cazneaux and thus was not presented for your
consideration at our last Annual Communication. Grand Master Doan elected
to extend the program through the current Grand Lodge year, and now, a much
broader proposal is before you for your deliberation.
In September, 1988, the Masonic Service Association published a
booklet entitled Allied Masonic Groups and Rites which lists approximately
59 organizations which require membership in one or more branches of
Freemasonry as a prerequisite to membership. If one reviews the stated
purposes and goals of each of these organiz.ations, there is much commonalty.
Each group purports to promote the principal tenets of the fraternity and
provide social opportunities.
Without studying the history of each organization in detail, it is
probably safe to assume that each organization gained recognition from a
Grand Lodge through some formal or informal process. In so doing, it may
also be assumed that each of these organizations expected to observe the
general regulations of the Grand Jurisdiction in which they operated. This
assumption is based on the fact that the members had to have some Masonic
tie.
Since these organizations are essentially dependent on Masons for
their membership, they must be prepared to accept the standards of
Freemasonry adopted by the Grand Lodges. They are in a sense, franchisees
of the fraternity of Freemasonry and would therefore be expected to comply
with the fraternity' s policies and practices.
As a practical matter, the large number of prerequisite organizations
recognized by the Grand Lodge of California, seems to necessitate uniformity
in the enactment and enforcement of our laws and regulations. It could be
very difficult for the prerequisite bodies to plan and implement programs and
activities if the laws and regulations varied from one organization to another.
And it probably would even be more difficult than it is now for Grand Lodge
to maintain any reasonable control over their activities.
At least one of the prerequisite organizations, the Shrine, has resisted
efforts by Grand Lodge to control their activities, on the basis that they have
special needs that must be met if they are to be successful in implementing
their programs and activities. They also complain about being required to

213

The policies of Grand Lodge relative to the prerequisite and other
affiliated Masonic organizations are based on at least two fundamental
principles.
I.

Prerequisite organizations and their members, all whom are
Masons, must conform to and obey the laws, regulations and
policies of the Grand Lodge of California.

2.

The laws, regulations and policies of the Grand Lodge of
California must be applied unifonnly to all Lodges and
prerequisite organizations.

The reasoning behind these principles was articulated by Grand
Master L. Harold Anderson in a 1957 decision in which he wrote, "prerequisite
organizations claim affiliation with Freemasonry and are believed by the public
to be Masonic, and it would be most unfair to Blue Lodges if their members
could band together in another body and endeavor to do what Lodges cannot
do."
In recent years a variety of legislation was proposed to give special
consideration to the Shrine in the areas of advertising, fund raising and the
serving of alcoholic.beverages. This approach was consistently opposed by the
Committee on Policy and General Purposes because, among other reasons, it
was contrary to the general policy of equal treatment for all.
It would appear, in view of the foregoing, that consideration for some
form of relaxation of our regulations as they affect our fraternity as a whole
might be in order. Grand Masters Cazneaux and Doan both have endeavored
to address this issue by entering into the aforementioned Memorandum of
Understanding. Grand Master Doan now proposes to extend this relaxation to
the entire Family of Freemasonry to include the Eastern Star, the Masonic
Youth Groups, the York Rite, the Scottish Rite, the Shrine and all other
Masonic organizations in California, other than Blue Lodges.

From a policy standpoint, we ask, is this proposal fair and equal
treatment for all? What reasoning is there for the exclusion of you, my
brethren, the members of our constituent Lodges in this noble experiment.
Your Policy and General Purposes Committee has determined that Grand
Master Doan' s Recommendation No. 4 is not consistent with the equal
treatment policy of your Grand Lodge since it specifically excludes the Blue
Lodges.
Recommendation APPROVED.

RECOMMEND ATION NO. 5

1.

If a man does not wish to be obligated on the Christian Bible, he
must select alternate Holy Writings from a list promulgated from time
to time by the Grand Master of the Holy Writings of other recognized
religions. The Grand Master's list shall at all times include the Holy
Writings of those of the world's major religions whose theology is not
inconsistent with a belief in a Supreme Being and a future existence.
In selecting alternate Holy Writings, the man must state that the book
chosen is the Holy Writings of his religious faith.

2.

The particular book selected for use on the altar during the
ceremonies of a man's degrees must be of a suitable size as
determined by the Ritual Committee.

3.

Grand Lodge will make available all books on the list. Grand Lodge
will loan any book on the list upon request to a Lodge which requires
it for a degree.

4.

The book selected should remain on the altar throughout the meeting
during which it is used for a man 's degree. However, if a Lodge
schedules more than one man to receive a degree at a meeting and all
men receiving a degree on that occasion will not be obligated on the
same book of Holy Writings, then the book should be changed when
the Lodge is at refreshment between the degrees.

5.

When alternate Holy Writings are used during a degree, a closed Holy
Bible of any size must be on the altar.

6.

Alternate Holy Writings may be used only at a Lodge meeting during
which a man selecting the alternate Holy Writings receives a degree
and on no other occasion.

7.

Most importantly, there will be no change in the wording used in the
Ritual during the ceremonies: the words "Holy Bible" will be used
in a generic sense referring to the Holy Writings then present on the

Use of Alternate Holy Writings
What makes a man a Mason? It is his obligation. His obligation
binds him to the Fraternity. His obligation is a solemn covenant which he
makes with every man who ever has been, is now or ever will be a Mason.
He promises to support a brother in distress. He promises to aid and assist a
brother's widow and orphans. He receives the same promise in return. This
covenant is so important that our Fraternity has strict anti-solicitation rules:
no man should ever have grounds to assert that he was pressured into
becoming a Mason and therefore that his solemn covenant is somehow
voidable because he was forced to become a Mason against his will.
The importance of a Mason's obligation is evidenced by the manner
in which it is given. A man swears to God to support it and it is repeated on
the Holy Scriptures, the rule and guide of a Mason's faith. In this jurisdiction,
the only Holy Scriptures permitted on our altar is the Christian Bible
containing the Old and New Testaments.
In Acts 4: 12 of the Christian Bible, we read that no person can be
saved unless he or she believes in Jesus. Jews obviously believe otherwise.
Should we ask a Jew to make a solemn covenant on scriptures which some
would interpret to mean that a Jew cannot go to Heaven? In Luke 9:20 of the
Christian Bible, we read that Christ is the Messiah. However, Muslims believe
that Christ was a prophet only and not the Messiah. Should we ask a Muslim
to make a solemn covenant on scriptures proclaiming a Messiah in which he
does not believe?
I am a committed Christian. But I am also committed to the Masonic
principle of toleration for the views of others. Just as I would want my
Christian beliefs respected, I respect the beliefs of Jews, Muslims and other
non-Christians. If given a choice, I would choose to take a solemn obligation
on a Christian Bible, and not on the Old Testament alone or on the Koran.
Should not our Jewish and Islamic friends have the option to choose their holy
writings when they become Masons? Should not every man be permitted to
take his Masonic obligation on the Volume of the Sacred Law of the faith to
which be subscribes? I recommend that you give him that right.
This proposal has been before Grand Lodge in the past. However, on
each prior occasion, various committees have recommended that you not
approve it because sufficient safeguards were not included. I believe that the
following conditions on the selection of alternate Holy Writings respond to
those concerns. I therefore recommend that every man be given the right to
select alternate Holy Writings on which he will be obligated, but only under
the following circumstances:

These standards are consistent with the generally accepted ancient landmarks
of Freemasonry.
On prior occasions, it has been reported to you that several, eminent
religious scholars have studied this issue and concluded that no change was
necessary. In their view, because no right thinking person could object to the
ethical standards set forth in the Christian Bible, no man should object to its
use during his Masonic degrees.

When alternate Holy Writings are used during a degree, a
closed Holy Bible of any size must be on the altar.

I believe that every good Mason should respect each of the Old and
New Testaments, the Koran and all other Holy Writings. However, the issue
is not respect. The issue is the solemn covenant which each man makes on
scripture. That covenant is sacred. Because it is sacred, the candidate should
swear to it on the Holy Writings which he holds to be sacred. I ask that you
give every man this right with the safeguards set forth in this recommendation.

219

Men, then, as now, are reluctant to throw anything away. The old
lectures, which were given in question and answer fonn, were assigned to the
candidates to learn in addition to the simpler and far older proficiencies. Thus
arose the requirement that our candidates memorize not only the historic
proficiencies which we inherited from operative Masons but also the displaced
lectures given to but not theretofore memorized by the candidates. With the
passage of time, it now requires the Masonic scholar to discern the ancient
from the modem in our candidate's lectures.
I believe that it is now time to return to our historic proficiencies as
they existed during the time of George Washington and Benjamin Franklin.
Our candidates should be required to memorize only those parts of the
candidate's proficiencies which are the most ancient and which have been
sufficient to prove a man a Mason "from time immemorial". This change
would bring our candidate's proficiencies closer to those now used in Great
Britain and in other English-speaking countries abroad.

ln returning to our historic proficiencies, we need not lose our current
forms of candidate' s lecture. There are many men in California who love
memory work, and they should from time to time recite our current candidate's
lectures at special Lodge meetings, much like they were recited in the
Eighteenth Century and before.
In theory, a candidate should advance once he has demonstrated skill
in two areas: reco8f1ition and education. Once a candidate has learned the
historic proficiencies to which I propose that we now return, he will be
equipped to recognize and be recognized by regular Masons, whithersoever
dispersed. The portion of our current candidate 's proficiencies now proposed
for elimination does not, in my opinion, give much educational value for the
considerable period of time required for its memorization. If you adopt this
recommendation, a more effective educational tool would take its place. Our
candidates would be required to study the teachings of our fraternity associated
with each of the degrees and then answer a series of written questions
appertaining to the craft as the Grand Master may promulgate from time to
time.
This recommendation was developed with the assistance of the Grand
Lecturer, the Grand Secretary, the Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens,
all of whom join me in asking for your support of it. Should you adopt this
recommendation, we believe that you will restore the candidate's proficiencies
to their oldest form, require the candidate to memorize all that he will ever
need to pass an examination before visiting another Lodge and, most
importantly, provide a far more effective means by which our candidates may
be taught what it means to be a Mason.
