Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The Grand Master recommends a return to "basics" and his
Recommendation No. 6 states that this would mean a return to Historic
Proficiencies as they existed during the time of George Washington and
Benjamin Franklin.
Certainly, to the best of our knowledge, candidates' proficiencies in
California Masonry do differ from those of the time of George Washington.
But then, so does California Ritual differ from the ritual of the historic times
to which he refers.
California Masonic Law requires that there be no change in the Ritual
with one exception and that exception is to return it to its original adopted
form. There is nothing in the Grand Master's Recommendation to indicate
that, when the Grand Lodge of California first adopted its ritual, it adopted that
of the Grand Lodge over which George Washington presided. California's

221

There have been nwnerous attempts in recent years to make changes
in the Ritual, particularly as it applies to candidates ' proficiencies. Numerous
reasons have been given for suggesting changing the candidates' proficiencies
to a shortened form . Among those reasons have been that the memory
requirements of our ritual impose too heavy a burden on candidates and this
is one reason why our applications for degrees have declined. No one has
provided statistics to prove that assertion. In fact, applicants for degrees are
not and should not be aware of the nature of the memory work to be required
of them. The relationship between candidates and their coaches contributes
greatly to the new members ' knowledge. This is an initial li nk in the chain of
candidatl! education. Another reason expounded is that some candidates
progress either slowly or not at all after having received a degree. This results
in the eventual loss of these candidates from our membership rolls. The loss
of membership experienced in Masonic Jurisdictions has been a source of
concern to many for some time. However, there are few men who can't
memorize a candidate' s lecture, the excuse being that they are too busy in
today's business and social lives to spend the necessary time. Your committee
is of the belief that a man too busy to learn a proficiency could well be too
busy to be of significant benefit to the fraternity. Frequently, many of the
leaders of a community also the leaders in Masonic Lodges. Certainly these
men are busy but still find time to devote to our Fraternity. If the desire for
dues, fees and other sources of funds is the primary interest, then we should
find some other means of increasing membership or revenues.
Some of our programs, such as Layman's Nights, have proven to
produce applicants. Your committee is disappointed to learn that many Lodges
have only one such night each year. We find that Masters who provide
interesting programs for their members do not have the same lack of
attendance or lack of applicants that a number of other Lodges experience.
Nevertheless, since none of the proposed changes have met the test
of conformity to our law they have not been approved by the delegates to this
Grand Lodge. In the future the delegates to this Grand Lodge may wish to
amend the law so that the ritual can be changed at their will. However, one
of the principal reasons for Masonry's success is its constancy over the years.
Changes do not necessarily enhance our Fraternity, but the solidarity provided
by traditional constancy does. A frequentl y changing ritual could only result
in chaos. There would be the constant question as to which ritual is the
current one and this alone, would put an added burden on Lodge Officers,
candidates, and those involved in teaching the ritual. Your committee realizes
that "change" is a popular buzzword in today ' s society, but change is not
necessarily beneficial.

RECOMMENDATION NO. 7
Discretionary Duties of the Assistant Grand Lecturers
There is a recognized need for the Grand Lodge to provide greater
emphasis, guidance and support to establish, develop and maintain the highest
possible standards for management and administration within each constituent
Lodge. This need is separate and apart from ritual but of equal importance.
The Grand Master cannot adequately supervise the Lodges as they
strive to meet these high standards, even with the assistance of the Deputy
Grand Master and Grand Wardens. Even when this supervision is delegated
to the District Inspectors, the Grand Master cannot adequately supervise the
District Inspectors in their supervision of the Lodges.
Accordingly, during the current Grand Lodge year, I assigned certain
additional duties to the Assistant Grand Lecturers with respect to management
and administration. These were in addition to the ritualistic duties which they
perform under the supervision of the Grand Lecturer as required by Section
3030 of the California Masonic Code.
During the current Grand Lodge year, each Assistant Grand Lecturer
supervised the District Inspectors assigned to his Division in each Inspector's
performance of his management and administrative duties. Each Assistant
Grand Lecturer was the intermediary between the Grand Master and the
District Inspectors of his Division with respect to such matters. Each District
Inspector reported to the Grand Master through the Inspector' s Assistant Grand
Lecturer. The Assistant Grand Lecturer was the first person contacted when
an administrative problem arose in a District in connection with the Inspector's
responsibilities as the Grand Master's representative. The Assistant Grand
Lecturers were asked to monitor, evaluate and measure the performance of
each of the District Inspectors assigned to his Division in each' s discharge of
his duties as the Grand Master's representative to the Lodges assigned to him.

The Assistant Grand Lecturers performed these discretionary duties
this past year under the supervision of the Grand Master.

It is the view of the members of the Deputy Grand Master, Grand
Wardens and l that this program has been successful. While future Grand
Masters have the right to continue, modify or discontinue this program at
each 's discretion, the Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens and I believe that
Grand Masters in the future might be assisted if at least the outline of this
discretionary program were in our Code as guidance for the possible
continuance of a similar program.
To accomplish that end, I therefore recommend that Section 3030.B
of the California Masonic Code be amended to read as follows:
8.

.

Examine and instruct the Inspectors within his
division in the performance of their duties with
respect to ritual and assist the Grand Master as and
to the extent that he may direct in the supervision of
such Inspectors in the performance of their duties as
the Grand Master's representative to the Lodges in
each ' s District;

Master's representative to the Lodges in each Inspector's District.
As the Grand Master stated in his Recommendation, "neither the

ritual. As long ago as 1963 the Special Commission of Masonic Practices
stated that "In too many cases, the problems of obtaining Lodge leadership ...
and its failure to sense and respond to the needs of the members and visitors
stand at the root of apathy, atrophy and absenteeism."
In 1990 the Committee on Long Range Planning recommended to this
Grand Lodge that a second structure, consisting of Grand Master's
Administrative Assistants, be set up parallel to the Jnspectoral corps, to
develop, establish and supervise a program for the management and
administration of lodges. This Recommendation was never implemented
because of cost and staffing problems. However, it seems clear that if the
Fraternity of Free and Accepted Masons is to survive and grow in the state of
California during the next decade, we must strive for the highest possible
standards of management and administration within the constituent Lodges.
Even though this Resolution is a change in our existing policy, your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes agrees with this need for this
Resolution.

Composition of Junior Grand Warden Recommending Committee
Many years ago, a system evolved in which Past Grand Masters fro':"
the northern portion of the state and those from the south met separately m
alternate years to recommend a member of Grand Lodge for election as Junior
Grand Warden. After agreement was reached among the Past Grand Masters
from both portions of the state, the name of the recommendee was circulated
mouth-to-ear. In later years, all Past Grand Masters have met collectively to
select a recommendee alternately from the northern and southern portions of
the state.
Jn 1974, these traditions were enacted into law. Provision was made
for written notice of the name and qualifications of the recommendee. Also,
three additional men were added to the selection committee, men who would
be appointed by the sitting Grand Master and who would not be p~t or
present elected Grand Lodge Officers. In 1980, the la_w was ch~ged a~am to
name the Grand Master as the chairman of the selection committee, with the
power to vote only in the event of a tie, as is normally the rule in such
circumstances.
This process has evolved because of a desire to pursue two goals: to
clarify the rules and to widen the circle of experiences represented at _the
selection meeting. "Tue addition of the Grand Master to the selectton
committee was particularly important in advancing this second goal. The
Grand Master is the one California Mason uniquely placed to observe the
performance and potential of the possible candidates for election as Junior
Grand Warden .
The Deputy Grand Master and the Grand Wardens potentially .have
much to contribute to the selection process also. They travel extensively
around the state. They sit on the major Boards of Trustees of this Grand
Lodge. They meet monthly with the Grand Master at Executive Committee
meetings. They too have a unique opportunity to observe the craft at work.
Their observations on occasion may differ from those of the Grand Master, and
those observations would be helpful to the selection committee.
In recognition of this potential, the Deputy. Grand ~aster and Grand
Wardens were invited to attend the selection committee meetmg last January.
Because our Jaw does not provide that they are members of the selection
committee the committee allowed them to attend its deliberations as observers
only. Wh'ite such observer status could continue in the future, an observer
does not have the same opportunity to contribute that a member has. The
participation of our Deputy Grand Master and Grand Ward~ns in the selection
process cannot reach its potential unless these men are voting members of the

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
Grand Master Doan recommends that the Deputy Grand Master and
Grand Wardens be included on the Committee for selection of a recommendee
for Junior Grand Warden.
The Selection Committee serves primarily as a Nominating
Committee. The voting delegates to Grand Lodge have the final word.
The procedure used by the Grand Lodge of California for decades has
served this Grand Lodge well. It is unique among the Grand Lodges of North
America and other parts of the world. It takes advantage of the accumulated
experience of all Past Grand Masters who have served the Grand Lodge in
many different positions culminating in the prestigious position of Grand
Master. The span of experience also covers a period of nearly half a century.
Some time ago, in response to a demand for wider representation of
the Grand Lodge on the Selection Committee, the Grand Lodge adopted a
change to include three other members of the Grand Lodge to be appointed
annually by the Grand Master to serve for a single tenn only and concurrently
with the appointing Grand Master and who are not past or present elected

Later, the Grand Lodge added the Grand Master to the Committee to
act as a non-voting chairman who would be responsible for arranging and
conducting the meeting of the Committee. This has been the procedure for the
past 12 years.
In 1992, an ad-hoc Committee of Past Grand Masters made a study
of the desirability of including the Deputy Grarid Master and Grand Wardens
as members of the Selection Committee. This study concluded that, because
these officers have the opportunity to meet many outstanding brethren in the
course of their service as Grand Officers, they should be invited to submit the
names of prospective candidates for the position of Junior Grand Warden to
the Grand Master, as chainnan of the Committee. However, it was felt that
their physical presence at the Selection Committee meeting, either as observers
or active participants, was neither necessary nor desirable.
There may be some merit in having the Deputy Grand Master present
as an observer so that he can properly exercise his responsibilities to the
Committee at the next meeting at which he would preside. However, previous
Grand Masters have had no difficulty in conducting the meeting without prior
attendance. We therefore see no need for an observer.
The presence of any of these officers is not necessary to learn the

RECOMMEN DATION NO. 9
Frequency of Lodge Secretary Reports to Grand Lodge
From the fonnation of our Grand Lodge in 1850 until 1942, Lodges
were required to send to the Grand Secretary an annual report only. Beginning
in 1942, Lodges were required to submit monthly membership reports. This
system has served us well over the years. However, with the advent of
computers, communicati on with our Lodges has become easier. The Grand
Secretary hopes to implement a system in the near future that will permit
Lodges to send information to the Grand Lodge Office by a computer modem .
We could thus not only accelerate the availability of information to Grand
Lodge, but also save money for both the indi vidual Lodges and Grand Lodge.
The California Masonic Code currently requires each Lodge Secretary
to send the Grand Secretary a monthly report as well as an annual report. It
is my recommendation that this requirement be changed to provide that the
Lodge Secretaries send reports to the Grand Lodge with such frequency as the
Grand Secretary shall determine, but no less often than annually. In doing so,
I also recommend that reports be required no more often than monthly. No
Secretary need therefore fear that this recommendation would permit the Grand
Lodge to require anything more of him than is presently required!
This flexibility will allow the Grand Secretary to take advantage of
new computer and electronic communication technology. This will eventually
allow the Grand Lodge Staff to devote time to more productive work than
tabulating the monthly reports which our Lodges are now required to submit.

Transmit reports to the Grand Secretary in
such form and with such frequency as the
Grand Secretary shall detennine, but in no
event more frequently than monthly nor
less frequently than annually;

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
This proposed , enabling change in current codific~tion ?f Lodg~
Secretaries' duties is, designed to implement a system which will permit
Lodges to send required information to the Grand Lodge office by computer
modem, and which will more efficaciously save time at both ends of such
communicati ons.
We agree with the Grand Master and the Grand Secre~ary that any
change which is necessary or desirable to increase the efficiency of our
operations or decrease the expenses of both Lodges and Grand Lodge should
receive favorable consideration .
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that the
style of the reports or their frequency is not a matter of policy, but should be
left to the discretion of the Grand Secretary.
Recommenda tion APPROVED .

ACKNOWLEDGEM ENTS

th:

It would not be possible to name every person to whom I extend
appreciation for their assistance during th is Grand Lodge year. Some of
have already been mentioned earlier in this message. Many Lodge Masters
Grand Lodge Committeemen and Inspectors have contributed much this
as they do every year. This year's Grand Lodge Officers have ~
particularly loyal in their attendance and helpful to Donna and me as we have
travelled throughout the state.

It is my hope that this past year will have been but one of many_years
en we meet the challenge to plan for the futur~ of the Family . of
ry as we prepare ourselves to lead Masonry mto the Twenty-First
wh
Freemason ,
centuTY·

yea:

The Deputy Grand Master and Grand Wardens have been ready
always with their wise counsel and with their support of the many changes
which were undertaken this year. Our Grand Secretary has been a friend of
mine since the late 1960' s when he was Master of one of the Lodges assigned
to my father's Inspectoral District. John Cooper has been of tremendous
assistance this year. Larry Adamson, the Grand Marshal, and his wife Lynn
have balanced their own work and family commitments to serve this year.
They anticipated every need and were available whenever Donna or I needed
them.
The greatest sacrifice has been made by Donna, Stephanie and Robert,
my wife and our two children. Since August of 1991 when Donna and I
began work on our Junior Wardens' Retreats, Grand Lodge has been all
consuming. With few exceptions since then, I have worked twelve hours a
day, most every day of the week, either at my profession or on Grand Lodge
business. Donna and the children were always understanding. They were
always at Grand Lodge events when wives and families were included.
Without their love and support, I could not have completed this responsibility.
Words could never express my appreciation to you for the opportunity
which you have given me to serve as Grand Master. I have enjoyed this past
year more than you can ever know. The Grand Master is the chief executive
officer of a major organiz.ation. l have enjoyed the opportunity to make
changes in the operation of that organiz.ation this past year which I hope will
improve Masonry for the future.
However, the greatest opportunity afforded any man as Grand Master
is the opportunity to express a vision. l have enjoyed this opportunity as
Grand Master more than any other. I have expressed this vision in my
writings. I have expressed this vision in the more than eighty addresses which
I have made this year, in each of which I have attempted to address something
different from any other speech. I have spoken on the future of our society,
including our system of government and public education . I have addressed
ethics. Most importantly, I have addressed the future of Freemasonry, as
expressed in the theme for th is Grand Lodge year: Masonry for the TwentyFirst Century.

231

. STEPHEN DOAN
ter of Masons in California

REMARKS AFTER INSTALLA TION

Grand Lodge Officers
Past Grand Masters
Distinguished Visitors and Guests
Members of the Grand Lodge
Ladies, Gentlemen, my brethren -"The Challenge of Change -- The Rewards of Renewal"

c

Deficit: A deficit is somewhat difficult to explain and understand.
"A deficit is what you have when you haven ' t as much as you had
when you had nothing."

We are now, in the year 1993, a Masonic Grand Lodge with just over
125,000 members belonging to 470 lodges located in or near every city, town,
and community in the State of California.
We are rightfully proud of our glorious past, equal ly proud of our
present and look with confidence to the future.
It has always been ou r practice over the past 143 years of this Grand
Lodge to begin anew at the conclusion of each Annual Communicat ion. So
it is that we are gathered together this afternoon, in this place, to install the
officers who w ill lead this Grand Lodge for the next twelve months. And to
consider our future.
Each of your· Grand Lodge Officers are committed to the service of
this Grand Lodge and its constituent lodges and members.
Most vo luntary organizations tend to reflect the society from which
they draw their support. Freemasonry is no exception. As the principles,
goals, objectives, and programs of our fraternity came to be considered by
society to be irrelevant we suffered a decline in active membership and in
member participation. Every similar institution encountered the same decline.
The reason is rather obvious, society changed.
The external or societal force during the period of the mid-60's to
what may well be the early to mid-90's was and is a self-centered , ME
generation. "If it feels good ...just do it." "Have it all...now.", "Free speech
for me ... but not for you." And, lest we forget, "Ent itlements!" was the cry of
the day -- little was heard or is about responsibiliti es and duty! We do hear
a lot about victims.
Over a 25 to 30 year period of our country's history, we created a
society that rewarded cleverness rather than honesty and ethical behavior. .. a
generation of celebrities, not heroes. Where family values were devalued and
television "sit-corns" reduced the American family to a joke with canned

260

261

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

laughter. It became and still is a world where you have to rea ll y loQ)s, and
look hard, to find an honest man.

~s they seek to serve others rather than self...the Masonic Lodge in each city,

We are all familiar with the story of Diogenes ...who, as you will
recall, was looking for an honest man, carrying a lantern at night to continue
the search. He was asked whether he was having any luck. Diogenes replied
'
"Oh, not too bad, 1 still have my lantern."
Perhaps you have also heard the story about the mother who was
overly protective of her children. If a child coughed once, it was TB. A
headache meant nothing less than a tumor. And one lie, and her child was
destined for Congress.
Wh at a sad state of affairs and one which sho uld mobilize all of us
to demand of our fellow citizens that they too exercise their responsibilities
and perform their duties as citizens as required for all of us who live in a free
society.
I think that you will agree with me that there are early signs of a
revival in America. A revival based upon time-tested and time-proven moral
and ethical standards. And with that revival or renewal will most surely come
a revival and renewal of Freemasonry -- if we are ready -- and we will be!
Freemasonry has always been unique for ...our hope and our optimism
are centered upon th e firm foundation of our Fraternity and its principles:
Brotherly Love ... Relief...Truth
Fatherhood of God ... Brotherhood of Man
Moral and Ethical Teachings
Fellowship, Fun, and Family
and the Knowledge that --

fright from wrong, as they seek to strengthen personal and family values and

town and community will come into its own and will once again return to its
traditional role.
For what will be sought is what we have always offered ...
Moral and ethical teachings centered upon the principles of
Brotherly Love ... Relief...Truth ... Brotherhood of Man
But here is a caveat! There always is!
We must...absolutely must...be a 9lli!li!Y organization. Quality must
be ingrained .. .qu al ity must be our culture. We must do everything better. .. the
best is none too good.
And we must treat our members and each other with a full measure
of brotherly love and fraternal affection as we carry o n the work of
Freemasonry.
The membership program of the Masonic R enewal Committee is the
keystone of my year as Grand Master. It is both membership centered and
The heart of this program is the ...T.L.C . of
membership driven .
them, how to get them involved a nd how to keep
attract
to
how
members ...
them invo lved and active. I hope the Masters, officers and members of our
lodges will give the program a fair chance. I assure them that it will give
them new insights into their members and how to meet member needs -thereby allowing them to gain members and member' s full support,
invo lvement and commitment.

We exist and prosper only in a Free Society where Responsibilities
and duties come first.

1 firmly believe that something great and wonderful and purely
extern al will never appear and solve our membersh ip and leadership problems.
The solutions are internal and require that we focus our full , undivided
attention upon our problems, and then discipline o ur efforts to solve them
through change, renewal, and quality-centered programs.

The former Chairman of the Board of Ford, Donald Peterson,
observed for corporations and all organizations what was needed for the years
ahead :

It has been said that success depends on -- not what we do but how
we do it. Our way of addressing our members and their needs must have
everything to do with quality and excellence.

"Those enterprises that don ' t adopt a qual ity c ulture simply are not
go ing to succeed ... " In the word of a recent Grand Master:

When we talk about membership renewal, we are reall y talking about
paying attention to our members in a special way ... abou t making every one of
them feel important, and about meeting their needs and thus supporting them
in meeting the needs of their families.

We must both renew interest and seek excellence.
As Americans return to moral and ethical standards, as they search for
fellowship and fun, coupled with a support system based on a strict separation

You know that everything each of us does relates to our personal
belief system . That is why you are here today! That is why I am here today!

The membership program will guide you and provide every tool
needed to involve our members in the great and good work of the Fraternity.
I trust that all of the delegates were able to visit the Lodge Resources
Development Committee's booth on "G" floor and that you have studied the
full page article in the latest issue of the California Freemason on the
Membership Program.

of the famous William Jennings Bryant (1860-1925). I suspect that either one
or both of my parents were impressed by his record as a U.S. Congressman,
as Secretary of State, as author of the "Silver Plank", and as a three-time
candidate for President. He joined the Freemasons at the age of 42 in
Nebraska and remained a member until his death in 1925.

The membership program requires discipline and hard work ...
everything worthwhile in this world always does. But if you are willing to
make things better for your lodge, it will provide every possible aid and
assistance you require. Bob Kulick, Chairman and the 20 Committeemen of
the Lodge Resources Development Committee are also ready to support your
efforts throughout this new Grand Lodge year. Please call on them for
whatever assistance or support you may need. Make them your partner in the
renewal effort.
The membership program is designed to assist you in rebuilding and
restructuring your lodge's approach to its members ... present and future.
Modem America has given discipline a bad rap. It is not fashionable
to be a disciplined person or be disciplined in how we deal with each other.
The membership program will encourage discipline with regard to how you
CARE for and about your members, their wives, and families.
Two Final Thoughts
First, as you approach the renewal effort in your lodge -Put to rest any conflict you may have between Ritual and Administrative
duties. Both are equally important.
There is an Amish proverb which says it as well as it can be said -"When you are making vegetable soup, you don't
ask whether the peas or carrots are more important."
have every confidence in the Grand Lecturer and the Ritual
Committee. They will renew the ritual when and as needed with quality the
only measure of success.
Second, be willing to challenge and even disturb the status-quo when
it becomes necessary -- and during 1994 please join with me as we all meet
the "Challenge of Change -- and enjoy The Rewards of Renewal."
1 would like to end this message on a personal note. My parents gave
me an unusual middle name -- Jennings -- and a set of initials to match those

263

1 commend to each of you for thoughtful consideration and appropriate action
th is quotation from the writings of William Jennings Bryant (WJB):
"... destiny is no matter of change, it is a matter of choice. It is not a
thing to be waited for, it is a thing to be achieved."
May each of us make the right choices and achieve our destiny!

REPORT OF THE GRAND TREASURER

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
The Grand Treasurer is charged with the responsibility of reporting
to the members of this Grand Lodge on the financial condition of Grand Lodge
and its entities, which include the Masonic Homes of California, the California
Masonic Memorial Temple, the California Masonic Foundation, and the Nob
Hill Masonic Management, Inc. (Please refer to the opinion letters attached
hereto by Deloitte & Touche.)

APPENDIX D

The reports and comments of the Grand Treasurer are based on the
official examinations and statements of Deloitte & Touche, Certified Public
Accountants of San Francisco, whose reports are an integral part of the Grand
Treasurer's Report. Their audits cover the years most recently ended and
contain a complete record of income and expenses for the period. This year,
the California Masonic Foundation Board of Trustees has elected to forgo an
audit because of the cost and limited risk.
The delegates to the Annual Communication are, in effect, the
stockholders of the entities of Grand Lodge and you are encouraged, and it is
recommended, that you read and review this report. Your observations are
appreciated.
Changes in economic conditions, especially lower rates of return on
investments are having a profound impact on the income of the
income
fixed
Grand Lodge and its entities. It becomes ever more important that California
Masons continue their generous support of the Masonic Homes of California,
the Homes Endowment Fund, and the California Masonic Foundation. In
today's economic environment, it is imperative that we all continue that
financial support.
In 1992, the Grand Lodge changed its fiscal year from June 30th to
October 3 lst to match the Grand Master's term. Therefore, our audited
statement of the Grand Lodge is for the period ending October, I 992.
In January of this year, Mr. Douglas A. Scott, a CPA, joined our staff
Mr. Scott, working with our veteran
as our Chief Financial Officer.
accounting staff, has enhanced our entire accounting function, bringing us
more timely and more useful reports.
Respectfully submitted,
Henry H.P. Wilkins, Grand Treasurer

317

REPORT OF THE GRAND SECRETARY

To the Most Worshipful Grand l odge, F& A.M. of California:
My Brethren:

APPENDIX E

Once again 1t 1s my pleasure to greet you as you attend the 144th
Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons of
California. As your Grand Secretary I am pleased to welcome you to the
California Masonic Memorial Temple, and to the Grand Lodge Office,
headquarters for the Grand Lodge of California since 1958. Members of this
Grand Lodge have gathered in this auditorium to decide some of the great
issues of the day, and decade after decade we have seen Freemasonry governed
by delegates from our lodges in this splendid auditorium. r hope that you will
take some time between sessions to visit your Grand Lodge Office on the third
floor, as well as the Library and Museum on the second floor. Your Grand
Lodge employees will be pleased to welcome you, and to make you feel at
home in "your" office. For it is truly that. The Grand Lodge Office is a
service agency for the lodges of this jurisdiction, as well as the headquarters
for the Grand Lodge of California itself.
As of June 30 of this year we have 128,060 members, in 470 lodges.
As in the past, the Grand Lodge has seen a decline in both the total number
of members of our constituent lodges, and in the number of lodges eligible to
attend. The consolidation of lodges continues, as does the overall decline in
membership. However, during the period of July I, 1992 through June 30,
1993, our lodges initiated 1,707 new Entered Apprentice Masons. These men
are now brothers amongst us, and have added their strength to our ranks.
They sought the Light of Masonry this past year because they saw something
worthwhile in the Fraternity. In my humble opinion, what they saw in our
lodges were Masons who lived the teachings of our Ancient Craft in such a
manner that these new Entered Apprentices asked to become Masons. That
vote of confidence in our Craft is perhaps more important in the long run than
The majority of our current
mere statistics of overall membership.
membership joined the Fraternity during the 1940 's and 1950's, when being
a Mason was much more of an accepted thing to do. Nothing should be taken
away from those who filled our lodges during these two decades as young
Entered Apprentice Masons, because they were, and are, just as enthusiastic
as our new Entered Apprentices are today. However, it does take some special
conviction, some special willingness to be different from the usual crowd
today, to ask for a petition and to become a brother amongst us. And so we
honor those who have been our long time members, as we specially honor
those who have newly chosen this Fraternity as Entered Apprentice Masons

PROCEEDfNGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

this past year. As our past is glorious, so must our future be, as long as men
seek the Light of Masonry, however few or however many their numbers.

Consolidation of Lodges

318

The Grand Lodge Office has continued to look for ways to reduce its
budget and to provide more services on a more cost-effective basis. This year
we were able to complete the rebuilding of the Membership Computer System,
and reload the Membership Database with the assistance of the secretaries of
our lodges who supplied the correct information. We also were able to
complete the networking of the entire office, and to develop an efficient
"Electronic Mail" system. We also introduced an "800" number to assist our
lodges in contacting the Grand Lodge Office, and are now expanding the use
of our Electronic Bulletin Board to provide timely information to our
increasingly computer-literate membership and lodges. We also have begun
the refurbishing of the Grand Lodge Office space, thanks to assistance from
the California Masonic Memorial Temple and the Nob Hill Masonic
Management Corporation, so that the Headquarters of our Fraternity in
California reflects a quality image to the public.
My thanks goes to all our staff members in the Grand Lodge Office
who have worked so hard for all of you. We are your representatives on a
day-to-day basis for hundreds of visitors to your Grand Lodge Office, and we
work hard to deserve your support and approval.
The balance of my report consists of lists and tables of essential
information about the Grand Lodge of California. This information records the
day-to-day activities of the lodges in our jurisdiction during the past year. We
hope that it also tells the story of Masonic activity in a condensed form,
Masonic activity that represents the life story of the lodges of the Grand Lodge
of California, and their members during 1992/1993.
Respectfully submitted,
John L. Cooper III, PM, Grand Secretary

REPORT OF THE GRAND LECTURER
Most Worshipful Brethren :
Another year has passed and time to present to you this annual report.
As required by our statutes, all of the Ritual to its minutest detail was
reviewed throughout the entire jurisdiction - conferences were held in each
division where each degree, lecture and candidates lectures was exemplified
by the Inspectors in an impressive manner. We are both fortunate and
appreciative of the servi ces of these dedicated servants of our craft.

APPENDIX F

As in prior years, seminars were conducted at randomly selected
These seminars afforded us the
locations throughout the jurisdiction.
opportunity to meet the brethren on a one-on-one basis to review and discuss
ritual and to create a closer relationship with the lodges. The program
continues to be well received and must be continued.
As we travelled extensively from one end of the jurisdiction to the
other conducting seminars and participating in and witnessing various
ceremonies, we were impressed with the enthusiasm and the tenacity of the
many "small" lodges struggling to maintain their identity in their respective
communities. We laud them for their efforts. Yet far too many lodges found
it necessary to consolidate and many more are now tottering on the brink of
extinction for lack of interested or qualified brethren who are willing to serve
as Officers.
Earlier this year, along with other Grand Lodge Officers, I had
occasion to visit Maya Lodge No. 793 to witness and hear the ritual performed
in the Spanish language officially for the first time, and while I do not
understand the language, I could follow to some degree the words, format and
rhythm of the work. I was delightfully impressed. "Mi Hermanos", please
accept our heartiest congratulations for all your efforts to bring your "dream"
into fruition.
At the outset of this Grand Lodge year, because of loss of membership
and lodge consolidations, the Executive Committee, after much deliberation,
found it necessary to "shrink" the number of divisions from six to four regretfully a change of this magnitude emotionally impacts someone, or a
group of individuals, or a closely "knitted" district. As a result many good
inspectors and two outstanding Assistant Grand Lecturers had to leave.
Hopefull y, time will heal these disappointments. To these Inspectors and
Assistant Grand Lecturers who have left our ranks we thank you most
sincerely for your time and talents.

348

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

I close this report with my thanks to all those who have given so
unselfishly of their time and talents to the furtherance of Masonry in this
jurisdiction - to the Inspectors both fonner and present, for their ever-willing
support; to our Grand Secretary and his able staff, who always seem to do the
impossible. To the Grand Lodge Officers who have acquitted themselves so
ably; to our Grand Master for his support and understanding; to my colleagues
of this ritual Committee the very able Stewards of the Ritual, my sincerest
"Thank you." I could not have this without you.
Respectfully submitted,
Ulysses G. Patropulos
Grand Lecturer

All right, let's bring that up to today.
Our Grand Master says we need better leadership, we need meetings
that will be so meaningful, so interesting, so vital, that our members, more and

Another reference from the Bible is a favorite of mine: "God is our

The operative mason makes certain that his stones or bric~s- are stron_g
and accurately cut. He uses his level, square, and plumb to be positive that his
wall is true and enduring. He may be making a house, a cathedral. or maybe
even a schoolhouse. He knows it will stand for a long time, centuries in some
instances.
We as speculative Masons are building our own individual temples,
our true quality of leadership, certain that it will be representative of the
teachings of our great fraternity: brotherly love, relief and truth .

So, it would appear that Freemasonry is in trouble. It's teachings
haven't changed, but in many instances the manner in which those teachings
are transmitted have changed with the times and will change some more when
we are ready for them. But the fundamental attraction and blessings are still
with us and are still needed by mankind. So let's put our thinking caps on,
listen for God's direction, and go forward with confidence, detennination and
joy.
Donald Douglas once said: "It's a hard rule of life, and I believe a
healthy one, that no great plan is ever carried out without meeting and
overcoming endless obstacles that come up to try the skill of man's hand, the
qualities of his courage and the endurance of his faith ."
So when we realize that the "qualities of his courage and the
endurance of his faith" directly come from God and God is an ever-ready help
in trouble, we can see the way open up and those fresh ideas which are needed
will come.

of how you can demonstrate the leadership skills you have and can manifest,
but this ~the time to get all the doubts out of the way, and listen, yes. listen
to God' s assurance that He is at hand and can lead you onto great
achievements.
We all recognize the great strides which have come in this arena
through the Wardens' Retreats. They are a magnificent help and undoubtedly
are giving many a greater degree of confidence in their ability to measure up

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON MEMORIAL SERVICE
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

.
Obviously, _a good leader would recognize the necessity of instructing
his fellow officers in matters which might not be covered by the Inspectors.
He would diplomatically guide them into the direction he has decided upon.

As we assemble today, it is fitting that we remember our brethren who
have preceded is on our eternal quest of life.

Humility, perhaps, is one of the hardest character traits for a true
leader to accept, but it really is one of the most important. Arrogance,
pomposity, pride, or vanity will never win the cooperation of your brothers.

We are reminded of the Master Teacher's words relayed to us by Saint
John that only those who are "faithful unto death" will "receive the crown of
life".

Another attitude which is all-too-common and restricting when some
progressive step is being contemplated, is to have someone exclaim: "But, it's
never been done that way before!" What an unvisionary point of view r What
a stumbling block to progress!

We are assembled here in this great Hall of memories to give honor
and tribute to our faithful, departed brethren. Our words can never do justice
to their lives of service and devotion nor can our hearts express enough thanks
for that dedication and Jove which they have shared.

Becoming a better leader depends upon whether one is willing to
study, to learn. to grow, to face his task, to work patiently and persistently.
There is no substitute for this.

They have used their Trowel well and have spread the mortar of true
brotherhood faithfully. Now, they have laid their earthly implements aside and
gone from earthly labor to eternal refreshment.

Yes, Steve is right, Freemasonry does need better leadership. Are we
all ready to accept the challenge and even if we doubt our own ability at this
particular time, realize that each one can build his own ladder to success?
Remember, success is a ladder we cannot climb so long as we keep our hands
in our pockets.

We come to pay them tribute an give our thanks to God for their
leadership and example of faithfulness.

Let's reflect on Moses. When God called on him to lead the Israelites
out of bondage in Egypt, Moses doubted his ability to perform such a gigantic
task . God assured him that He would be with him and told him exactly what
to do, what to say to Pharaoh, and how to prepare the Israelites for the
journey. He gained confidence in his ability to perform, he trusted God's
promise of support, and they undertook that 40-year trek through the
wilderness to the Promised Land.
Lead on to victory in the Twenty-first Century starting now!

A recent song writer has penned the words, "May all who come
behind us find us faithful."
It is for us, the living, to remember that we are following the path that
has led is up the winding staircase by faith and in the footsteps of those who
have gone this way before us. They have followed the light, they have
finished the course and, we trust, they have kept the faith.
It was R :. W :. Raymond who wrote:
"Crowned, Son of God! Behold They friend Departs from us, to bide
with Thee, Trusting Thy Word, that to the end Where'er Thou art,
Thine own sha ll be.
And by Thy promise sure, we know That he on whom we leaned in
love Shall stand, as in thy Temple below, A pillar, in Thy Temple
above"
A pillar, always in its place, Steadfast and strong, and true in line,
Firm-founded in Thy changeless grace, High-towering to Thy full
design!

EULOGY
He nry C. C lausen, 33°, Past Grand Master
and Past Sovereign Grand Commander,
Supreme Council, A.A.S.R., Southern Jurisdiction, U.S.A.

The cold wind of winter swirls. The days shorten. The life so
abundant around us just a few months before has died, or has it? A seed
remains to sprout anew in spring. The human form decays and wastes away,
yet the eternal, the spirit of man lives forever. His life and death in this world
is but a prologue to the dawn of a new life in eternity. This world is but the
pathway of discovery to th e mansion of eternity where live the good servants
of our heavenly father.
Among them now is one more: our Illustrious Brother, Henry
Christian Clausen, 33°, Past Grand Master of Masons in California and Past
Sovereign Grand Commander of the Supreme Council, 33°, Ancient and
Accepted Scottish Rite of Freemasonry for the Southern Jurisdiction of the
United States of America who departed this earthly life on the morning of
Friday, December 4, 1992 at his home in San Francisco.
As he passed through our lives, Henry C. C lausen left many indelible
marks. His strength, his wisdom and his character inspired all who knew him.
He lifted our hearts. -He lightened our labors. He gave of his time and energy
endlessly to assist in our successes. As a Mason, as a lawyer, as a worker for
home, state, church or community, Brother Henry knew that tasks shared
become mutual triumphs.
Henry C lausen was born in San Francisco on June 30, 1905. He
attended the public schools. As a you ng boy, he sold newspapers on the
streets of San Francisco. The death of his father interrupted his high school
studies, whereupon he assumed the support of himself, his mother and s isters.
He completed h is high school, college and legal education at night, while
employed during the day. He was admitted to the bar in 1927 and embarked
upon a private law practice. His practice very quickly became one of
prominence.
He served a tenn as Assistant United States Attorney for the Northern
District of California. When the Golden Gate Bridge was under construction,
he served as general counsel for its chief engineer, Joseph 8. Strauss.

HENRY CHRISTIAN CLAUSEN
PAST GRAND MASTER
June 30, 1905 - December 4, 1992

On July 17, 1926, Henry married Irene McDonald. They had two
sons, Henry Jr. and Donald, and one daughter, Florian. On August 17, 1935,
he was remarried to Virginia Palmer, the mother of Henry's daughter, Karen.

360

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Henry had sixteen grandchildren: Bruce, Barry, Brett, Brian, Caroline and
Cathy Clausen, Henry Junior's children; Eric, Rene, Amber, Christian, Laurel
and Sarah Clausen, Donald 's children; Jeffrey and Eric Thede, Florian's
children; and Loren Freeman, Karen's son.

All of this is not to say that Henry's only interest was in service to
others. Not true ! He was an avid golfer. Many an unsuspecting golfer was
shorn like a Iamb, playing against Henry on his beloved Burning Tree Golf
Course in Washington, D.C., or at the San Francisco Golf Club.

Henry was raised to the Sublime Degree of Master Mason in Ingleside
Lodge No. 630 in San Francisco on May 31, 1935. He very quickly took an
active part in Lodge activities. He was elected Master of that Lodge in 1940.
Grand Master Wilson appointed him as the Grand Orator of the Grand Lodge
of California in which capacity he served until October, 1941. In preparation
for higher positions of leadership which were foreseen for him, he was
assigned service on many of the important committees of the California Grand
Lodge, culminating with his election as Junior Grand Warden in October,
1951. He progressed through the various elective offices, until his election and
installation on October 15, 1954 as the eighty-ninth Grand Master of Masons
in California.

At its Biennial Session on October 23, 1969, the Active Members of
the Supreme Council elected Henry Clausen as the sixteenth Sovereign Grand
Commander of Scottish Rite in the Southern Jurisdiction, thus commencing a
sixteen year tenure of inspired leadership, leadership which would mark Henry
Clausen as one of the greatest minds of this century, leadership which wou ld
elevate the prestige of the Supreme Council for the Southern Jurisdiction to
prominence and acclaim among Masons worldwide. As Sovereign Grand
Commander, he associated with Kings , Princes, and Presidents. His leadership
was acknowledged in every country of the World where Freemasonry exists.
He was a prolific author, and wrote many books on Freemasonry. His works
were a great source of inspiration and instruction to all members of the Craft.

Henry Clausen paralleled his Grand Lodge interest with activity in the
Ancient and Accepted Scottish Rite. He was coroneted a Thirty-Third Degree
Inspector General Honorary on October 23, 1953. The Supreme Council of
the Southern Jurisdiction soon took note of his extraordinary leadership
abilities. He was appointed a deputy for the Scottish Rite in California
succeeding Past Grand Master Francis V. Keesling. At the Biennial Session
of the Supreme Council held in Washington, D.C. in October, 1955, he was
elected an Active Member and designated Sovereign Grand Inspector General
for the State of California.

One of his proudest accomplishments was the establishment of
Childhood Language Disorders Clinics throughout the Southern Jurisdiction of
the Scottish Rite. At present, there are over one hundred Childhood Language
Disorders Clinics in operation . Thei r existence is due in great part to the
determination of Henry Clausen to spread this great work to every place where
there was a need.

During World War Two, Brother Clausen volunteered his services to
the United States, and was assigned to the Department of the Judge Advocate
General. He served in Washington, D.C. and overseas. He was appointed a
member of the special Presidential Appeal Board for Spy Trials and afterwards
served on the Army Pearl Harbor Board of Inquiry. In this assignment, his
work was so noteworthy that Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson appointed
him to chair the Secretary's investigation into the Pearl Harbor disaster,
pursuant to a joint resolution of the Congress of the United States.
Interestingly, Henry had just recently completed his final book, Pearl Harbor,
Final Judgment, an account of the events surrounding the attack on Pearl
Harbor. From all indications, this book will soon make its way to the best
seller list.
Perhaps his greatest service in civic affairs was on behalf of free
public education, of which he was an outspoken advocate. He championed
public schools, not only statewide, but nationally as well. He devoted his time
and talent without compensation to the protection of free public schools, and
to the protection of another source of our freedoms, the Constitution's
guarantee of our freedom of faith: the separation of Ch urch and State.

361

Most men leave footprints in sand, the marks of which are swept away
by the tide at night. ·Some men embed their footprints in clay which the sun
dries and preserves for a season or two. Henry Clausen left his footprints in
indestructible stone. They challenge us to follow where he lead. They
challenge us to open our minds. They challenge us to be of good courage.
They challenge us to study. Most importantly, they challenge us to look to the
future, to make the world a better place for all who shall follow us.

seeker of truth, always striving to improve himself, to be better than he was
before, seeking that perfection denied all of us at birth, that perfection for
which we strive but do not attain, until, as Joe did on November 5, 1992, we
pass from this imperfect to that all perfect, glorious world which follows.

Joseph R. Lenninger, Grand Tiler

R. Stephen Doan, Grand Master

Joseph Richard Lenninger was born on July 9, 1937 in Munich,
Germany. His family immigrated to America when Joe was a small child and
settled in Los Angeles. Joe attended public schools and graduated from
Fairfax High School. In 1963, he married his wife Barbara. Their sons,
Joseph Junior and Eric, are now twenty-seven and twenty-six years of age,
respectively.
Joe worked for Ralphs Markets for over thirty-seven years . At the
time of his death, he was a store director, responsible for managing the Ralphs
Market in Santa Clarita. Joe was active in the community, having been a
member and active in the committees of the Canyon Country Chamber of
Commerce.
Joe became a Mason in Reseda Lodge No. 666 and was its Master in
1977. He served Grand Lodge on the Masonic Widows Committee for four
years and was a member of the Public Schools Committee at the time of his
death. He was a Di strict Inspector from 1987 until recently.
Joe' s first Masonic office was as Tiler of his Lodge, a job Joe enjoyed,
as you might expect. Enjoyed? He enjoyed it because, as Joe once told me
he could thereby personally greet every man who came to Lodge. It w~
probably fitting that Joe's last Masonic office should also be as Tiler, the
Grand Tiler of the Grand Lodge of California.
If I were asked to draw a portrait of the ideal Master Mason, I do not
believe that I could find a better exemplar than Joe. Faithfulness marked
everything that Joe did. He was faithful to his wife and his sons. He was
faithful to his work, as evidenced by his thirty-seven years of service.
Joe was faithful to his Masonic obligations. He served with distinction
as a District Inspector and undertook his new responsibilities as Grand Tiler
with equal zeal. He was always willing to do whatever job might be asked of
him with enthusiasm and commitment.
Few men could hope to live a life more committed to brotherly love,
relief and truth than did Joe. I never heard Joe say a bad word about anyone.
He was tolerant of the views of others, even when he might disagree. He was
willing to give of himself to help those less fortunate. Joe was truthful and a

363

Whence did Joe's faithfulness spring? It sprang from the example of
another Master Mason. Joe' s father was a noted physician in Germany. Soon
after Joe was born, the Nazis came to the hospital and took Joe' s father away
for a few days. Why? Because Joe's father was a Freemason. Under similar
circumstances, there were German men of wealth, education and social
standing who renounced Freemasonry. Other men accepted the loss of
personal and intellectual freedoms which Masonry has championed throughout
the world to preserve material comforts. Joe' s father would not renounce
Freemasonry. Instead, he surrendered the material. He abandoned his career,
his wealth and his position to come to America. He abandoned his
possessions but not his honor; he was faithful to his beliefs.
Joe met adversity with that same faith . Men who have had the same
heart surgeries that Joe had often give up. Not Joe. He jogged daily. He
received the President's Council on Physical Fitness Award in 1990 and 1991.
He pursued his work. He pursued his Masonry. Knowing that his physical
condition might shorten his life, Joe lived his life to the fullest.
Joe was faithful to God in fulfilling His commandments. Joe lived by
truth. Joe lived by-his regard for his fellow creatures, by brotherly love and
charity. Joe set an ethical standard by which all of us who survive may
measure our lives.

GRAND ORATION
Frederick L. Sorsabal, Grand Orator

Prior to commencing this Grand Oration, may I say to you Most
Worshipful, on behalf of all the appointed Grand Lodge officers for 1992-93,
thank you for giving each of us a fantastic opportunity to serve our Grand
Lodge and the wonderful, dedicated Masons of California. This time of
service has been an opportunity for each of us to feel the real vibrance of our
great fraternity. It truly has been an exhilarating year, and we thank you for
allowing us to be part of it.

APPENDIX H

The theme for the 1992-93 Masonic year has been "Masonry in the
21st Century." Many ofyou probably are worried that because of the decrease
in the membership of your lodges, there will not be a Masonic Order in the
21st century. I now want you all to dream about the future and nurture those
dreams in Masonry. We must encourage the dreams of others -- don 't feel you
brighten up a room by leaving it. We in Masonry have a message of good
things -- great philosophies. Share this message with all those with whom you
come in contact. Remember that a broken clock is right twice-a-day. God has
given us the ability to share -- share our Masonic teachings of brotherly love,
relief, and truth. After this sharing, show how you can help the other person
rather than just yourself. You will have then fulfilled our dream. Give thanks
to God for the benefit to dream.
History is but the prologue for the future. Our Masonic history has
been phenomenal. From small groups of workmen primarily concerned with
preserving their status as highly-skilled craftsmen, it has evolved over the
centuries into a fraternal and philosophical society covering a major portion of
the earth. Our past is secure. Masonry in the United States had a silent but
large part in shaping this country, its fundamental life, and certainly its laws.
Would the American Revolution have been different if Washington and most
of his generals were not held together by that peculiar tie which Masons spin
and weave between men?
But, my brothers, what of the future? What of our dreams? Gillet has
said, "We are always looking to the future; the present does not satisfy us.
Our ideal, whatever it may be, lies further on." This is certainly true of
Masonry. The golden age is not in the past but in the future. Longfellow
said, "Look not mournfully to the past -- it comes not back again; wisely
improve the present -- it is thine; go forth to meet the shadowy future without
fear and with a manly heart." My brothers, this should be our determination.

Relief -- nothing need be said beyond the words of an eastern seer:
"When man will not help man, the end of the world has come."
By "relief" we mean the urgent necessities of humanity in time of woe
or disaster, which may, any day, devastate any part of our world, helping not
only our brethren in dire plight but all who are made helpless. An unknown
poet puts it vividly:
"Men in the street and mart
felt the same kinship of the human heart
that makes them, in face of flame and flood,
rise to the meaning of true brotherhood."
By "truth" I mean the important things in the service of which the
modem Masonic craft is enlisted and devoted. First, Free Masonry stands for
those great freedoms of the mind by which men arrive at the truth. Our craft
is utterly committed to the principle of freedom of thought -- unhampered by
political or religious dictation -- the right, and yes, the duty of man to seek
everywhere and in every way the truth by which no man is injured, but by
which we have the only basis for freedom and faith. Second, we mean by
truth our devotion to the enterprise of public education without which
democratic societies cannot permanently endure. By letting in the light all the
way, we will be successful in driving ignorance, intolerance, superstition, and
despotism off the face of the earth.
Now, let's get back to the future -- the future of Masonry depends
upon many things. Today, we live in a technological age. Scientific research
has given us vast knowledge in a short time. These strides in science have
brought us prosperity beyond our wildest dreams, even though we are
presently in a recession. While we have seen changes in our society, some of
which we don ' t like, our population has a fluidity and mobility which is
without precedent. Youth is again full of unrest. Protests are increasing in
number, and violence ri ses like an ugly serpent.
All of these changes require different uses of our talents, our time,
ourselves, and the ways in which we are family members. Either we change
and adapt ourselves to these changing times, or we die. The same is true of
our great philosophical order. No one is asking Masonry to change -- only
that it adapt to today's and tomorrow's world. We must change our approach

Some of you say "if it ain't broke, don't fix it." Doesn ' t this really
mean we are do ing the same thing over and over again? The U.S. Auto
Industry is a prime example of this approach. Look how long it took them to
realize that the auto-buying public had shifted from gac; guzzlers to little cars.
The foreign auto manufacturers had seen this shift and adapted early on.
Masonry must adapt to these shifts also. Remember, I did not use the word
"change".
The futu re of Masonry depends upon leadership -- your leadership -your direct ion . We must have good leaders at the grass roots of our order.
We need men full of energy, vision, and a willingness to work. We need a
base o f younger men who speak out and are not "put in their place" by older
Masons. Young men who know that one of our ancient landmarks is not "we
can't do it, because it has never been done that way." We need to focus our
attention upon the young men in our lodges by giving them increased Masonic
knowledge an d an Qpportunity to become participants and not mere spectators.
This is the work, and should be the goal, of every leader. Any organization
is but th e lengthened shadow of its leaders. Its success or failure depends
almost entirely upon what they do. If they start out with the command, "Come
on, men", success is sure; however, if the command is, "Go on, men!", the
organization will be assured of total failure.
Our leaders will prov ide the necessary goals and programs for our
lodges t o attract and retain its members. We should remember to make our
meetings more than just boring repetition of our ritual or degrees. Good lodge
leaders will provide an avenue for the family to enjoy our Masonic heritage.
Bring ing non-Masons into those activities could well provide a cadre of
potential members. Quality leadership will provide the desire for members to
attend and also find the opportunity to provide for our families and our church
and/or social life. Begin by developing fellowship in your lodge. Remember,
you can 't shake hands with a clenched fist.
The future of Masonry depends also upon education. The necessary
education and instruction to our new members and officers is needed to
understand the meaning of our very important Masonic lessons. Let us not be
like the small child who has learned to count to ten but cannot recogn ize .,.,iy

In our Masonic educational programs, are we giving too much
emphasis to a fixed course or routine, a repetition of forms or phrases, without

The supreme architect has given each of us three great gifts, some to
a greater degree and some to a lesser degree. The first gift is a span of time
to live out our lives during which we can decide to be selfish, grasping for
worldly possessions, or we may decide to have a genuine concern for our
neighbors. The latter requires a sharing of time. If we are to get the most out
of life, we must share our time and ourselves with others. The second great
gift is our talents or abilities. We differ in abilities. Some of us may only be
able to listen. Some of us may use our vocational skills to help our fellow
worker. And some may be called upon to lead. The last great gift is our
worldly possessions. Often we think of these only in terms of money.
However, to relieve the needs of others, we can use our money and our other
material possessions. If we employ our abilities, possessions, and time to help
others, we need not proclaim what we have done for the cause of good.

The future of Masonry also depends upon dedication and service -dedication to the point of faithfulness to the tenants of our fraternity, which
begins with faithfulness in attendance at the regular meetings of your lodge.
I know I am preaching to the choir, as most of you are faithful attenders. But
why aren't the other members of your lodge attending? Are your meetings
dull and boring?
Dedication to the fundamental principles of Free Masonry. Showing
and practicing these principles in our homes and our communities. Masonry,
we are told, strives to make good men into better men. It is my hope that as
Masons we try to practice the virtues and to display sound moral judgement,
not only within the lodge but outside it as well.
The fundamental principles of Masonry are the foundation of a healthy
society. Whenever the guidelines of society are bent, redirected, or removed
too far, then society tends to return to absolute standards which are proven.
As Masons, we must promote these fundamental principles! Each of us must
commit to make a difference. We must be reassured that every Mason
practices the virtues for which we subscribe and display a sound moral
judgement, not only within our lodges but outside as well. We must have a
genuine concern for our neighbors. We can no longer live within ourselves,
even though we may want to, remembering the phrase, "no man is an island,
entire of itself." We must have a genuine concern for our neighbors. This
requires a sharing of time.
By helping and sharing with others, we influence them. You will
continually influence through your words and actions. You are constantly

GRAND BIBLE BEARER'S MESSAGE
Ronald L. Koretz, Grand Bible Bearer
There is an oil painting hanging in the hallway of the Masonic Home
in Union City. It is a still life, painted by one of the former residents and
dedicated to the memory of her deceased son. She originally kept it in ber
room, and, after she passed on, the picture was put in storage. It lingered there
for years until it was recently found. It was repaired and redisplayed, allowing
a small portion of the world to enjoy it and to continue to remember both the
woman and her child, people who otherwise would have passed into oblivion.

APPENDIX I

I saw this picture when I visited the Home last August, and it caused me
to reflect on the specialness of every human life. It is easy to lose sight of the
fact that each person around us uniquely interprets the world in ways that are
just as important to him or her as your or my unique interpretations are to you
or me. This morning, I would like to reflect on what happens when an
individual specialness ceases to exist.
A few years ago, a movie came out called Enemy Mine. Dennis Quaid
portrayed an earthman, and Louis Gossett, Jr., a Drac, an alien from another
civilization. The two races were at war, and these two characters found
themselves stranded together on a barren planet. The movie dealt with the
ability of members of different races to be able to find mutual interests and
respect, and even to establish a bond of love and concern. As the plot
develops, we find out that a Drac cannot become a member of his society until
he has learned and recited his entire lineage, and the names of all of his
ancestors are thus passed on from generation to generation, so no forebear is
The Drac teaches his lineage to the earthman, and
ever forgotten .
subsequently dies.
The earthman ultimately becomes the surrogate father to the Drac's
son, to pass on the genealogic history. I mention this film to contrast the Drac
practice to our own; in our society, identities qui ckly disappear after people
die, and anonymity becomes our destiny.
How many times have you looked at the newspaper obituary column and
scanned over a host of unknown names looking for one with which you are
familiar? Have you ever paused to reflect on any of the unfamiliar ones or
read his or her brief biography to see what that life was all about? Each one
of those names was a person whose life was meaningful, not only for him or
her, but also for family and friends. They all once were children who played,
laughed, and cried. Each had desires and aspirations which may or may not
have been realized. They no doubt touched many other lives, sometimes for
better, occasionally for worse.

386

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Like that woman at the Home, some people leave behind a material token
of their presence. This memorial may be very simple, such as a painting, or
it may be much more complex, especially if the individual has a large fortune
to expend in this undertaking. In the latter case, the memorial may even be
a gross misrepresentation of who that person really was. Andrew Carnegie did
not always behave in the noble fashion that his Carnegie charities may suggest.
More recently, we have the Milken Foundation, which, a century from now,
may cause the world to consider Michael Milken a great philanthropist and
forget that all of its funding came from the scandalous and unethical behavior
of a confidence man who never contributed anything of value and really has
no claim on a favorable place in history.
More often people leave behind only intangible, hazy memories of what
they said or did. A generation later, these are incorporated into, and diluted
by, the mores and behaviors of society. In fact, these contributions can often
no longer even be traced back to that one person. But the good deeds of
individuals are far more important to the survival of a society than any
physical monument.
Let me read to you an obituary notice from the Los Angeles Times of
April 21, 1993:
"McCuish, John Angus passed away April 16, 1993; was born in
Dawson, Yukon Territory, Canada. He is survived by his wife,
Virginia and his son, Rick. A 44-year resident of Culver City/ West
Los Angeles, he was an active member of the Triangle-Palms Masonic
Lodge (Master in 1964), Eastern Star, Rainbow Girls, Staff Club, and
Masonic Service Bureau. He was a recipient of the Hiram Award, and
in 1991 he was awarded his fifty-year Masonic Membership Pin. He
was with the Army in the Philippines during World War II. John will
certainly be missed."
Those of us who are Masons may have some notion of the value of a
Hiram Award and of being a Past Master, although a Fifty-Year Pin is more
a divine decision than a reflection of the work that one does. Nevertheless,
even a Mason could not begin to fathom who John Angus McCuish really was
from this brief description.
It was my good fortune to learn about this man from his friends, and I
would like to share some of his life with you. John did not simply serve with
the Army in the Philippines. He was trapped there as a civilian when the
Japanese invaded, and he spent 18 months behind the lines, living in the jungle
and sabotaging Japanese installations. He finally had to surrender himself
when his mother-in-law became too ill to continue to endure this primitive life
style and John could no longer carry her around on his back. John and his
wife survived the Bataan Death March, and, after the war, they settled in

387

southern California.
As is apparent, John became an active Mason and a productive citizen who
never made any claim to becoming a footnote in a history book. He dedicated
He played Santa Claus for
most of his 76 years to helping others.
long that he wore out three
so
disadvantaged children every Christmas for
Santa suits in the process. He donated countless hours to the Masonic Service
Bureau. Every morning, for years, he went to a blind woman's house and took
her for a walk. For years, he also o versaw the business affairs of another
elderly woman with Alzheimer's Disease whom fate had put in his path.
Outside of his small circle of friends, no one knew that John did these things,
and John never made a big deal out of them. Through John's terminal illness,
he always had a chuckle in his voice and a warm regard and concern for
others.
As I said, it was my good fortune to hear his story. It was my misfortune
that I was never able to meet this man myself and be able to thank him
personally for his contributions. In fact, my talk today is stimulated in part by
a belief that such people deserve societal immortalization far more than do
Andrew Carnegie or Michael Milken.
I ran across an anonymous quote that is quite applicable to John, and
which I would like to share with you. Before doing so, I cannot help but
notice that the fact that it is anonymous makes the point of how we can be
touched by people we do not even know. The quote is: "What you do, what
you say, what you'are, may help others in ways you never know. Your
influence, like your shadow, extends where you may never be." John McCuish
never tried to influence most of us in any way, but he left us all with a great
inspiration.
When I was a youngster, my parents taught me that, if you borrow
something, you should always return it in better condition than that in which
you received it. Let all of us who can now remember John McCuish in 1993
silently thank him for returning the world in a better condition than he
received it in J916.

CARRY-OVER LEGISLATION

1992 ANNUAL COMMUNICATION
Grand Master Cazneaux's Recommendation No. 4
Amend CMC to Require Three "Black Balls"
For Rejection of a Candidate

APPENDIX J

It is my belief that all too often, potentially good applicants are being
rejected by virtue of a "black ball" vote cast by one biased, angry or
unreasonable member who has pennitted his personal feelings to interfere with
a dispassionate and realistic consideration of the contributions that the rejected
applicant could make to Masonry. O n several occasions this year I have been
notified by Brothers of this Grand Lodge of the rejection of candidates because
of obvious religious or racial reasons. However, the most serious incident
occurred when a Brother hid behind the ballot box and rejected a total of five
(5) candidates at two consecutive Stated Meetings just to get at the officers of
the Lodge. O ne of those candidates was a member of the City Council. It is
my thought, therefore, that thi s problem could be solved by eliminating thi s
"one man" control and requiring the negative vote to reject a candidate by a
realistic three or more "black balls" or by three or more members filing a
"person to person" objection to the Master of the Lodge prior to the day of the
vote.
Accordingly, it is my recommendation that our California Masonic
Code ( 1991 edition) be amended to provide that three or more brethren must
cast "Black Cubes" at the time of the ballot, or object in person to the Master
before ballot, to constitute rejection o f an applicant.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
In 1992, Grand Master Cazneaux recommended that the California
Masonic Code be amended to provide that three or more brethren must cast
"Black Cubes" at the time of the ballot, or object in person to the Master
before ballot to constitute rejection of an applicant.
Grand Master Cameaux stated that he believed that "all too often
potentially good applicants are being rejected by virtue o f a ' black ball' vote
cast by one angry or unreasonable member who has permitted his personal
feelings to interfere with a dispassionate and reali stic consideration of the
contributions that the rejected applicant could make to Masonry."
If this Recommendation is approved it would still permit one member
to cause the rejection of an applicant by making an objection to the Master.
If the objection is made prior to balloting or prior to initiation, the member

392

PROCEEDfNGS OF THE

need not state a reason and would remain anonymous.
In considering changing the requirement for a unanimous ballot, we
agree that there have been abuses of the process. However, it can also be said
that the requirement for a unanimous ballot has worked well in California for
more than 140 years. While changing this requirement might prevent an
occasional abuse of the process, it could also impose troublesome restrictions
upon those who have legitimate Masonic reasons for the rejection of an
applicant.

Had Resolution 92-10 merely authorized the establishment of Table

Our Masonic Law clearly states that the Ritual can be changed solely
for the purpose of returning it to what it has been in this jurisdiction from time
immemorial. Therefore, it is the opinion of this committee that modifying our
established ritual to develop a Table Lodge Ritual is contrary to our Law and
the policy of this Grand Lodge.
Your committee still believes that there is merit to having a Table
Lodge Ceremony and a future resolution to adopt a "ceremony" as opposed to
changing established ritual could receive favorable comment. Note however,
that there should be no requirement to open Lodge on any degree as a part of
the ceremony.
Resolution 92-10 is contrary to the policy, rules and regulations of this
Grand Lodge, and does not merit your approval.

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
Before discussing this Resolution, we need to make a small, but
important, distinction. Strictly speaking, a Table Lodge is a formal, tiled
Lodge meeting, often involving degree ritual, held around a dinner table. In
fact, in the early years of Masonry, the First Degree was conferred in such a
lodge. As our ritual work evolved, though it became apparent that our
purposes would be better served by conducing our degree ritual in the lodge
room and leaving the eating and drinking to another time and place.
This developed into the ceremony with which we are familiar in
California, the one involving a meal and a series of ceremonial toasts.
Although we commonly refer to it as a Table Lodge, it properly called a
Festive Board. We believe that this Resolution addresses this Festive Board.
With that distinction in mind, in order to conform to the wording of the
Resolution, we will continue to refer to it as a Table Lodge.

(1)

To formally open a Table Lodge on the First Degree, and

(2)

To prepare a specific ritual for use at a Table Lodge.

Table Lodge meetings are currently being held throughout the
jurisdiction so they obviously are permitted by our law. We have personal
knowledge of at least half a dozen. Although no two use exactly the same

395

A Table Lodge is a social event, not a lodge meeting, and should be
allowed to follow whatever form is most appropriate to its purpose. We see
no reason to impose a set ritual on a table Lodge, any more than we would a
Hiram A ward ceremony.
To insure that propriety is observed, we will
continue to require that the "ritual" part of every Table Lodge program be
approved by a member of the Committee on Ritual.
Your Committee on Ritual feels that both a formal opening of lodge,
and a prescribed ritual, would be counter-productive to the purpose of a Table
Lodge and recommends a "no" vote.
Resolution NOT ADOPTED.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to have the duties of the Grand
Secretary recodified, reorganized, modified and clarified.
We agree with the proponents of this Resolution that it is necessary
to be constantly alert to changes which are periodically necessary or desirable
in increasing the efficiency of our operations and which will assist in reducing
the cost and expense of operating Lodges and Grand Lodge.
We note also that, because of the complexity and broad
responsibilities with which the Grand Secretary is charged, they have consulted
extensively with the present Grand Secretary, immediate Past Grand Secretary
and members of the staff in the Grand Secretary's office respecting possible
recodification of the duties of the Grand Secretary. Concurrence was reached
with respect to the language of this Resolution.
Basic changes, additions, or deletions to the present codification have
been minimal.
The Grand Secretary expressed to our Committee no discomfort with
any of the job description duties outlined.
Your Committee agrees with the need for and the clarifying proposals
