In the event that the Master of a Lodge detennines that inclement
weather, including ice, snow, and flood conditions, existing on the
day established in the By-Laws of the Lodge for its Stated Meeting,
make~ it hazardous for members of the Lodge to attend the meeting,
he may, with the consent of the Inspector of the District to which the
Lodge is assigned, postpone the Stated Meeting to the same day of
the week next following the week scheduled for the Stated Meeting.
Upon such postponing, the Master shall notify, to the extent possible,
all members of the Lodge residing within 50 miles of the meeting
place of the Lodge.
Should a Stated Meeting be postponed, the business transacted at the
postponed Stated Meeting shall be limited to the reading of the
minutes of the last Stated and subsequent Special Meetings, action
thereon, payment of the invoices of the Lodge, and such other
business of an emergent nature as determined by the Master to require

§26040. UNIFORMED SERVICES RESIDENCE.
A member of any uniformed service of the United States, whose duty
station is at a facility or on a vessel having an officially designated
home port, may apply for and receive the degrees of Masonry in any
Lodge having jurisdiction of the location of such facility or home
port. If the member of any such uniformed service has not resided at
such facility or been attached to such vessel for at least six months
immediately preceding the date of his application, a dispensation from
the Inspector GraRe Mash!r is required. Uniformed Service of the
United States includes the U.S. Anny, the U.S. Navy and Marine
Corps, the U.S. Air Force, the U.S. Coast Guard, the U.S. Public
Health Service and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric
Administration.

Resolution No. 93-03
Make Fee For Life Membership
Automatic Upon Increase in Dues

1be proponents of this Resolution seek to eliminate the du~licate proce~ure of
ldopting a resolution to raise th~ dues and ~lso ad~ptmg a ~esolut10~ to
mcrease the minimum fee for a life membership. This R~so lut1on pro~1des
that, when the dues are raised, the minimum fee for the ltfe membership is
artomatically raised .in proportion.
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge F.& A.M. of California:
WHEREAS, Section 27020 of the California Masonic Code provides
that a Lodge may adopt a standing resolution for a life membership plan wit~
the minimum fee being in the same proportion to the Lodge dues as $250 ts
to$12, the $250 being the minimum fee for a life membership and the $12 the
minimum dues; and
WHEREAS, when a Lodge raises its dues and has a life membership
resolution in effect, the minimum fee for life memberships must also be raised
proponionately by a separate resolution; and
WHEREAS, many Lodges now overlook the need to adopt a separate
resolution to raise proportionately the minimum fee for life memberships when
the Lodge dues are raised.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Section 27020 of the
California Masonic Code be amended to add the following new sentence to the
end of the section:

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

408

When the annual dues of the Lodge are increased, the Lodge's
standing life membership resolution shall be deemed to have been
amended without further action of the Lodge to increase the dollar
amounts required for a life membership by the same percentage that
the Lodge dues have been increased.
Respectfully submitted,
H. Francis Lewis, PM No. 192
Andrew M. Smith, JW No. 191
Joel H. Springer Ill, PM No. 462
Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
TI1e proponents of this Resolution seek to eliminate the duplicate
procedure of adopting a resolution to raise the dues and also adopting a
resolution to increase the minimum fee for a life membership.
This resolution does not change either the minimum fees or the
minimum life membership fees or the proportion of one to the other.
A "No" vote will continue to require a separate resolution to amend
life membership dues every time lodge dues are increased.
A "Yes" vote will no longer require a separate resolution to amend life
membership dues as life membership dues will automatically be changed by
the same percentage as the annual dues are changed.
This Resolution is consistent with our general purposes and policies
and should simplify the process of changing dues.

§32030. NOT UNMASONIC CONDUCT.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to modify the procedure to be utilized
for Masonic trials to provide additional due process protections.

An act does not constitute a Masonic offense that neither violates this
Code nor involves a breach of faith or moral turpitude.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

WHEREAS, the Code Revision Committee has been created to study
designated portions of the California Masonic Code and to recommend
desirable changes, as appropriate, so as to have our law stay abreast of changes
in the world around us and the economy; and

The following do not constitute unmasonic conduct sufficient to
support the fifing of charges against a Mason :
A.

A business dispute not involving fraud or one that involves
the innocent inability to pay a just debt as promised;

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

410

B.

Political differences and acts in respect thereto;

C.

A possible conflict of interest arising from a transaction
between a Mason in his private capacity and his Lodge or
Temple Association where a full disclosure of the possible
conflict has been made prior to the transaction; or

D.

Actions allegedly violating the laws of other fraternal or
social organizations, including Masonic Organizations.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

411

If he the member was a multiple member in the other Jurisdiction, the
provisions of this Code relating to multiple memberships shall be
applicable.
§32060. CHARGES.

A charge or charges of unmasonic conduct may be preferred against
any member of a Lodge or any Mason residing within the Jurisdiction
of a Lodge by any Master Mason in good standing. All charges shall
be in writing over the signature of the accuser.

§32040. FOREIGN CONVICTION.

Whenever it appears by the record for conviction from another Grand
Jurisdiction, recognized by this Grand Lodge, that a member of one
of our Lodges, resident in that Jurisdiction, but not a multiple
member, has been suspended or expelled for unmasonic conduct in
that Jurisdiction while a resident thereof, it shall be the duty of Junior
Warden of his Lodge in this Jurisdiction to procure two certified
copies of the record of conviction, which shall include the charges or
complaint and the judgment or order of expulsion or suspension.
Notice in writing shall be given to the member by registered mail,
forwarded to his last known place of address, notifying him of the
record of conviction and requiring him within 60 days to elect in
writing, if he so desires, to have a trial on the charge of unmasonic
conduct based on the offense or offenses of which he was convicted
in the other Jurisdiction. The written election shall be filed with the
Secretary of his Lodge in this Jurisdiction.

Charges to be preferred upon the Grand Master, as Grand Master, or
a Master, as Master, shall be preferred as provided for elsewhere in
th is Code.
If facts, from any source, are brought to the attention of the Junior
Warden of a Lodge showing any Mason, over whom his Lodge has
jurisdiction, to be guilty of unmasonic conduct, and if, for the period
of 30 days following the bringing of such facts to his attention, no
Master Mason in good standing has preferred charges against such
Mason, then it shall become the official duty of the Junior Warden to
prefer the charges. He does so as a Master Mason and remains the
accuser throughout the proceedings.
If the Junior Warden is the accused, or the information is against the
Jun ior Warden, it shall be the official duty of the Senior Warden to
prefer such charges.
§32100. PRESENTATION OF CHARGES.

If the Mason elects to have a trial, it shall be the duty of the Junior
Warden of his Lodge to prefer charges based on the offense or
offenses of which he was convicted in the other Jurisdiction. The
proceedings shall be as provided for elsewhere in this Code, except
that the record of conviction in the other Jurisdiction shall be received
as prima facie evidence of his guilt.

§32240. AUTOMATIC DISSOLUTION OF COMMISSION.
A Commission is automatically dissolved and all future actions
attempted by it are void if it fails to meet on the date appointed by
the Master or Trial Master, or if it fails to meet on the adjourned date
and no further time is granted by the Trial Master. A Trial Master
shall have the power to grant reasonable continuances of the trial
upon request of either the accuser. the accused or a member of the
Trial Commission.

§32270. COUNSEL.
Any Master Mason in good standing may, at the request of the
accuser or the accused, appear as counsel to assist in the prosecution
or defense. No Lodge funds shall be used to pay the expenses of an
accused resulting from the trial. Such counsel may not, without
pennission of the accused, testify to facts disclosed to him by the
accused or discovered by him as a direct result of any such disclosure.
but may . be compelled to disclose any facts otherwise in his
knowledge.
Such counsel need not be any attorney at law. He may appear and
represent the accused if the latter cannot be present at the trial. The
summons served on the accused shall give notice of the provisions of
this section.

The accuser has the burden of proving the charges. The counsel for
the accuser has the duty of first presenting evidence to support the
charge, after which the counsel for the accused ~ may present
evidence in defense. The counsel for the accuser shall, at the
conclusion of the testimonyL have the right to first make an oral
summation. The counsel for the accused shall thereafter have the
right to make such a summation after which the counsel for the
accuser shall again have the right to make a final summation.

§32320. GENERAL PROCEDURE.

§323IO. TESTIMONY.
The Trial Master shall, at the request of either party, summon
witnesses who are Masons residing in the Jurisdiction of his Lodge to
appear and testify before the Commission.
Whenever the attendance of a witness who is a Mason and who
resides out of the Jurisdiction of the Lodge in which the trial is held
cannot be procured, his testimony may be taken. This testimony may
be taken before the Master of the Lodge within whose Jurisdiction he
resides and upon notice to the adverse party by the Master of the
Lodge in which the trial is held. His attendance may be compelled
by summons to testify. His testimony shall be written in full, signed
by him, and authenticated by the certificate of the Master before
whom it is taken, under the seal of the Lodge. Whenever the
testimony of a witness residing out of the State is desired, it shall be
taken upon interrogatories, agreed upon by the parties or settled by
the Trial Master.
If the testimony of witnesses who are not Masons is desired, such
witnesses may appear before the Commission and, after having been
put under oath or affirmation by some officer authorized by the laws
of the State wherein the testimony is taken to administer oaths, and
at such time and place and upon such notice to the adverse party as
shall be designated by the Trial Master.
Witnesses who are Master Masons in good standing shall testify upon
their honor as such, and all others shall testify under oath or
affirmation .
All oral testimony will be written in full by the Secretary or
stenographer, and c.e rtified as correct. A tape recording, properly
monitored and certified, may be used in place of a written record.
The documentary testimony, including interrogations, depositions and
affidavits, will be made part of the record by incorporating it, or a

419

Any Master Mason in good standing may be present at all times at a
Masonic trial. The Trial Master may, for good cause and in the
interest of justice, exclude any person whose presence is not necessary
to the actual conduct of the trial. Under no circumstances shall one
who is not a Master Mason be pennitted to be present at a Masonic
trial except for the limited purpose of testifying.
The Trial Master shall decide all questions o0.4aseAiG law which may
arise during a trial, decide what and how much testimony shall be
allowed and ensure that the trial is conducted in all respects with due
order and propriety.
The ordinary rules of evidence employed in the courts of the State of
California shall be followed as nearly as the circumstances permit.
Admissions or confessions of the accused that would be admissible in
the courts are admissible. The records and reporter's transcripts of
test imony made in the Courts in criminal cases, but not in civil cases,
properly authenticated, may be allowed in evidence. A witness shall
not be examined or any testimony taken without an opportunity given
the accuser and the accused to be present. Affidavits or depositions
taken withQut notice cannot be received. Technical objections as to
fonn shall not be permitted. Hearsay evidence is not admissible. The
certified record of final conviction in criminal proceedings is prima
facie evidence in a Masonic trial of guilt of the offense covered in the
criminal proceedings. The accused has a right. as a part of his
presentation,_ to introduce testimony which explains his actions and
has the further right to introduce evidence in extenuation and
mitigation.
No Mason, the accused or otherwise, against whom charges are
pending shall be required to be a witness or to testify to facts tending
to incriminate himself. Before such testimony is accepted, the Trial
Master must be satisfied that the accused has been advised of his right
to remain silent.
Where guilt is sought to be proven by one witness, great caution is to
be exercised.
Except in those cases wherein the parties have agreed that the trial be
conducted before the Trial Master alone, the....::i:A& Commissioners are
the sole judges of the facts proven, and the Trial Master shall have no
vote in decision of the case.

§32350. VERDICT.
After all testimony has been received in a trial , when before Trial
Commissioners, the Commissioners shall proceed without delay to
deliberate upon their verdict and sentence. During deliberations._ only
the Commissioners, the Trial Master, arui th• Sesretary may be
present. The Sesretary shall ha>1e Re vei10• iR the ~re&HeiAgs.
The guilt or innocence of the accused must be determined by the
Commissioners. Only those Commissioners who have participated in
the entire trial are entitled to participate in its deliberation and
findings. The Trial Master, being only the presiding officer, cannot
decide the facts or dismiss the case at the conclusion of the trial,
except in the case of a trial held before a Trial Master alone, where,
following a trial conducted in accordance with the procedure set forth
elsewhere in this Code for trials before a Commission, the Trial
Master alone shall determine the guilt or innocence of the accused and
shall decide on the penalty.

§32410. TRANSCRIPT OF RECORD.
After sufficient consultation and deliberation, a vote by ballot for
"guilty" or "not guilty" shall be taken upon each specification, and
each vote shall be recorded. A separate vote shall be taken upon the
charge of unmasonic conduct and be recorded, to determine if the
facts proven and found constitute a Masonic offense. A majority vote
of the original number of Commissioners elected is required to find
a verdict of guilty. If the Commissioners cannot find the accused
guilty of the charge or specification, they may delete any part which
they do not find against the accused, and return a verdict, or
judgment, for that portion of the specification or charge of which they
find the accused guilty.
Should the accused be found guilty of one or more of the
specifications, and of the charge of unmasonic conduct as originaily
charged, or as modified by their findings, the Commissioners will
proceed to vote upon the sentence. A majority of the original number
of Commissioners elected will be required to determine the sentence.
The vote shall be by ballot and the ballots shall have written on them
"aye" or "no." The first vote will be upon the question by the Trial
~ - "Shall the accused be expelled?" If there is not the required
majority vote for expulsion, the question will next be - "Shall the
accused be suspended?" If there is not the required majority vote for
suspension, the last question will be - "Shall the accused be
rep rim anded?"
All questions and votes shall be recorded, giving the number of votes,
both aye and no, upon each question.

In all cases, the Trial Master shall cause the Secretary to prepare a
transcript of the trial record.
The transcript shall consist of:
A.

A· copy of the proceedings of the Lodge at the Special
Meeting held for the election of Trial Commissioners, as
recorded in the minutes;

B.

A copy of the record of the proceedings before the
Commissioners as recorded in the minutes, including copies
of the charges, summons, notices, and Certificates of Service._
including the written record of testimony or tape recording;
and

C.

All original papers in the record.

The Trial Master shall carefully examine the transcript to see that it
is fairly and legibly written, and that it otherwise complies with this
Code, and shall endorse his approval.
As soon as possible after the next Stated Meeting, the Secretary shall
forward a copy of the original record, together with a certified copy
of the minutes relating to the announcement of the result of the trial
and a copy of the stenographic reporter's transcript or tape recording,
if any, to the Grand Secretary.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this resolution seek to modify the procedure for a
Masonic Trial and to provide due process protection.
The amendments to our California Masonic Code are housekeeping
in nature to hopefully clarify some of the procedures in Masonic Trials as well
as increase due process for the Mason to be tried and who is tried.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believes that
previous rules regarding Masonic Trials have been arn.biguous and n~t prepar~d
in language suitable for laymen . These changes will and do clanfy certain
matters and assure an accused Mason of due process during his trial.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

423

present a frugal program to assure the desired result.
We have a minor concern about one other point. Section 32030
would define conduct which is not unmasonic. Subsection A will provide that
among the conduct not constituting unmasonic conduct sufficient to support
the filing of charges against a Mason is a "business dispute ... that involves
the innocent inability to pay a just debt as promised." While we like the
sound of the words "innocent inability" we see this as a new source of
confusion in an already confused area. However, if it proves to be such it can
then be remedied.
Your Committee on Trial Review approves the proposals contained
in this Resolution and heartily recommends a "Yes" vote.
Resolution ADOPTED.

§33010. GRAND LODGE ACTION ON REVIEW.

All transcripts of trial records of individual Masons shall be
transmitted to the Grand Secretary and shall be forwarded by him to
the Committee on Trial Review. That Committee shall examine them
with such statements or arguments,_ in writing, if any, as may be
presented and shall report its recommendations at the next succeeding
Annual Communication. Grand Lodge may affinn, modify, or reverse
the judgment of the Lodge or may make such other order as it deems
proper. When a new trial is ordered or a judgment of reprimand is
affinned, the Grand Secretary shall send a copy of the opinion and
judgment of Grand Lodge to the Lodge as soon as possible.
Pending the report of the Committee on Trial Review, a Lodge may
not take action toward the modification of the penalty or upon the
restoration of a member under penalty of suspension.

§33080. LODGE RESTORATION OF SUSPENDED MASON.

A Lodge may, at any Stated Meeting taking place 90 days or more
after the sentence of suspension has been imposed and affirmed by
Grand Lodge. by the votes of two-thirds of the members present,
annul any such sentence of suspension and restore the Mason thus
suspended to all his Masonic rights and privileges. Notification of a
resolution for such restoration must have been given at the flFiliiEliag
Stated Meeting next preceding the meeting at which the vote is taken.
In case of restoration, the Secretary shall at once notify the restored
Brother and the Grand Secretary thereof. If the Mason suspended was
not a member of the Lodge by which he was suspended, the
application for restoration shall be refused unless the consent of the
Lodge in which membership was held, if it is in this Jurisdiction, is
given. The request for such consent shall lie over at least one Stated
Meeting.
Restoration need not be reviewed by Grand Lodge.

In essence it calls and designates transcripts of trial records of all

Report of the Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation:
The proponents of Resolution No. 93-06 propose two housekeeping
modifications of the California Masonic Code. They seek to increase the
dollar amount of expenditures on a local temple that would be free of statutory
oversight of the Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation, and they seek
to codify the long-standing practice of the committee's review of sales of
temple property.
Your Committee on Temple Properties and Taxation believes that the
Directors of a local Temple Association know best what is needed for the
maintenance of their property. The language of this Resolution prudently
reduces a restriction on the decision-making of local Temple Association
Directors. It recognizes the influence of monetary inflation on the cost of
routine repair projects, thereby making maintenance projects easier to achieve.
This Resolution reduces the burden of oversight on local lodges.
Also, the proponents ask that the current regulatory practice of the
committee' s review of property sales be added to the California Masonic Code.
Temple Associations and the committee have, for years, cooperated in the
review of such sales. Because specific language in our California Masonic
Code requires the committee's approval of the creation of a mortgage, should
a sale agreement create one.
This revie~ process, by real estate experts on the committee, seems
more important today as a way to reduce, to decrease risk to a lodge from an
unintentional mishandled sale. The recent growth of new liability laws allow
buyers to contest a sale after the fact if the proper disclosure of haz.ardous
materials are not made.
The continued cooperation between Temple
Associations and the committee will reduce future liabilities for lodges.
We recommend a "Yes" vote.

The proponents of this Resolution seek to permit Masonic Temple
Associations to invest in and own real property other than real property
suitable for use by a Masonic Lodge.
At the present time the California Masonic Code Section 22020 only
allows Temple Associations to own real estate which is suitable for the
occupancy by a Masonic Lodge.
This limitation has come about over the years because of financial
problems that Lodges have found themselves in due to imprudent investments.
As long ago as the 1928 Annual Communication, Past Grand Master William
Rhodes Hervey, reporting on behalf of the Committee on Policy and General
Purposes, said "Many Lodges have become seriously involved by reason of
unwise and imprudent investment of their funds in corporations organized to
build halls for the use of Lodges and, also, in many instances, to build
premises for rental purposes . If a Lodge is plunged into debt, or falls into
distress, or meets with disaster by reason of its building operations, it causes
a reflection, not only upon the Lodge and its membership, but upon Grand
t
Lodge and Masonry in general. The financial distress may be more poignan
far
to the Lodge than to Grand Lodge, but its influence and effect is felt
beyond the limits of the subordinate Lodge."
Admittedly, Past Grand Master Hervey was talking about new
building projects, not the acquisition of existing buildings. However, the same
,
comments apply. We must be cautious that we don 't acquire real property
of
whether through gifts and bequests or consolidations, that will be the cause
a Lodge plunging into debt. On the other hand, it could be detrimental to the
financial condition of a Temple Association and thus to a Lodge to have to sell
a valuable piece of rental property that it had received as a gift, merely
because it did not meet our California Masonic Code requirements.
During this same time period a Grand Lodge Building Committee was
established, requiring subordinate Lodges to submit the plans and proposed
final arrangements of future building projects for approval. Today that
Committee is know as the Grand Lodge Committee on Temple Properties and
Taxation. By including the requirement that all Lodge investments in real
property must have the specific approval of the Temple Properties and
Taxation Committee, any concerns along the lines previously stated should be
eliminated.
It has also been said that - The business of Masonry is Masonry not

business - and that we should not be permitted to won real property if it is not
to be used for Lodge purposes. Today, however, because of the escalation of
taxes, water and power expenses and general building expenses most Temple

432

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Associations have to be concerned with the operation of the building for profit
otherwise they would find themselves in the same conditions described by Past
Grand Master Hervey 65 years ago. In fact, some Lodges are already in dire
financial straits because their property has not been operated in a fiscally
prudent manner and some have even lost their buildings due to poor business
management. Obviously if a Temple Association owns real property, whether
or not it is used for Lodge purposes, then its members have to be concerned
with the operation of the property in a prudent business manner. The proposed
legislation does not change this fact.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents seek to permit the active solicitation of men to join
Masonry.
Freemasonry has several unique characteristics, one of . whic~
distinguish es it from all other fraternal organii.a~ions. That c~aractenst1c is
that every applicant must seek membership of his own free will and acco~d.
This is expressed in our unwritten law against active solicitation of potential

434

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

members. Unfortunately , this law has been carried to extremes by many of our
members who still regard Freemasonry as a secret organization and refuse to
talk about it, even to a prospective member.
Like all Masons today, the proponents of this Resolution are
concerned about the decline of membership in the fraternity. While this is a
concern of Freemasons throughout the world, membership decline is not
limited to Freemasonry. All organizations , including those which actively
solicit members by inviting them to join, are experiencing the same problems.
This would suggest that solicitation is not the answer to the membership
decline. In fact, the opposite conclusion could be drawn from statistics which
show that, among business leaders, membership in the Masonic fraternity far
exceeds membership in all other fraternal organizations.
There is a fine distinction between solicitation and providing
information to a prospective member. In the broadest sense, solicitation may
include many different means of persuasion, ranging from mild suggestions to intimidation - to the use of threats. In the extreme, it may tum a
prospective member away rather than attract him to the fraternity.
A prospect is more likely to become interested in Freemasonry if he
is impressed by the character and integrity of its members, is provided with
information, suitable answers to his questions and the experience of fellowship
which Freemasons claim to be one of their basic attributes. Having this
information, he may then make up his own mind whether he wishes to make
application. An invitation to attend a Masonic Information program or a
discussion with a prospective member about the purposes and practices of
Freemasonry do not constitute solicitation.
The Committee on Policy and General Purposes recognizes that some
members of the fraternity now use persuasive methods of enticing a
prospective member to complete his petition to receive the degrees of
Masonry. This is a violation of the solemn vows taken by every Mason. The
Committee is concerned that complete removal of the solicitation restriction
from the ritual may result in more widespread indiscriminate use of the
practice of solicitation in its worst forms.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

This resolution is a matter of policy - not ritual. The Committee on
Ritual makes a "no" recommendat ion.

Report of the Committee on Policy and General Purposes:
The proponents of this Resolution seek to amend the California
Masonic Code whereby a joint lodge installation of Lodge officers may take
place.
To become Master of a Lodge or for that matter any elected or
appointed office is an honor usually due to the fact of service to the Craft of
which the Master's election and installation is the culmination.
Your Committee on Policy and General Purposes believe that a joint
installation would take away from that crowning moment in a Master's life.
Two such moments in a single evening would diminish the honor and the
event for the Masters.
In addition there are practical problems.
Would there be two
Installing Officers, etc.?
There are not sufficient guidelines for your
Committee on Policy and General Purposes to support this Resolution.
Further there is a concern of the Committee that with the "or more
Lodges" in the proposed Resolution the joint installation include 3 or more
Lodges. This "mass production" would take the dignity and respect out of the
ceremony.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

437

singular for good reasons, and we should consider them before changing it.
The retiring Master is responsible for all issues concerning this
installation. This includes the form, the installing officers, the amount and
selection of music, etc. Although these decisions are usually deferred to the
incoming Master, the retiring Master still has the last word. We can easily
foresee disputes arising among the Masters, both retiring and incoming, with
lodges involved in joint installations.
The retiring Master should deem it an honor and privilege to install
his successor. Obviously, there can be only one Installing Officer. I know I
would deeply resent being deprived that opportunity because tradition dictates
a joint installation for my lodge. I also know that any Master who breaks with
tradition for personal reasons is going to subject himself to a lot of
discontented grumbling.
Rewriting the installation to accommodate two or more lodges will
indeed be difficult, particularly in delivering the floor work. For example, how
would 39 or 52 chairs be arranged in the semi-circle? How would you
distribute rods to, and escort to their seats, six or eight deacons? Many, if not
most, of the lodges have one fixed chair for each Warden and Master. How
would you seat three or four of them?
We rarely see an installation which is correct in every respect. We
hesitate to encourage a condition which can only lead to increased error and
confusion, and recommend a "no" vote.

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

WHEREAS, Masonry is full of symbolism and allegories used when
teaching our candidates to better understand those lectures presented to the
candidate during his lecture; and
WHEREAS, the importance of physical teaching aids has proven
invaluable from time immemorial, as presented to the candidate during his
lecture; and

440

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

WHEREAS, the wages of a Fellowcraft Mason as presented in the
Second Degree Lecture are com, wine and oil. The candidate receiving this
information from the Master will have a greater appreciation and a clearer
understanding of the wages of a Fellowcraft if the receptacles containing com,
wine and oil were lifted for display as they are referred to; and
WHEREAS, Masonic history previously allowed for the display of
com, wine and oil during the conferral of the Second Degree; and
WHEREAS, Masonic Ritual for the Second Degree currently prohibits
the display of containers representing com, wine and oil; and
WHEREAS, the display of containers representing com, wine and oil
is currently allowed by Grand Lodge Ritual during various Grand Lodge
ceremonies, such as the Cornerstone Laying Ceremony, Lodge Hall Dedication
Ceremony and the Constitution of Newly Chartered Lodges Ceremony; and
WHEREAS, there is no prohibition against the display of containers
of com, wine and oil in Masonic law.
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Masonic Lodges may,
as an option, allow the Brother conferring the Second Degree to display on the
Master's podium containers representing com, wine and oil and to lift them for
display when referred to during the Master's Lecture.

441

Report of the Committee on Ritual:
The tools and implements displayed during the Three Degrees are
generally those with which the candidate is probably not familiar (the 24"
gauge, for example) or which have some amount of associated ritual, such as
the trowel. Com, wine and oil meet neither of these criteria, all are well
known and easily recognized and the ritual references to each is so brief as to
give scant time for their individual display.
The recent tendency of the Ritual Committee has been to try to
simplify our ritual, removing confusion and extraneous movements whenever
possible. As we have continued in the past years, the introduction of new
elements creates new areas of confusion and difficulty. This resolution
proposes new ritual movements, and does little, if anything, to enhance the
lessons of our ceremonies. We find no compelling reason to adopt it and
recommend a "no" vote.

California to change the Ordinances in the California Masonic Code during
this revision , but merely to simplify the language of the Code; and

This proposal is prompted by a substantive change revealed in Section
3030 of the 1991 California Masonic Code as a result of the Special
Committee 's revision of Section 1116 of the 1975 issue of said Code.

WHEREAS , the revised Code was not to become effective until the
close of the Annual Communic ation in 1992 to provide a one year period of
review by the appropriate committees of the Grand Lodge of California for any
inadvertent errors or omissions; and

The charge and guidelines for the Special Committee are properly
stated in the preamble of Resolution 93-12, in part, stating that during the
revision process it was not the committee 's prerogative to make changes; that
removal of ambiguitie s, redundanci es and inconsisten cies, simplifying the
wording, etc. were the main thrust of the assignment ; and that it was not the
intention of the Grand Lodge to change the ordinances. Now, it appears that
errors, changes and omissions, unknown to the voting delegates, prevailed at
the time of considerati on and adoption of the 1991 Code during the Annual
Communic ation in October of 1992. The main issue at stake is the concern
that the delegates and the constituent Lodges were denied their right to vote
on a matter that seriously impacts and has a profound effect on the quality of

of this nor any reference to monetary savings whether real or imagined should

Section 810 of the 1991 California Masonic Code outlines the proper
procedure for proposed amendmen ts to our Ordinances by presentatio n of
written resolutions by members of Grand Lodge, decisions and/or
recommend ations by the Grand Master and such emergent matters which may
be presented and deemed proper by the delegates of Grand Lodge. Section
6180 states that the Committee on Masonic Code shall edit and prepare for
publication the annual changes in our laws and submit to Grand Lodge any
revisions that may seem necessary or desirable.

We spent considerable time and effort on the budget process and all
aspects of financial planning. Now every Trustee has a thorough knowledge
of the source and amounts of revenue as well as a full understandin g of every
budget line item.
We undertook the task of drafting standard forms of agreement to be
used in negotiating the terms and conditions for all future individual funds.
In order to qualify for an individual fund a minimum $50,000 donation is
required .
We established commitment, encumbrance and accrual reports for all
individual funds and for the general fund. This allows the scholarship renewal
process, for those qualified, to move through the system smoothly and
facilitates the work of the scholarship selection committee.
We restructured the scholarship process with timelines, and cut-off
dates for submittal of applications and issuance of checks .
All of the above steps were taken to reduce staff time and more
importantly to reduce and control administrativ e costs.
All of us realize that the current low level of interest rates has been
a serious problem for all foundations, including ours. The need to reduce all
areas of expenditure except for scholarship grants has been fully addressed and
appropriate actions taken.

Board Meetings
Meetings of the Trustees are usually held on the first Wednesday of
the month, alternating between the Union City and Covina Hornes.
Committees of the Board usually meet the day before Board Meetings
to review or prepare reports for Board consideration.
You will note that the Administrators and members of the Board of
Trustees have been given the opportunity to participate in the preparation of
this Annual Report as follows:

Admissions Committee
by Victor Howard, Ph.D., and Ver/ Lobb, Co-Chairmen
The Admissions Committee of the Board of Trustees meets on the
first Tuesday of each month. This informal meeting allows for a free
exchange of information about each of the applicants between the Trustees of
the north and the south and the Homes Administrators, Representatives and
Medical staff.
Prior to the Tuesday meeting, the eight Trustees who fonn the
Admissions Committee (four from the North and four from the South) have
received and carefully studied the applications for prospective residents and/or
non-resident assistance. These Trustees evaluate the applications and pass
their comments and votes to the two co-chairmen. The co-chairman in charge
for that month (the co-chainnen alternate responsibility) then produces a
preliminary Admissions Committee Report.

458

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

This Preliminary Admissions Committee Report may be modified to
reflect the discussions during the Tuesday Admissions Committee Meeting and
the inputs received from the medical staff at the Home. The revised
Admissions Committee Report is then presented to the full Board of Trustees
at the formal Board Meeting on Wednesday. where the final decision is made
on each application.
The number of applications handled by the Committee for couples,
individuals and children varies from month to month. This past year the high
was 10 applications handled in one month.

Purpose

Over the past year the number of persons admitted to Assisted Living
has significantly increased as the age of our applicants has gone up - and the
level of their physical ailments becomes more serious. During this year we
gradually increased the number of residents in the adult section of Covina,
although at present we are limited in the level of applicants we can accept by
the absence of on-site medical and nursing facilities.
The co-chairmen sincerely thank the other Trustees who labor long
and hard over these applications. These Trustees try to make a thoughtful
judgement for what is best for the applicants. During the past year Trustee

6.

The Committee will provide consultation and assistance to
the Board of Trustees in reviewing potential Health Care

Physical Facilities Committee
by William W Dickson, Chairman

This year the next two steps were taken to further develop the Covina
site into a complete facility with Assisted Living and Skilled Nursing.

Union City
Last year it was mentioned that we expected to do some precautionary
strengthening on several of our buildings due to the proximity of the Hayward
earthquake fault.
After considerable analysis and discussion we realized it would be
difficult to accomplish this without several moves of residents and probably
having to outplace some residents in the community during construction.
This was not an acceptable option for the Board of Trustees so we
adopted a multi-year plan to address the entire site.
The first step will be to remodel the upper floors of the Wollenberg
building to an assisted living non-ambulatory facility which will give us some
rooms to permit movement of residents. On the ground floor in addition to a
physical rehabilitation area we plan to create a preventative health maintenance
area for the residents. We feel this will promote their well being.

The Board engaged a specialist in the field of geriatrics to survey our
residents both at Union City and Covina. This was done to allow the residents
opportunity to express their priorities with suggestions as well as listing
shortcomings. Staff, Administrators and Trustees also participated in the
survey to determine the extent to which we understand the residents needs.
The survey was toJally anonymous and the results became the foundation for
space planning at Covina as well as for improvements we could make at Union
City.
A further step taken was architectural development of a master site
plan for best use of our property. It takes into account the building space
program and preservation of the existing site character. This is currently under
review.
Some observations by consultants both geriatric and architectural
mentioned above are worth noting:
1.

The residents have a high degree of life satisfaction
compared to national norms.

2.

The residents have a high degree of trust and feel they made
the right decision to locate at the Homes.

3.

The consultants without exception were overwhelmed by
what they saw. It was not what they expected. It was not
just a home - it was a community for living.

Following this the upper floors of Adams will be addressed,
eliminating shared bathrooms and adjusting other features.
Then in order the North, Administration and South buildings will be
addressed. Structural strengthening will be accomplished, room sizes adjusted,
air conditioning added, telephone outlets installed and various adjustments
made to enhance the quality of life for our residents.

Real Estate Committee
by Stanley M Cazneaux, Chairman
The Real Estate Committee of the Masonic Homes of California
Board of Trustees presently includes the Chairman and two members, Alvin
J. Weis and Ver! Lobb.
The Real Estate Committee is charged with the responsibility of
disposing of all real estate made available to the Masonic Homes through asset
assignment, wills and bequests, gifts and grants.
During the past year, July I, 1992 through June 30, 1993, we sold
thirty-two (32) pieces of property for a total of $2,988,257.34. In addition we
sold 37 motor vehicles for a total of $48,507.50, and home furnishing in the
amount of $6,193 .19. Total sales for 1992-1993 , equal $3,042,958.03.
We always have an inventory of unsold properties, due to the Life
Care Contract signed by each new resident of the Home. This affords them
a ninety (90) day period to adjust and satisfy their own minds that they have
no intention of withdrawing from the Masonic Home. The resident then signs
a release authorizing the sale of the property.

The members of the Real Estate Committee, wish to express their
deep appreciation to Brother Hambleton Leas, Past President of the Board of
Trustees, for his continued assistance in the sale of real estate. As a consultant
to this Committee, he continues his dedication to our Masonic Homes.
Scholarship Committee
by William W. Dickson, Chairman
This past June we again had the pleasant opportunity of meeting with
some of our young people who wish to further their education.
The discussion of their needs, their objectives and what we can do to
help them follows somewhat the same pattern as happens in many households.
The main difference being we are concentrated in a one-day meeting.
Our young lady majoring in International Studies spent a semester at
sea as sponsored by the University of Pittsburgh. A trip around the world and
exposure to different cultures will be most beneficial to her further endeavors.
She considers it the opportunity of a lifetime and has resumed her studies at
Humboldt with great enthusiasm.
Our young man who was studying at Sacramento State has realized
that his interest and aptitudes are not in the area of pure accounting but more
along business analysis lines and will be switching his major without too much
lost academically.
As a result of his experience we are considering expanded aptitude
testing for all our junior year residents.
The other two young men having just graduated from high school will
be entering the fields of Forest Management and Police Science at a local
college.
Of note should be the completion this past year by one of our former
residents at Covina of the academic portion of the requirements for a Doctorate
degree at the University of California. As reported last year his studies at
Berkeley were in applied mathematics in the field of applied dynamical
systems, neural networks and bio-genetic algorithm s.
Perhaps some new thought, new direction will come from his efforts
for the good of our society or for that matter from the efforts of any of our
young residents.

1992/1993

General

This past year has been one of both "Implementation" and "Planning."
We have been refining the growing Adult program which has entered
its third year of service.
We are participating with the Board of Trustees in planning for
service in the 21st century. This will include expanded adult Assisted
Living service and a new, state-of-the-art, Skilled Nursing Facility.
As well, we have been planning how to implement and evaluate the
admission of children who are not Masonically related. This amended
admission program was initiated through a special trust from our
deceased arother, Herman Tate of Seafaring Lodge No. 708. Brother
Tate and Seafaring Lodge obviously understood that to relieve the
distressed is a duty incumbent upon us all and that charity is love.
Our efforts to assist Masons and their wives, widows and children are
an obligation as well as a charity. Seafaring Lodge also has shown
us that our Masonic teaching does not suggest charity is due only to
Masons and their wives, widows and children, and that charity lies
beyond an obligation.
Given the current and projected growth and development at Covina,
every management team member will be receiving specialized training in his
or her area of expertise. This will allow them to direct, to a more complete
and professional extent, their departments.
This year we have made significant progress toward compliance with
new regulations relating to Worker's Illness and Injury Prevention Programs,
Hazardous Materials Programs and Employee's Rights Programs.
Adult Services
As Administrator, it was necessary that I become qualified to
administer the planned expansion programs. With the encouragement of the

472

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Board of Trustees, I have completed and passed both the State and National
Skilled Nursing Examinations and the State Residential Care Facility
Administrator's Certification program. I have also completed the curriculum
for a Master's Degree in Public Administration .
In the Adult Program we have continued to implement the "Choice"
philosophy program among adult residents. Having choice enhances our
resident's control over their lives and personal dignity. The Masonic Homes
at Covina is sensitive to these issues. In my Grand Lodge Report for 1992 we
stressed the importance of our philosophy on choices. The following are some
of the examples of Covina's pursuit of this philosophy:
Residents wanted a choice of physician and collectively did
not appreciate the services of one approved physician . We
now offer two Health Maintenance Organizations for Seniors
which now gives residents a choice of primary physician.
We have implemented an appointment system and residents
now can make their own doctor's appointments.
We have implemented a menu selection program and a
resident now selects a choice of menu items such as entrees
and desserts.
Residents can choose to prepare two meals daily for
themselves. we will soon commence a pilot project where
residents may order breakfast between 7:30 a.m. and 9:30
a.m.
Residents in this Home choose whether or not to have a
private telephone and also choose a long distance carrier.
Residents have their own patios and choose if they prefer
gardeners to maintain the patio or what plants they wish to
plant and maintain themselves. As well, they choose their
own tools and gardening equipment.
A resident and retired R.N., serves on a committee to study
and evaluate HMO programs. This committee will inquire as
to how an HMO can factor into the planned Covina Skilled
Nursing Facility.
We have a Dietary Committee and a CARE (Covina Adult
Resident Evaluation) Committee.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

473

Residents may choose to use Dial-A-Ride or the Covina
Trolley which stops immediately in front of the Masonic
Home.
Residents may choose to participate with the Joslyn Senior
Citizens Center in Covina.
An Expansion Planning Survey is a good example of
empowering and hearing residents.
We will continue to be attentive to opportunities where "choice" can
be the operative word.
We have been attentive to the quality of educational, cultural, spiritual
and recreational activities of adult residents through use of a volunteer
chaplain, resident participation in planning, reassignment of certain staff and
planning for employment of a Recreation Leader in fiscal year 1993/ 1994.
We are pleased to introduce Carolyn Tolcher, our corporation's Homes
Representative. Mrs. Tolcher's position is funded through the retirement of
Mrs. Sue Dean, who was located in San Francisco. We will miss the services
of Mrs. Dean, but are encouraged by the employment of Mrs. Tolcher. Mrs.
Tolcher is assigned to Covina to assure that applications for Masonic
Assistance in Southern California are completed as thoroughly, professionally
and as quickl y as possible. As well, she handles matters related to nonresident
assistance and Outreach Services, e.g., identifying and arranging for needed
human service resources available through the local, county, state and federal
government or private agencies. Mrs. Tolcher is available to constituent
lodges and members for advise relative to such resources.

Children's Services
To continue our service in this era of domestic stress, there has been
more formalized in-service training of Houseparents on subjects appropriate to
the Child Care mission.
A revised academic assistance program was evaluated this year with
quite positive results. We have met and exceeded our goal for each child of
having at least a 2.0 grade point average or better. Brother Ronald T. Bunte,
Director of Children's Services, believes that we should provide an incentive
and encourage each child to pursue academic excellence based upon the full
potential of each child in our care. As well, we are working closely with the
Charter Oak Unified School District and assuring that vocational aptitude and
interest tests are conducted on children in our care.
The first draft of a measurable developmental key milestone program
which identifies and defines age appropriate general development and skills in
preparation for independent living has been completed. We consider this a
bold step forward in stating our goals and objectives in such a sensitive area.
A revised program statement has been provided to our licensing
agency and reflects the many program modifications made over the past 13
years. We have reviewed the formal - legal relationship of the Masonic Home
to the children in our care. Although we are not the legal guardian nor a
conservator, we are empowered to make specific decisions on behalf of these
children. Other decisions must be made only by legal guardians. We are
reviewing who makes what decisions on behalf of children to assure that no
confusion exists and that harmony between the Home and guardian remains a
strength and support for children. This is particularly important for children
who have already experienced too much domestic stress in their lives.

The following are more than names. They, in part, represent our
future. The entire staff of the Masonic Home is delighted to have been a part
of their lives.

Other Items of Interest
The father of one of our 16 year old residents, Appl. # 1782, Consuelo
Lodge No. 325, has suddenly surfaced. He is claiming his right as a guardian
(joint custody). He suddenly does not want his child in " ... a place like that."
Our child is afraid of his father due to previous physical abuse, drug and
alcohol dependency and a lack of consistency. He does not want to be
withdrawn from the Masonic Home and we have assured him that with his

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

mother' s cooperation he will not be. His father says he is living with a fine
woman and her three children and that he is free of chemical dependency and
is now working. Being 16 years of age, our child has certain controls and
choices. We have assured both parents that the Masonic Home will act in the
best interests of the child and will encourage reestablishing a healthy
relationship between father and son if the father will participate as a stable
participant

REPORT OF THE AnMINISTRA TOR

478

We have received an unsolicited donation of $100.00 from the Dreier
Family Foundation . David Dreier, a United States Congressman, sent us a
personal note as Secretary of that foundation . It is wonderful to know that our
Congressman finds our philanthropy to be worthy of his family's attention .
A pilot project has commenced at Covina. Commencing August 23rd,
breakfast is served between 7:30 a.m. and 9:30 a.m. A menu is being used
and the residents may select the food items they wish. We think this may be
efficient and more effective while allowing adult residents the opportunity to
make more choices.
Respectfully submitted,
John Rose, Administrator

MASONIC HOME, UNION CITY
1992-1993

As your recently appointed Administrator, l am extremely proud to
provide all of our brethren with this annual report on the status of our residents
and facilities at Union City. Of special note this past year is the fact that on
March 13, 1993, we celebrated the I OOth anniversary of the purchase of the
287 acres our Home occupies.• This event was publicized by a full page
advertisement in the local newspapers, acknowledging that the Home is
supported by the 132,000 Masons comprising the Masonic Grand Lodge of
California.
l am also pleased to report that since our last annual communication,
30 Lodges, Eastern Star Chapters, various youth groups, and other related
groups have visited and toured the Home. We are hopeful that next year we
will have even more visitors at this great Home. Visits from sponsoring
Lodges and concordant bodies are always appreciated by our residents .
During the past twelve month period the efforts of our staff were
devoted to improving the quality of life for residents and upgrading our
facilities.
By keeping abreast of the latest gerontological and health care issues,
and relaying this infonnation to our dedicated employees, we are able to
continually improve our care to the residents.
Our employees receive ongoing trammg to facilitate their
understanding of the needs of our residents. This is especially important in
our Skilled Nursing Facility where our Brothers and Sisters sometimes
experience difficult adjustment periods. Employees who work in this area are
taught:

"A nursing home isn't a place where old, sick. people come to die;
it's a community of men and women with memories and experiences
they treasure; people who once were part of the neighborhoods and
churches the rest of us inherited. .. in short, people like the rest of us
except that they are older than most of us. and living through
complications that very possibly await you or me." • •

••Quote from an article entitled "Nursing Homes--What's Good About Them" by
Olaf J. Kaasa. President of lhe American Assn . of Retired Persons.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Later this year, we will implement a Pre-Certification Program to
enable our employees in various non-nursing departments to take courses
conducted by our Staff Development Department to train to become Certified
Nursing Assistants. This is a first step in creating a career ladder for our
employees who wish to enter the Health Care Profession at our Facility.

of our clinical data. A multi-disciplinary team approach is utilii.ed, with data
access provided at a moment's notice to those staff persons providing resident
care. According to the chair of our Medical Advisory Committee, ..."it is
anticipated that this system will become a model for this and other facilities
in California in the future .."

Another example of our efforts to improve the quality of life for our
residents is through our CPE Program (Clinical Pastoral Education Program)
which was started two years ago. The Masonic Home is already an accredited
CPE Center and is due for a full accreditation in 1994. Four programs have
been completed over the past two years; two extended units from October to
May, and two summer units from June to August. Sixteen students have
completed our programs.

Over the past twelve months, improvements to our physical facilities
were made in the following areas:

480

The CPE Chaplains serve in conjunction with our two full time staff
Chaplains. They participate in Sunday Worship, structured pastoral groups
such as grief groups, study and meditation groups; and provide one on one
pastoral counseling and spiritual guidance to residents at all levels of care.
The CPE Chaplains also actively participate in all the Health Services
interdisciplinary meetings.

a complete renovation of our recreational area on 2-Adams,

the purchase of a new 35-passenger bus to accommodate
increased outings to plays, baseball games and tours to local

Because of this direct interaction, some residents develop lasting
relationships with the CPE Chaplains who continue to reside in the area, and
the students leave with an expanded understanding of Masonry. Given the bad
press our craft has received in recent controversies within certain portions of
the Southern Baptist denomination, this awareness is an opportunity to
gradually correct misunderstandings and develop appreciation on the part of
present and future religious leaders.

new medication carts for our Assisted Living section of the

I am proud to report that our program has had students from a wide
variety of religious backgrounds: Pentecostal, Unitarian, United Church of
Christ, Roman Catholic, United Methodist, Lutheran, Presbyterian, and
Episcopal. The variety reflects the diversity of religious backgrounds among
our residents.

new tables and chairs fo r our Sedam auditorium.

From the professional health care standpoint, the Trustees established
a Medical Advisory Committee in July 1992 consisting of a physician,
psychiatrist, dentist, psychologist, and an Associate Clinical Professor from a
local School of Nursing to provide "advisory assistance and guidance" to the
Administrator and our Medical Director. Through this committee and our
Medical Director, we are assured that our ongoing medical services are
consistent and in accordance with the best medical practices.
Our goal is to have the best medical practices in the state. This past
year we implemented a new Long Term Care Computer System in our Skilled
Nursing Facility which provides for a thorough communication network for all

a new EKG machine for our medical clinic.
a complete renovation of our laundry department with new
washers and dryers.

a covered walkway from our Lorber Building to the parking
lot.
As we look to the future, we are making plans that will provide even
more enhanced services to our Brothers, their wives and widows. As a greater
percentage of our Brethren live in Southern California. the Trustees have
decided to expand our Covina Facility to include the services of Assisted
Living and Skilled Nursing. This will greatly reduce "transfer trauma" among
our Brothers who, in the past, had to be transferred from Covina to Union City
when either of these two services were required.
After the Covina expansion is complete, Union City's population wi ll
gradually decrease, and our facilities will be remodeled to provide larger rooms
for our residents, complete with private phones, individual controls for heating
and air conditioning, and cable te levision. At the same time, the Main

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Administration building, North and South Wings, and the Adams Building will
undergo earthquake retrofit work.

We plan to begin the first phase of our remodeling later this year
when the Wollenberg Building is remodeled to accommodate our growing
population of Assisted Living residents. Initial plans call for a new Physical
Therapy area, and exercise/gym area complete with juice bar and a hydrotherapy pool.
As you have just read, we have had a busy year at Union City, a
proud 100-year heritage, and we look forward to a bright future.
On behalf of all our residents and employees at Union City, I invite
all Brothers and their families to visit "their Home" at Union City during this
year's annual communication, or whenever they can .
As residents and employees, we are "thankful to all California
Masons" for their contributions which make the Masonic Home for Adults at
Union City a great place to live and work.
Respectfully submitted,
Kelly Wiest, Administrator

Your Masonic Homes Endowment Board is pleased to submit its
62nd Annual Report covering the fiscal year ending June 30, 1993. Through
the commitment of many of the Brethren of this great Fraternity to the support
of the residents of our two Homes, their contributions through their Lodges
to the Endowment Fund, were over one and a quarter million dollars. Also,
the amount of bequests, gifts and memorials was the fourth largest ever
received in recent years over two and a half mill ion dollars. It was indeed
a satisfying year!

Income from the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund amounted to
$5,922,814 which will be transferred to the operating accounts of the Masonic
Homes of California. This income is an extremely vital and important factor
in providing the Homes' Trustees with a portion of the funds necessary to
maintain the exceptionally high quality of health care and services afforded
to the residents. Another use of this income is to help provide nonresidential
assistance for those who are not able to become a resident. This income also
assists in providing money for present as well as future construction and
enhancement of the facilities at our Homes.

Considering the depressed state of the economy, the demands placed
on our money avai lable for contribution to other charities and programs within
Grand Lodge, and our co ntinued dec line in membership we are pleased with
what we have achieved. The contributions through Lodges only decreased 6.4
percent while the percentage of members contributing decreased 6.9 percen t
with a decrease in membership of 4.4 percent.
Your attention is directed to the United Way data given above. The
full amount of the pledge is used for the purpose of Honor Roll status of the
Lodges. The actual cash receipts are less than the pledges because of United
Way administrative costs. The concern arises because of the large disparity
of pledge vs. receipts.
One explanation could be the designatio n Mason ic
Homes vs. Masonic Homes Endowm ent Fund. The brethren sho uld verify
with their United Way to be sure the recipient is the Masonic Homes
Endowment Fund.
The presentation of the book "The Greatest Of These Is Charity" - a
history of the Masonic Homes of California - is being widely accepted as one
of great enli ghtenment to both the new Entered Apprentice as well as the
This program was so s uccessful that a second
seasoned Master Mason.
printing of the book was made. Lodges can receive these books by contacting
their Endowment Board member whom will be pleased to make the
presentation to the !)CW Entered Apprentice.
The response to th e Mason ic Homes Endowment Lapel Pins and the
Appreciation Certificates is continuing to be strong. The Lapel Pin for 1994
is of a new design and should contin ue to appeal to our contributors. It is
oblong with a map of California and stars locates our two Homes and Grand
Lodge.
We are pleased to report that the average contribution per contributor
increased to $22.87, up 5.1 % from the previous year. However the average
contribution per membe r decreased 2 . l % to $9.84 , and the percentage of
Lodges making the Honor Roll decreased 1.3% to 46.3% . The really bad
news is that the percent of members contributing declined 6.9% to 43.0%.
Also of interest is th e fact that of the four divisions in the jurisdiction,
only one of them had an increase in contributions.
Division II had an
increase of 9.1 %, and interesting ly enough this area is not recognized as an
economically strong area of the state.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Planning For The Future
The Individual Contribution Incentive Program is progressing very
well and tbe majority of tbe Lodges are participating in the program. On the
side opposite to the calendar is the Masonic emblem and inscription "Let us
soar in ' 94 to new heights for the Masonic Homes Endowment Fund".
A number of calendars, in excess of the membership of each Lodge,
were again sent to the Secretary of each Lodge with the hope that they will be
included in the dues envelope (or Lodge Bulletin or in the dues receipt
envelope) to each Mason in California. Hopefully, we will convince the non
participating 57% of our members to contribute something to the support of
the Endowment Fund.
The reporting and recording of contributions and the number of
contributors for Honor Roll recognition has improved over the past year. We
still urge the Lodge Secretaries to make their checks payable to the "California
Masonic Homes Endowment Fund" and in the "memo" section on the lower
left side of the check indicate the number of contributors. Think about it, that
would be a pennanent record.
In planning the printing budget each year we look at the historical
orders of pamphlets from the Lodges. One way that Lodges can help the
Endowment Board is to order only the quantity of envelopes and pamphlets
that it intends to use in one year.
Also, if your order is not filled in a
reasonable time please do not place another order until you have verified with
the supplier as to status of your order.
The presentation of the book "The Greatest Of These Is Charity" to
the newly initiated Entered Apprentice has been a great success . There are
many Lodges in the jurisdiction that still do not avail themselves of this
program. Our Board members will endeavor to see that each newly initiated
Entered Apprentice has the opportunity to receive a copy of the history of the
Masonic Homes of California.

the Endowment Board.

This past year was marred by the untimely death of our Board

REPORT OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS

Noe HILL MASONIC MANAGEMENT
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
Nob Hill Masonic Management, Inc. ("NHMM") is a California forprofit corporation wholly owned by the Grand Lodge of California. It was
formed to operate essentia.lly all of the physical assets of the California
Masonic Memorial Temple ("CMMT") including the Auditorium, Exhibit Hall,
parking garage and Pine Street apartment rental properties and has been operational since May l, 1992.
NHMM directors are five in number and are appointed annually by
the Grand Master. The Junior Grand Warden serves as a director by virtue of
his office, and the Grand Treasurer and Grand Secretary serve respectively as
the Chief Financial Officer and Secretary of the corporation by virtue of their
offices.
It has been an interesting and extremely busy year. Great credit is
given to Ray W. Ward, C.F.E., our Executive Vice President/General Manager,
and his staff for their diligent efforts and many accomplishments.

Much deferred maintenance has been undertaken including completing
the reroofing, te.a ring out and replacing the leaking terrazzo porch on the
Taylor Street side, ~ainting the California Street pedestrian entrance into the
parking garage, refinishing the wood paneling on the lobby interior walls, tying
the emergency generator into the ventilation system to remove automobile
exhaust, putting emergency lighting in the stairwells and installing an
emergency sound system.
A comprehensive insurance survey was undertaken by the Travelers
Insurance Company together with our insurance brokers, Thompkins &
Company and we responded promptly to each loss control recommendation.
We have substantially complied with the Americans With Disabilities
Act ("ADA") requirements by lowering drinking fountains and telephones,
installing stalls for the handicapped in the public restrooms, providing for
wheelchair seating in the auditorium, setting aside parking spaces for the
handicapped in the garage, lowering the elevator buttons and installing the
necessary hearing and Braille equipment, and completing and submitting
architectural and engineering studies for a ramp at the building entrance to the
city for approval, and much more.
We have painted and carpeted the meeting rooms on "G" floor and
converted the women's restroom and adjacent room behind the stage into a

518

PROCEEDINGS Of THE

star's suite, making these areas much more marketable to prospective tenants.
We rehabilitated the un sightly bathrooms in the parking garage and converted
one-half of the men ' s restroom on "G" floor so that it may be used as a
women 's restroom when we have public events. All of thi s work was
undertaken by the new corporation but financed by the CMMT with the
complete cooperation of President Robert A. Bush and its Board of Trustees.
We can be proud of the appearance and integrity of thi s magnificent edifice
and we hope that the Brethren will be as well.
Routine maintenance in the Pine Street apartments is now
accomplished by our maintenance personnel instead of contracting th at work
to the others, all at a considerable savings.
Our staff under the direction of Ray Ward has responded with great
dedication to its tremendously increased work load. Training and safety
prog rams arc in place as are personnel policies and compensation adju stments
have bee n made to recognize staff contribution to the revi tali zed operations.
The parkin g garage had been subject to a 10-year lease which expired
at the end of March this year. When our corporation was fo rmed, the Grand
Master and the Executive Committee recognized the parking operation as a
significant revenue center, if properly managed and controlled, so that we,
rather tha n the operators, could set parking fees and use it as a marketing tool
in combination with renting the auditorium and exhibit hall. We there fo re
entered into a Man agement Agreement with AMPCO Auto Parks, Inc. so that
for a monthly fee they care for the day to day management, staffing, cleaning,
collection of parking fees , acco unting subject to audit, and pay ment to us of
net receipts, all subject to the general supervision of our Executive Vice
President/General Manager.
As a part of the agreement with AMPCO, they installed and paid for
compute rized stat e of the art parking equipment which g ives us an accurate
accounting of auto mo biles in and out, and itemization of receipts at any given
hour. During our first full two months of operation in the fi scal year ended
June 30, 1993, our net receipts increased from an average of $20,000 per
month to $48,000 in May and $44,000 in June. We expect th is trend to
continue with our new rate structure which was effective on September 1 aided
by the new parking equipment.
Professional marketing brochures have been distributed to prospective
tenants. The advertising budget has been greatly increased and hundreds of
telephone calls have been made by Ray Ward to his colleagues an d others to
solicit business. Also, an open house was held for some 300 members of the
San Francisco Convention and Visitors Bureau to show off our facility to a
myri ad of businesses which can refer ten ants to us.

GRAND LODGE OF CA LIFORN IA

519

T he parking receipts are direct ly t ied to the number of events in the
auditorium and exhibit hall . In this regard, the new corporation improved the
count from I 06 event days of operation before our management to 237 event
days in our last fu ll year of operation. Among the quality tenants was IBM
Corporation which rented the auditorium and exhibit hall and much of our
sound and lighting equipment for 49 days.
To test our value as a management company, we compared our first
full year in business with net income from operations before we started up and
found that we netted from operations $271,954 (before rent, interest and taxes)
c.o mpared to a fiscal year 1990-1991 net operating loss of $40,44 7 and a loss
exceeding $147,000 for the first 10 mo nth s of the fiscal year 1991- 1992 .
We paid in rent to the CM MT $305,435 last year wh ile re liev ing it of
the exp~nses and bu rdens of operation and resu lt ing significant losses. Long
term th is method of operation w ill greatl y benefit ou r Masonic Homes and
Mason ic Foundatio n who are the beneficiaries of C MMT income production
while at the same time prod ucing what we expect to be substantial div idends
to assist in the operation of our Grand Lodge.
We are grateful to Grand Master Doan for his interest, cooperation
and professional adv ice. Likewise the Grand Secretary and G rand Treasurer
an.d thei r person~el have been of great help in the formidable task of bringing
this new Masonic venture to its present position of successful operation.
Respectfully submitted
Donald B. McCaw, President
W illard Vausbinder, Vice President

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON Aw ARDS AND REcoGNITION

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

APPENDIX L

This committee has been reestablished from the old "Certificates,
Awards and Special Presentations Committee." We feel that our new name
"Awards and Recognition Committee'' better describes our labors. We added
a new member and the purpose of the committee is to make our Grand Master
and Grand Lodge look good. The members of our Lodges do need recognition
for their labors and we hope that our committee will help in establishing some
of this much needed recognition.
Our members have been busy helping Grand Lodge with designing
certificates and helping with the design of metals etc. Gavels, name badges,
and special presentations have been fabricated by our members. We look
forward to helping the Grand Master and the Grand Lodge with projects in the
future.
Respectfully submitted,
Ken Kessel, Chairman
Glenn C. Johnson

Albert G. Cowan, Jr.
Thomas J. McKimson

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

It is with a great deal of pride that I submit the following report on
the activities of the Charters Committee. With your excellent leadership, many
of the Lodges of California have considered the benefits of consolidation.

The members of this committee have performed in an exemplary
manner in assisting the Lodges in their endeavors. I would especially like to
recognize the efforts of Brother Harold Hand and Brother Haskell Goodman.
Brother Hand processed 7 actions and Brother Goodman handled 5 actions.

Each Division had an agenda arranged for training activity in their

REPORT OF THE SPECIAL
COMMITTEE ON INSURANCE STUDY

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F& A.M. of California:
At th e request of Grand Master Doan, a special committee was formed
in October, 1992 to complete a comprehensive study of our Grand Lodge
insurance program. Specifically, the committee was asked to consider all
insurance programs covering Grand Lodge, the Masonic Homes, the Memorial
Temple and Masonic Hall Associations. Questions to be explored included the
adequacy of coverage afforded, the competitiveness of the premiums paid and
coverage provided, the future direction of insurance in the marketplace and the
adequacy of our internal structure to monitor our fraternal insurance needs in
the future.
BACKGROUND
From time to time our Grand Lodge has addressed its concerns over
the manner in which we provide insurance protection for our liabilities and for
our extensive portfolio of real and personal properties owned by the Grand
Lodge, its affiliates and our Masonic Hall Associations. Over the past two
decades, the insurance industry in California has been plagued by major price
increases, runaway litigation and a movement toward increased governmental
regulation.
•
In response to these troubling trends, at the I 30th Annual
Communication, Grand Lodge mandated the study of a self-insurance program
for the Masonic Hall Associations within our jurisdiction. During the ensuing
year, a Special Committee on Insurance Study was formed. At the 13 lst
Annual Communication, this committee made two recommendations based
upon its study of the prior year. The first was the continued study and
preparation of a proposal for the formation of an insurance trust. The second
called for an appraisal of Masonic Hall Associations within this jurisdiction to
determine an adequate insurance valuation of their properties. Such appraisals
were vital to the committee's evaluation of the cost benefit of the first
recommendation. The proposed establishment of an insurance trust would
have provided for an alternative self-insurance structure with the possibility of
controlling future costs of insurance.
After considerable study, which included the consulting services of
Mr. Harry 0. Miller, a fonner C hief Deputy Insurance Commissioner for the

532

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

State of California, the Special Committee concluded its work and reported at
the 132nd Annual Communication. Its report concluded that an insurance trust
should not be fonned at that time and included a very convincing business
case in favor of its findings. It did, however, recommend that Grand Lodge
periodically evaluate alternative insurance structures to insure that the Grand
Lodge was properly positioned to guarantee maximum cost benefits for its
insurance portfolio.

Primary Comprehensive Liability, (e) Excess Comprehensive Liability, (f)
