coverage to evaluate the adequacy of coverage and form. This committee was
unanimous in its conclusion that the Fraternal Comprehensive Liability Policy
form currently recommended by the Insurance Committee and in force
provides insured benefits which are substantially better than all known
commercial liability policies in the marketplace. Although a review of specific
coverage requires the steady vigilance of the Committee charged with this
important responsibility in order to address changes in asset mix and our
business environment, the fraternal policy form is very favorable and should
be preserved.
Our review of the policy form and coverage provided to California
Masonic Hall Associations was equally positive. The Memorandum of
Insurance in force at the time of our review {Aug. 1992 thru Aug. 1993 - The
Travelers Insurance Companies) offered Masonic Hall Associations a broad
policy form, very limited exclusion provisions and coverage adequate to
address most loss scenarios anticipated (excepting Earthquake and Flood).
When compared to standard commercial policy forms, the Fraternal policy
affords substantial coverage benefits. As of the 1992-93 policy year, the

A concern was noted during your committee' s preparation of this

participate in the fraternal insurance program . We reach this conclusion
because the number of covered locations is fewer than the number of Masonic
Hall Association properties disclosed in Grand Lodge records. We need to do

COMPETITIVE PRICING IN THE MARKETPLACE
In the Special Committee on Insurance Study report to the l 32nd
Annual Communication in October 198 l, the Committee found that "our
Masonic insurance has not been adequately marketed in the past". The
Committee encouraged Grand Lodge through its committee structure to
negotiate "between carriers for more favorably priced insurance to be
purchased by any Masonic organization in the state which wishes to
participate". Since this report, progress on this recommendation has been
noted. The Insurance Committee has been effective in developing a unifonn
premium pricing standard for Masonic Hall Associations participating in the
program. The area that remains unaddressed is the competitive positioning of
carriers in pricing our Masonic insurance book. For the past thirty-one years,
the Traveler's Insurance Company has been the sole provider of the fraternal
broad form policy.

534

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Although Traveler's has performed admirably during this period, we
believe that marketplace competition is extremely important to insure
competitive pricing. A review of available loss data suggested to your
committee that other insurers would compete for our insurance business if they
were encouraged to review the fraternal insurance program . More competition
would increase the opportunity for more favorable pricing. The Grand Lodge
Insurance Committee should therefore establish a competitive environment
where multiple insurers bid for our insurance on a regularly scheduled basis.
ALTERNAT IVE STRUCTUR ES AND FUTURE TRENDS

In the 13 lst Annual Communication Report by the Insurance Study
Special Committee, focus was centered on the potential of a self-insurance
structure. Two steps were identified, starting with the establishment of an
insurance trust, followed by the eventual formation of an Inter-Insurance
Exchange. As previously indicated, the following year, and after additional
study, it was determined that there were sufficient complications to this
alternative and no future action was pursued.
Your committee began its look at the question of alternative structures
by again addressing the "Insurance Trust" and "Inter-Insurance Exchange"
concepts. Although there have been many changes to the Fire/Casualty
insurance market in California, particularly after the implementation of the
Proposition I03 regulations, there still appears to be no change in the
fundamental underlying concerns over the Insurance Trust structure. The issue
of a lack of insurable interest remains a roadblock to this type of structure. It
should be noted, however, that provisions for "group rate factors" are a
recognizable structure under these new provisions and may be advantageous
in the pricing of insurance premiums for "California-only" Masonic Hall
Associations in the future.
Your committee also looked at the possibility of establishing an InterInsurance Exchange to act as our insurer. In essence, an Inter-Insurance
Exchange is an internally funded insurance entity providing coverage for the
Grand Lodge, its affiliates and participating Masonic Hall Associations.
Discussions were held directly with the California Department of Insurance's
Regulatory Chief. Currently, it is the Department's position to oppose the
establishment of any additional Inter-Insurance Exchanges for a multitude of
policy reasons, including the more favorable regulations on reserve levels and
premium taxing rates. Depending on the number of lines of insurance and
forms being offered, the Department indicated that reserves exceeding
$8,000,000 would be required. Your committee found it logical to conclude
that this alternative structure would not be viable at this time and could only

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

INTERNAL MONITORING STRUCTURE
The question of the adequacy of our current internal structure to
monitor this highly complex need is both timely and prudent. Over the years,
our Grand Lodge has been served well by the large number of brothers who
have possessed impeccable credentials in the insurance field and dedicated
their time and expertise to the Insurance Committee. Currently, the Insurance
Committee is blessed with that same high level of professional expertise and
their committee actions are certainly demonstrative of their capabilities in
protecting our interests.
However, as we assess our future and look at the alarming reduction
in the number of our members, the increased median age of our membership,
and the diminishing number of insurance professionals affiliated with the
fraternity, your committee questions whether governance by a committee
structure will continue to be practical. For this very reason, Grand Lodge has
begun to shift its financial management from Grand Lodge committees to a
We suggest that our long-term strategic planning include
paid staff.

integrity of our insurance programs.

ON INVESTMENT

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The Investment Committee has the responsibility of reporting annually
to Grand Lodge on the condition of the various funds of Grand Lodge and
those of its entities.
During the year quarterly meetings are held by the committee with its
investment counselors. At each meeting an independent analytical consulting
finn reviews the performance of the various funds as compared with similar
funds, ie., endowment, non-profit and trust funds, in the United States.
The primary concern of the committee is the preservation of the
principal of the various funds together with the highest rate of return
commensurate with safety and good investment practice.
Three funds, Masonic Homes Endowment Fund, Masonic Homes
General Fund and the Hugo M. Loerber Union City Fund constitute 91 % of
the total investments.
Among other funds supervised by the committee are the General Fund
of Grand Lodge, the ,funds of the California Masonic Memorial Temple, and
the California Masonic Foundation.
The market value of the total portfolio on June 30, 1993, was
$322,593,000 compared to $304,006,251 a year earlier, an increase of 6.1%.
The 1992-1993 cash yield from the total invested funds was 6. 1%.
Fixed income securities, including government and corporate bonds
composed 47.2% of the total portfolio. The remainder consisted of common
stocks and cash equivalents.
The Pooled Income Funds is of particular importance to the Masonic
Homes. On June 30, 1992, the Fund had a market value of $4,988,000. The
cash yield was 7 .02%. The Pooled Income Fund gives Masons and others in
California the opportunity to create a lifetime income for themselves and for
one-time designated beneficiaries. Certain tax advantages may accrue to the
contributor. Eventually, the Masonic Homes becomes the final beneficiary.
The rewarding accumulation of assets in the various funds of Grand Lodge has
been the result of the efforts of Masons and their friends . The operations of

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

the Masonic Homes at Union City and Covina are financed almost entirely
through the income from the Endowment and General Fund investments. The
expansion at Union City in the last several years was funded entirely from the
Hugo M . Loerber Fund. Other revenues furnish support for the charitable
activities and educational grants of the Grand Lodge of California.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE

538

The Funds' investments rank among the highest in quality because the
Investment Committee exercises the utmost prudence and care in their
overseeing of the management of the funds. The cash yield and the total
return have been satisfactory in view of the committee' s conservative
investment policy and the securities markets.
During the past year a great deal of study has been made to regarding
the benefits and flexibility gained with the use of mutual funds rather than
individually managed portfolios and some funds have been converted to that
investment medium. It is anticipated more will follow. Consideration has also
been given to the conversion of funds to equity investments away from fixed
return in the smaller accounts under our responsibility and to the acceleration
of that conversion in the General Fund and the Endowment Fund.
During the 1992-1993 year the Investment Committee along with the
Executive Committee of Grand Lodge re-evaluated and re-wrote the
Investment Policy of the Investment Committee. This policy provides for
specific guidelines, and specific performance evaluation.

ON JURJSPRUDENCE

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F& A.M. of California:
Most Worshipful, with your permission I wou ld like to introduce the
members of the 1992-93 Committee on Jurisprudence.
As is apparent to you all, the need for efficiency and economy has
been seen in many ways already in this communication . The report of your
Jurisprudence Committee will be in keeping with the overall need to more
efficiently handle our business. Therefore, this will be the only report given
by Jurisprudence and of necessity, it will have to cover a number of issues at
one time.
The decis ions and recommendations of our Grand Master have been
distributed to you and I know have been reviewed by you with care. In each
case, the language presented is adequate to carry out the intent of the Grand
Master. Since decisions of the Grand Master do not change our ordinances,
a majority vote only is required for adoption.
Recommendations of the Grand Master fall in a different category.
They change our ordinances and therefore a five/sixth vote is necessary.
The next category of business which will come before you is the
"carry over" matters from our 1992 session. Once again, these items have been
forwarded to you from the Grand Secretary's Office in the package containing
the Resolutions.
These are the two items on the blue paper, namely
Recommendation No. 4 by then Grand Master Cazneaux and Resolution No.
92-10. Each of these matters required a five/sixth vote for adoption. Neither
achieved that level of support but did receive a majority vote, therefore, under
the provisions of our California Masonic Code, each was automatically carried
over for reconsideration. Carry over matters such as these require only a
two/thirds vote for adoption. Again, in each case, the language presented to
you is adequate to carry out the intent of the proponent of the legislation.
Finally, the last items to be voted upon are the 1993 Resolutions. The
legislative style of presentation used by the Grand Secretary's Office makes
immediately apparent the changes which will be required in our Code either
by way of deletion or addition if a Resolution is adopted. The Resolutions as
presented to you are in a form adequate to carry out the intent of the
proponents and are presented to you for action by your Committee on

540

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Jurisprudence. A five/sixth vote is required for adoption.
There are several additional comments which should be presented for
your general background and understanding. You have heard a great deal of
comment, and perhaps more will be forthcoming, about Past Grand Master
Ron Sherod's Recommendation No. 2 on advertising. Regrettably, we find
ourselves in a predicament which is a result of a combination of factors,
among them being imprecise recollection on the part of many, some human
error, lack of documentation of act:ions which are believed to have occurred or
not depending on which side of the issue you're on, faulty procedures and
possibly other ingredients including the changeover from the 1975 Code to the
1991 Code.
The issue revolves around what the Grand Lodge actually voted on in
1991 and again in 1992. There was a discrepancy between the written
presentation by then Grand Master Sherod which he read to the Grand Lodge
and the written Resolution which was read by the Committee on Jurisprudence
to the Grand Lodge based on what it believed to be an authorized amendment
to the Recommendation. Because the Recommendation did not receive a
five/sixth vote but did receive a majority vote, it was carried over and
regrettably, both versions were distributed to the Craft before the 1992 Annual
Communication.
Faced with this unprecedented situation, and in order to resolve the
matter, the Grand Master undertook the responsibility of determining what had
occurred.
Following extensive investigation, it was the conclusion of the Grand
Master that the language which had been adopted did not contain the words,
"and Masonic organizations" so that restrictions on advertising did not apply
to concordant bodies.
Because the Grand Master felt it was solely a matter of legal
interpretation as to what had occurred, he felt no further vote was needed since
the Recommendation had been properly adopted.
Your Committee on Jurisprudence was unable to reach the same
conclusion as the Grand Master, inasmuch as the California Masonic Code
requires that all business shall be referred to and reported on by committees
before any vote shall be taken and only the language containing the words
Your Committee on
"and Masonic Organizations" was reported on.
Jurisprudence therefore felt that to delete the words "and Masonic
Organizations" would require a vote.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

541

Reasonable minds have reviewed this issue in exhaustive detail. In
cooperation and in an effort to move forward in harmony, your
of
spirit
8
Committee on Jurisprudence and the Grand Master unanimously agreed to an
unprecedented solution to an unprecedented problem. The solution is to have
a vote with only a majority required for adoption.
I caution you that not everyone agrees that this compromise is the best
or most appropriate way to solve the problem but it appeared to your
Committee on Jurisprudence that rather than maintain a rigid position and
perpetuate a controversy, we could best serve the Grand Lodge as your
lawyers, but more importantly as your Brothers, by reaching this solution.
Your Committee does not view this as a precedent which will
fundamentally weaken the voting process set forth in the California Masonic
Code because the existing controversy is unprecedented and we felt called for
an unprecedented solution. Procedures and practices have been put in place
to insure that this situation never arises again.
Before passing on to the next subject, I cannot help but comment that
most, if not all, of those involved in this controversy are not strong advocates
of one position or another on the merits of the issue of restrictions on
advertising applying to the Concordant Bodies however, many are fervently
concerned about the integrity of the process and have an honest and deeply felt
concern that this process not be compromised.
I wish to thank the Grand Master for allowing me to serve as
Chairman of the Committee this past year. It has been an interesting one with
more than a few major challenges. I also wish to extend my heartfelt thanks
to the members of the Committee who have assisted me and served this Grand
Lodge with the highest level of professionalism and dedication. They are a
very talented group of men whose only concern has been the well-being of our
beloved Fraternity and this Grand Lodge.
Respectfully submitted,

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
There are 15 committee members presently serving on the Lodge
Resources Development Committee.

1.

We must find a way to let the lodges and inspectors know
that we are available to assist them with their problems.

We meet with a full committee three times a year. We hold two
meetings in Southern California and one in Northern California. Our Northern
meeting is held during Grand Lodge Week. Our annual budget is $4,500.

2.

The developm'e nt of the "Lodge Leadership Handbook."

3.

The development and review
Achievement Awards.

4.

This committee will lead the drive for the new "Membership
Development Program" in the year 1993 - 1994.

Major subjects and actions by the committee for the Masonic year
included:
1.

2.

We revised the Grand Master's Achievement Award form
and the eligibility point system to being more equitable to
the smaller lodges. This years program was set to coincide
with the Grand Masters edicts. The annual reporting period
was changed from July lst to July 31st. The new reporting
period is from January I st to January 3 lst, corresponding
with the term of office of that years Master. This action was
proposed by the Grand Lodge Executive Committee.
We have continued to promote the committee's "Lodge
Leadership Handbook" for improvement and better access to
lodge officers.

3.

This year we have continued the new Award, which we have
presented to the inspectors whose Districts had I 00%
participation in the Grand Master's Achievement Award.

4.

Our committee this year has continued the program of lodge
contact. Each member of the committee has selected 5 lodges
in hi s division who have not participated in the Grand
Master's Achievement Award program. Our members then
tried to encourage and assist those lodges to participate. I
feel we have met with success.

One of the best services our committee provides is to meet with
various lodges that are in trouble and need help. As Grand Lodge
representatives we are able to show them that Grand Lodge cares. In addition,

of the Grand Master's

being of service. Thank you for the opportunity.

ON MASONIC EDUCATION
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The 1992-1993 Masonic Education Committee consisted of 24
committeemen assigned to 21 of the 26 Masonic Education Areas in
California. Assisting the committeemen were 93 Area Instructors.
lo
February, six Divisions and 143 Masonic Districts were reduced to four
Divisions and 112 Masonic Districts.
At the time of this report there are still five Masonic Education Areas
without committeemen; 83 of the 112 Districts have members serving as
Masonic Education Area Instructors assisting our Committee.

545

Workshops were conducted in 15 of the 26 Masonic Education Areas.
Evaluation fonns revealed the workshops were successful in every respect
except in attendance. Those attending indicated that the infonnation they
received was well worth the short time spent in attending the workshops, and
that those not attending missed out on some good ideas for educating the
members of their Lodges.
Lodges were requested to designate one of their meeting nights each
month as a Masonic Family Meeting night. At least one hour on six of these
nights should be spent discussing information contained in the Masonic
Education Manuals. The intent of this fonnat is to allow Entered Apprentices,
Fellowcrafts and Master Masons to meet, discuss and answer questions
regarding Freemasonry not pertaining to the Ritual.

books for a Lodge or a District Library and to make use of the Grand Lodge
Library for educational material for their members.

29

The major problem facing this committee is how to convince our
members that education is not a "nasty" word and that education is equally as
important as Ritual. Every hour spent on perfecting our Ritual must be
matched with equal time educating our members. Ritual teaches us the
principles of Masonry in the Lodge room. The recitation of the ritual, without
education, will accomplish very little. Masonic Education teaches us how to
explain and apply those principles in our daily lives. Progress has been made
during the last four years toward the attainment of this goal. However, we
have only climbed the hill to get a better view of the mountain.

546

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

Many Lodges are already benefitting from the rewards of the
participation, the dedication and the leadership of educated members. We are
proud of the Masonic Education program, material and dedicated members
who have been working to assist the Lodges in the education of their members.
Looking back on our accomplishments this year we realize we still have a long
way to go. Working together, the committee, the Lodge and the members
have been ''Building Masonry for the Twenty-First Century." Now we must
look forward to "The Challenge of Change - The Rewards of Renewal" and
educate our members to truly understand "What it Means to Be A Mason."
Respectfully submitted,
Robert L. Sorensen, Chairman

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON MASONIC SERVICE BUREAUS
To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

The Committee on Masonic Service Bureaus is pleased to submit the
following data as its Annual Report for the Fiscal Year ending June 30, 1993.
The Committee is in its 66th year.
The Committee takes its directive to supervise the operations of the
various Masonic Service Bureaus in the State of California very seriously.
This includes the Relief of Distressed Worthy Brothers and their families
residing in the Jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge F & AM of California, both
Sojourners as well as California Members; when the situation requires it. the
Committee also assists the Masonic Service Association in the development of
its "Hospital Visitation Program" at the Veterans Administration Facilities in
the State of California. Members of the Committee and Executive Secretaries
of the Bureaus participate in the work of the Masonic Relief Association of the
United States and Canada.

COMMITTEE MEMBERS
The 1993-1994 Committee consisted of Wor. Paul Brown of San
Diego, Wor. Howa.Td Dumont of Sacramento, Wor. Thomas Hart of Torrance,
Wor. Ray H. Rookard of Oakland, along with Wor. A. Bruce Ivie of Newhall
as Committee Consultant, and Bro. Arthur H. Rumsey of Los Angeles serving
as Committee Chairman.

EXECUTIVE SECRET ARIES
There are several new Executive Secretaries in place as of this writing,
who are new since last year's report. Wor. Glen E. Le Beck has replaced
Wor. Bill Carnot, and is bringing the San Gabriel Valley Bureau back on lone
in fine shape. In San Jose, Wor. Leslie S. Wilson has replaced Wor. ~ird~ll
Wilson who resigned due to his wife's health and subsequent death, and 1s still
having a problem getting the Bureau reorganized. Wor. Bro. John Thornton
has replaced Wor. John A. McCuish after Bro. McCuish passed away. The
Santa Monica Bureau is in good hands .

548

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

COMMITTEE MEETINGS
The usual four Committee Meetings were held during the 1992-1993
year. The first was a two day session held in the Monday and Tuesday of
Grand Lodge, where problems of the past year were discussed. A meeting
with the Chairman of the Grand Lodge Committee on Insurance, along with
the Grand Treasurer was held and the problems regarding the Workers
Compensation Insurance and Liability Insurance were resolved.
This
resolution assured the continued existence of several Bureaus who rely on "Per
Capita" to remain functional. Again, a booth on "G" Floor was in operation
from Sunday through Tuesday for the purpose of enlightening the Brothers of
what the Masonic Service Bureau are, what the Masonic Service Association
is, and what the Masonic Relief Association is an how all three assist the
members of the fraternity. Brother Tom Wier, the newly appointed Director
of Hospital Visitation Program of the Masonic Service Association was an
invited guest and brought the Committee up to date on this major part of the
Committee's Annual Activities.
The Southern Regional Committee meeting was held in Pasadena on
April 24, 1993 with four of the five Committeemen and the Committee
Consultant present. All Southern California Bureaus were represented and the
Morning session was Given over to instruction on the preparation of various
Bureau Reports, Federal, State, and Grand Lodge; where to and when they
should be submitted. The afternoon session was limited to Committeemen and
the Consultant discussion of two Los Angeles Bureau By-Laws Changes. Both
requests were turned down by the Committee and the Los Angeles Bureau was
so notified.
Between the April 24th Meeting of the Committee and the scheduled
Committee meeting on May 1I, 1993, a Survey of the Committee was made
regarding the request of Damascus Lodge No. 648 . The Committee Members
gave verbal approval to the Committee Chairman;s action of May l 0th,
whereby the authorized Damascus Lodge No. 648 to withdraw from the San
Bernardino Masonic Service Bureau.
On May 11 ,1993, the Committee met with the Northern California
Bureaus in Oakland and discussed the necessary reports, and their due dates,
etc. Committee Chairman Rumsey was unable to attend due to family medical
reasons, however, all other Committeemen and the Committee Consultant
were present; as were seven of the Executive Secretaries, and MSA
Coordinator for Northern California, RW Robert Klinger.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

549

On June 22, 1993, the Committee' s annual Bureau Budget
consideration meeting was held in the Pasadena Scottish Rite Library. After
considerable discussion all Budgets were approved, and for the most part in the
same form as submitted. The approved Budgets amounted to slightly over
$6,000.00 more than for 1992-1993 due to renewed activity in both San
Gabriel Valley and Santa Monica Bay Bureaus; and the San Francisco need to
up-date their computer system with Bureau owned equipment.
TAXES
The Committee was advised that all Federal and State Tax Returns
have been submitted and fi led. This is an item that the 1993-1994 Chairman
must address himself to as dealings with the Federal l.R.S. and State E.D.D.
can get out of hand very easily.
BUSH MASONIC RELIEF, INC.
As has been the case for many years, the Los Angeles County Service
Bureaus; Long Beach, Los Angeles, San Gabriel Valley, and Santa Monica
Bay, have been financially supported by the Bush Fund, and the members of
this committee appreciate this generous contribution to our activities.
BLOOD BANKS
Blood Banks are now operated by the Bakersfield, East Bay, Fresno,
Sacramento, San Francisco Bay, and So. Alameda County Masonic Service
Bureaus. During the period July 1, 1992 - June 30, I 993, 732 united were
collected and only 321 units were distributed. The Santa Monica Bay Bank
was closed by Bureau Action.
UNIFORM COMPACTS
Several new "Un iform Compacts" were submitted for approval of the
Grand Master during the past year. There were all the results of "Mergers".
West Covina-La Puente #446

South Pasadena # 290
West Beach # 616
BUREAU OPERATING EXPENSES

As can be seen from the "Recapitulation of Service Bureau Operating
Expenses" report for the period July 1, 1992 - June 30, 1993, the operating
expenses were $190,928.28, as compared to expenses of $182,883 .37 for the

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

previous period from July l , 1991 to June 30, 1992. This $8,044.91 Increase,
can be attributed to increased cost of operating the Los Angeles County
Bureaus, in particular the San Gabriel Valley Bureau, and the Santa Monica
Bay Bureau which had little or no expenses during the previous year. The
increase does not include the San Jose figures as they were not received prior
to September 5, 1993; the date of preparation of this report.

This Committee's Budget of $2,941 .00 for the 1992-1993 period
extending through October 30, 1993 was very, very tight and it can only be
hoped that Airline "Price Wars" will still be going on in 1994 which will
permit a slight reduction for 1993-1994.

550

551

Respectfully submitted,
Arthur H. Rumsey, Chairman

M.S.A. HOSPITAL VISITATION PROGRAM
This program is proceeding along at good speed with new units at the
Fresno Veterans Facility and the Bakersfield "Out Patient" Unit. There is still
a great need for assistance in all fields of endeavor not just "Visitation".

CONCLUSIONS
We did solve our Insurance Problems, thanks to efforts of the Grand
Master, Grand Treasurer, and Chairman of the Grand Lodge Insurance
Committee.
We lost the San Bernardino Masonic Service Bureau when a Member
Lodge decided to withdraw, leaving only three Lodges; two of which have
since "Merged." We have been Unable to get the San Jose Bureau formally
reorganized, but we believe the 4th attempt scheduled for early/mid September
1993 will accomplish the fact.
This Committee appreciates the support given to it by Most
Worshipful R. Stephen Doan, and his corps of elected and appointed officers,
along with the several Committee Chairmen with whom this Committee has
had direct dealings during the past year. The Officers of each of the Masonic
Service Bureaus are to be Congratulated on their continued efforts on behalf
of the many little known facets of Masonic Service Bureau Activities,
including but not Limited to, Funeral Services for the many Sojourning
Masons living in California.
The Bureau Executive Secretaries are the ones who face the brunt of
our fraternal and charitable business, and are on call every day and night of the
year. Each Lodge member should give them a vote of thanks.
An attempt to organize an "Inland Empire" Masonic Service Bureau
should be considered during the 1993-1994 year, using the two San Bernardino
Lodges as a base, and looking for membership from Lodges in the Riverside
Area.

Howard Dumont
Ray Rookard

Paul E. Brown
Thomas Hart
A. Bruce Ivie, Consultant

Donor Club #69 IS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:
At the beginning of the Masonic Year, I distributed to all the then
Senior Wardens master copies of the new evaluation fonns for their Masonic
Information Programs. They were to be completed and returned at the
conclusion of the program. However, confusion has again reared its ugly head,
because members of the Education Committee members took it upon
themselves to conduct Masonic Information Programs and did not tum in any
reports with the lodges doing the same. Therefore, I am hard pressed to give
an actual count on the number of Programs held this year. But, I am sure it
exceeded 100.
From the correspondence I received, several of our lodges went that
extra mile and did a lot of advertising in their local medias about their
individual Masonic Information Programs.

(I) Bakersfield Bureau coordinates release of Blood Bank accounts of six Masonic Family Bodies.

Of the reports I received, over 20 lodges had 10+ Non-Masonic
Guests and a number of Lodges saw an increase in applications from the
programs. Three such programs were by I) Vista Lodge #687 that had over
100 in attendance and received 8 applications for membership; 2) the 293rd
District that had over 300 in attendance and received 28 applications for
membership and turned people away; and 3) the Stockton Lodges in the 28 lst
District that had over 100 in attendance. Congratulations for a job well done!
I have had several complaints from the committee members that a lot
of the Lodges are not putting forth their best effort in attracting their members
and guests to these programs. I would hope that the Masters for 1994 will
take into consideration that the members of this committee are volunteering
their valuable time and that it would be nice to see the Lodge halls filled to
capacity with most of those being non-masons and their wives. The Lodges
need to ensure that their programs are successful, the speakers can only
enhance the evening.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

As of June 30, 1992 there were I 779 first degrees conferred and as
of June 30, 1993 there were I 707 degrees conferred. We were hoping that our
Masonic Information Programs for the current Masonic year would show an
increase, but such was not the case. We hope that with a little more effort on
the part of the Lodges, the 1992 figure will be surpassed and the 2000 plateau
reached. All it will take is going that extra mile.

ON PRJNCE HALL RECOGN ITION STUDY

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M of California:

This special committee was formed in October 1990 at the direction
of the Grand Master as a result of a verbal agreement between the incoming
Grand Master and the proponent of Resolution 90-07, calling for the
recognition of Prince Hall Masonry, when it was withdrawn from consideration
before the 1990 Annual Communication.
The original purpose of the committee was stated as:
I.

To study the future relationship between the Grand Lodge of
California and the M : . W :. Prince Hall Grand Lodge F.&
A.M. State of California, Inc. and their constituent lodges;

2.

To meet with representatives of the M :. W :. Prince Hall
Grand Lodge F.& A.M. State of California, Inc.; and

3.

To report to the 199 I Annual Communication of the Grand
Lodge of California its findings.

After delivering that report at the 199 l Annual Communication of our
Grand Lodge the recommendation was adopted that your special committee "be
continued for the 1991 /92 Masonic year, as presently composed, with explicit
charge to bring before the 1992 Annual Communication its proposals and
recommendations respecting some form of recognition of the M :. W:. Prince
Hall Grand Lodge F.& A.M . State of California, Inc. and also that the Grand
Master, the Deputy Grand Master and their designees continue to meet
informally with corresponding representatives of the M :. W :. Prince Hall
Grand Lodge F.& A.M. State of California, Inc." Your special committee
complied with that recommendation.
After delivering our report at the 1992 Annual Communication the
recommendation was adopted that your special committee "be continued for
the 1992/93 Masonic year, with explicit charge to bring before the 1993
Annual Communication its further proposals and recommendations. And also
that the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand Master, and their designees, continue
to meet informally with the corresponding representatives of the M :. W :.
Prince Hall Grand Lodge F.& A.M. State of California, Inc. for the 1992/93

PROCEEDINGS OF TIIE

560
Masonic year."

Since shortly after our formation we have met with a like committee
from the M :. W :. Prince Hall Grand Lodge F.& A.M . State of California, Inc.
After our initial request for these meetings the formally arranged meetings
have been supplemented by informal meetings and conversations between
individual members of both committees. We continue to distribute our formal
meeting minutes as a joint committee. With each meeting the joint committee
obtains a better understanding of the other's fraternal culture and the meaning
and importance of the words being used in our discussions.
This committee has met four (4) times over the past Masonic year
during the months of November, January, March, and July with the similar
committee of five of the M :. W :. Prince Hall Grand Lodge of California , Inc.
Through all our deliberations we continue to be impressed with the quality,
depth, and sincerity of the commitment of these men representing Prince Hall
Masonry.
Currently our JOmt committees have developed a Joint Mission
Purpose, Initial Goals, and an Initial Agenda for Future Relations.

A.

Joint Mission Purpose

To study the future relationship between the Grand Lodge of F.&
A.M. of California and the M :. W :. Prince Hall Grand Lodge of F.&
A.M. State of California, Inc. and to report progress and mutual
proposals to the forthcoming Annual Communication of each.

B.

561

14th, 1993 luncheon. Prince Hall Masons were invited for our
October I 0th Vesper Service. When questions are directed to your
committee we have sought to obtain appropriate correct information
from our counterpart Prince Hall committeemen.
The joint committee, while it continues its pursuit of its mandates, has
recognized that the Mason of the twenty-first century will be faced with new
and perplexing challenges as never before. He will be forced to think about the
basic principles of Freemasonry and examine his relationship to those
principles. He will be required to justify his actions to the uninitiated observer.
The uninitiated observer will be a strong critic where the practices and cultural
activities do not align themselves with the lofty ideals which Masonry
proclaims. The uninitiated observer will not have the patience to ask why
things are the way they are. Your committee believes that as new situations
arise Masonry must develop new solutions. Your committee has taken the
initial steps, as you directed, to be the catalyst through which dialogue with
Prince Hall might take place. The timing of future contacts remains at the
direction of Grand Lodge.
During the process of our study and communication with the Prince
Hall committee we have asked general questions about the applicability of the
American Doctrine of Territorial Jurisdiction, as well as, how suitable are our
current day social interaction practices. We have been informed of, or
observed, actions at variance with traditional CMC interpretations. We inquired
as to whether the I ?75 CMC Edition annotations, or previous Grand Master's
decisions, or original interpretations of CMC provisions reflected the manner
in which a number of our members currently deal with Prince Hall and other
non-recognized Masonic entities.

Initial Goals

Three goals were established . Understanding the history and
evolution of each entity. Documentation of joint actions of other
Grand Jurisdictions. Understanding the term "recognition" and of its
meaning and application as used in Freemasonry. The first two are
approaching closure. The last item will remain in discussion. The
current comments focus on visitation as that is reflected in the eight
(8) jurisdictions that have granted recognition.

C.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

An Agenda for Future Relations

We have worked for joint agreement on areas where we can plan
activities with each other. With your approval we have planned a
third consecutive meeting with both Grand Masters for an October

As a committee we reviewed the origins of the American Doctrine,
including inquiries made to research libraries in other jurisdictions. As a
committee we discussed, from an historical perspective, the current day
impacts of a strict observance of the American Doctrine. From our
consideration of the American Doctrine we noted that events of our time tend
to sway us from a concept of strict adherence. Recognizing our limitations
your committee asked for guidance, and input, from others.
Following full discussion and consideration your committee has
accepted as legitimate the origin of what is now Prince Hall Masonry, through
its original charter, through the United Grand Lodge of England. We accept
it, not because it can withstand all counter claims and questions, but because
Prince Hall Masonry has withstood the test of time. Its continuous history and
the acceptance by eight (8) other American grand jurisdictions which we

recognize have subdued many arguments that we have read or heard.
The words contained in our simple report to Grand Lodge are not

Words come up short trying to describe the positive feelings we have toward
one another- those of mutual understanding and trust. We are decidedly
impressed with those with whom we have become acquainted as citizens and
as members of their Fraternity.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON PUBLIC SCHOOLS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A. M. of California:

The charter for the Grand Lodge Committee on Public Schools is
found in Section 6060 of the C.M.C. and reads as follows, "The Committee on
Public Schools shall developed and promote methods of increasing interest in
and support for the Public Schools. " The activities and achievements outlined
in the following report are founded on these 20 words.
PACKETS FOR SENIOR WARDENS

We started our year at the October 1992 annual communication of
by making sure that the Senior Wardens (who were to be
Lodge
Grand
Masters during the following calendar year) were supplied with the necessary
information and materials to get them started on preparations for their Public
Schools Week Observance in April. Packets of printed and other materials
were assembled by members of our committee on the Saturday prior to the
opening of Grand Lodge. The many successful Observances that follow justify
these procedures.
PUBLIC SCHOOLS WEEK

By far the most important event of the school year is the annual
observance of Public School Week in April. To promote this affair, all
committee members were assigned to lodges in their areas with instructions to
contact them at their District meetings. Essentially these meetings were pep
rallies at which the committeemen displayed their promotional material and,
while so doing, instructed the lodges how to make use of the material to
promote successful Observances. The results were highly satisfactory.
MEETINGS

Three meetings were convened by our committee during 1992/ 1993.
The first was February 28, the second May 23, and the third July 18. They
were highly productive, A fringe benefit of such meetings are that they unify
our committee. We came away with an awareness of that other members have
done, are doing and what they will do in the future. Another benefit ts a
feeling that none of us work in a vacuum; we are a cooperative group.

564

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

SCHOOL BOXES
Our committee has been asked by the Masonic Foundation and the
Executive Committee to help in the distribution of school boxes. Of course,
we readily agreed. Each box contains a pencil, an eraser, a ruler, and crayons.
As part of our drug abuse prevention program there is a prominent warning on
each box: "DRUGS ARE FOR LOSERS". Although these boxes are
distributed free to elementary school children at cornerstone laying, our
committee urges lodges to buy them at $1.50 per box and distribute them to
pupils in elementary schools in their areas. To encourage lodges to participate
in this endeavor, the members of our committee are, at this time, contacting
them at District meetings throughout the state to impress upon them the
importance of this project. Each lodge will receive 1 box to allow the brethren
of his lodge to be aware of the school box program and ergs them to
participate in this program.

LITTLE RED SCHOOL HOUSE PINS
Another give-away item that has met with enthusiastic reception by
our lodges is the Little Red School House lapel pin . In view of their
popularity we have urged the lodges to purchase them in quantities at $ l .25
each, for distribution to those attending Public School Week Observances and
other Masonic gatherings. When worn by members of our craft, the message
is clear: "The Masons are strong supporters of the Public Schools!".

THE "CHOICE" INITIATIVE
On November 2, 1993, the voters of California will make a
monumental decision. On that date they will go to the polls and cast their
ballots for ...or against...a California Constitutional Amendment called the
"Parental Choice in Education Initiative (Proposition 174 ). Its outcome will
profoundly affect the future of our Public Schools favorably ... or adversely ... for
years to come.
In the Autumn 1993 issue of the California Freemason, our Grand
Master, R. Stephen Doan (featured in the centerfold), has written a detailed
critique of the measure. At this time each Master Mason, Inspector, and Grand
Lodge Officer of California has received infonnation regarding the pros and
cons of this pending proposition. In addition, two thousand copies have been
distributed among public schools and the citizenry.

GRAND LODGE OF CALJroRNIA

565

The Public Schools committee members have voted to not support this
initiative. But are supplying supporting and non-supporting infonnation so the
citizenry may make an educated choice.

PIPELfNE TO THE SENATE
Our committee is fortunate in having a direct contact with the
California State Legislature, Senator Ralph Dills, a member of our fraternity
who is also a longtime member of our committee. His interest in and support
for our Public Schools is well known. Because of this interest and support we
are kept infonned of all pending legislation whose passage would affect our
schools.
His most recent contribution to our committee and to the welfare of
our Public schools was his diagnosis and critique of the up-coming "Parental
Choice in Education Initiation" on which voters will cast their ballots on
November 2nd. Senator Dills' input is invaluable.

PROCLAMATIONS
We have long been aware of the publicity value of Public Schools
Week Proclamations. This year, as in all previous years, we urged lodges to
obtain such proclamations from local city and county officials. Our committee
set a good example by obtaining similar proclamations from the state governor
and the state legislat~re . In addition we drafted a proclamation for our Deputy
Grand Master to use as his Public Schools Week Proclamation during his year
as Grand master in 1994. After editing, it was accepted.

PAMPHLETS
This year we printed 10,000 pamphlets extolling the achievements of
our Public Schools and expressing Masonry's interest in their welfare.
Although these pamphlets were intended for distribution throughout the year,
they were especially effective at Public Schools Week Observances where they
were handed out at "open houses"or used as part of table settings at dinner
meetings.

FILLERS

CONCLUSION

Many Masters have difficulty in filling out their lodge bulletins. As
a service to these Masters we supplied them with what we call "fillers" to fill
in the gaps in their trestleboards. These fillers contain interesting infonnation
about Public Schools and were written with the Master in mind. It is pleasing
to note that many Masters used them as part ...or all...of their Master' s message.

Several words of Thanks are in order. The first is to Brother Clyde
M. Stine (494), (my ghost writer), and his wife Audley for there untiring
efforts for over two decades on the Public Schools Committee.

A NEW IDEA
We are always on the lookout for new ways to "Develop and promote
methods of increasing interest in and support for Public Schools". To this end
we recently laid in a supply of white jackets, white shirts, and white hats, each
bearing the Little Red School House and the message in bold lett~rs:
"SUPPORT PUBLIC SCHOOLS". The jackets will sell for $22,00, the shirts
for $15.00, and the hats for $6.00. It is too early to report on the results of this
new venture because it was initiated only a few weeks ago. To date there has
not been sufficient time to make known to the brethren that these items are
now available. We are now making plans for a vigorous campaign to
distribute these items and we hope that next year we can make a full and
favorable report.

MASONS ON CAMPUS
A pilot program has been commenced in the Los Ang~es U~ified
School District titled "MASONS ON CAMPUS". This program 1s designed
to unify the students in the classrooms and on school property ~y the
association with adults on campuses. Due to the number of masons available,
the number of schools, and the diversity of the students, people of all
influences are encourage to participate. At this time we have a fine working
relationship with the School Board of Education , the Prince Hall Masons, the
citizens in the area and, the students and staff.

SUBSTANCE ABUSE GRANTS
Due to the lack of available funds, the annual Public School Grants
of $15,000 to the IO State of California' s Healthy kids Regional Centers were
not awarded.

CHANGE IN LEADERSHIP
On 9 November 1992, Dare! N. Reynolds PM, relieved Joseph
Silveira PM, as Chainnan of the Public Schools Committee.

Second is to Brother Don Pollock (721) and all the brothers who are
working so hard to promote Public Schools in the Los Angles Unified School
District.
Thirdly is to my wife Elizabeth and all the other wives whoever
husbands have served on this committee with diligence and honor since its
inception in 1920. Without their support and understanding we would not be
able to carry on our mission.
A special thank you to all who have participated in the logistics of the
School Box efforts.
It is evident from the foregoing that membership on the Public
Schools Committee is no sinecure; we are a hard working committee. In
reality this report has no closing date. Ours is not a committee that winds up
its business at the end of the year, closes up shop and goes home. Even as
this is being written our members are still working.
Our notable projects are still under way and will not be completed
until well into the next Masonic year. One is our assignment to help the
California Masonic Foundation distribute school boxes. Another is our
campaign to inform the brothers, our ladies, and the citizenry of the "Parental
Choice in Education Initiative". And lastly is the sincere efforts to expand our
Masons on C ampus Program and promote Public Schools in the Los Angles
Unified School District.
We've had a very successful year but as this report draws to a close
we're planning for an even more successful 1993/ 1994 !
Respectfully submitted,
Darel N . Reynolds, Chairman

TEMPLE PROPERTIES AND TAXATION

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M. of California:
The state of the Craft's Temple properties is generally good. In
making this assessment we recognize that the process of erecting, maintaining,
changing, selling and rebuilding is a never-ending process among a constantly
changing membership.
We have met with success in our continuing education activities
among the membership. We are committed in the coming year to continuing
our efforts to offer guidance and counsel to Inspectors, to educate Directors of
Temple Associations through the Officers' Administrative Seminar program
and to speak directly with each Masters' and Wardens' Association, if invited.
These allow us to transmit the business, legal and taxation reasons for
our standards of operation of Temple properties within the laws of our nation,
state and craft, so that our Temples are as free as possible from unforeseen
legal and taxation liabilities.

571

Thus, we consider changes in our practices that might convince
outside parties of our fraternal use of our properties. Because there are real
cases of multiple property ownership by Temple Associations, through
acquisition by bequest, consolidation or contemplation of future building, we
feel that the California Masonic Code should adequately provide for and
characterize such holdings. You will note that legislation has been introduced
to remedy this problem and, hopefully, to forestall future legal and taxation
problems through adequate regulation of such multiple ownership for fraternal
purposes.
Respectfully submitted,
C. Richard Hutchinson, Jr., Chairman
Larry L. Adamson
Frederick Kao
Donald B. Mcclary
Bill L. Tool

Don A. Geiger
Thomas J. Luby
David A. Poole, Jr.
Anthony P. Wordlow

However, success requires problems to overcome and your Committee
on Temple Properties and Taxation envisions possible other future problems.
We Masons are humans embedded in American culture and our Lodges and
Temples are organizations that form part of the fabric of that culture. Each
Mason feels that, to the extent our Craft has been successfully engaged in the
operation of the warp and woof of the operation of our American culture, all
Americans have benefitted from our principles.

To the Most Worshipful Grand lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

Alas, brethren, we have ample evidence of our Craft 's declining
importance to the fabric of contemporary American Society and that our
culture suffers because of our principle's relative eclipse in public life.

The Tournament of Roses Float Committee has the responsibil ity of
arranging all of the details necessary to put a Masonic float in the Rose Parade
in Pasadena on New Year' s Day.

And so we must assess the future, as reasonable men must do, and
attempt to perceive where, in this less Masonic American culture, legal and
taxation danger may lay for our Craft. And we must attempt to avert those
damages.

The scope of the Committee's tasks includes the selection of the float
theme, design of the float, negotiation of a contract with the float builder, fund
raising from members of the Masonic fraternity on a voluntary basis, liaison
with the Tournament of Roses Committee and the float builder, selection of
float riders, selection and plans for music on the float, publicity, float
decoration, food service for the decorators, costumes, accommodation and
transportation for riders, photography and videography, design and sales of
merchandise relating to the float, and many other details.

We perceive that, because our non-profit Lodges are often most
visible in their communities because of the operation of their Temple
Properties (often with commercial rentals involved), our intolerant critics might

consisted of three connected gazebos resembling the band rotundas found in
community parks. A musical group was riding in each of the gazebos and that
were dressed in costumes of the period represented by their music.

Special thanks are due to a number of people or organizations for the
assistance that they provided. In particular, the 800 or so members of the
Masonic youth groups who decorated the float did an outstanding job of
decorating and also acted as ambassadors for Freemasonry by assisting on
other floats as well. Members of the Shrine and York Rite performed the
almost impossible task of providing food for the decorators under somewhat
inclement weather conditions. Three members of Al Malaikah Shrine provided
motor homes at the start of the Parade to keep the riders warm until it was
time for them to board the float for the 2.5 hour journey down the Parade
route.

make use of the working tools of Masonry prominently displayed on the float.

2345, 2346, 2346A, 2351, 2353, 2354, 2358 and 2360 and finds that in each

Constitution and Ordinances, and the result is supported by the evidence in the
records of each case and that there are no miscarriages of justice.

Trial Record No. 2347
In Trial Record No. 2347, a member of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42
was charged in two specifications with unmasonic conduct. The accused pied
not guilty and a Masonic Trial by Commission was begun.

579

We therefore submit the following Resolution :
Resolved, that in Trial Record No. 2348, the penalty be raised from
reprimand to expulsion.
Resolution ADOPTED.

During the Trial by Commission, the Trial Master ruled that the
evidence of unmasonic conduct was not sufficient to convict and directed that
a not guilty verdict be entered. The California Masonic Code states in Section
32320, "The Commissioners are the sole judges of the facts proven, and the
Trial ~~ter shall have no vote in the decision of the case." Once a Trial by
Comm1ss1on has begun, only the Commissioners can decide a verdict. The
Trial Master's directed verdict violated this principle and prevented the accuser
from presenting all of his evidence.
Your Committee, after extensive review and discussion, finds that
there is sufficient evidence to warrant a Trial by Commission and that the Trial
Master exceeded his authority by entering a directed verdict of not guilty. To
allow this not guilty verdict to stand denies the right of the accuser to present
his case to a commission for judgment.
Based upon the foregoing, your Committee submits the following
Resolution:
Resolved, that the findings of the Trial Master of not guilty be set
aside, new charges be prepared, and a new Masonic Trial be
conducted in accordance with the California Masonic Code.

Trial Record No. 2350
This very troublesome trial record presents multiple problems.
On September 2, 1992, a member of Westminster Fairview Lodge No.
629, now WestBeach Lodge No. 616, was charged with unmasonic conduct.
No specification of the charge was made. The accused member was served,
a Trial Master was appointed, the member was found guilty on October 6,
1992, and the penalty was fixed at suspension .
On November 12, 1992, the Grand Secretary's office pointed out that
the absence of specifications was a fatal defect. Amended charges were filed
on November 18, 1992. They were properly served. So far as the record
shows no trial was held on the newly filed charges and specifications. Thus
no findings were ever made on the specifications which were not filed until
November 18.
On the original charge, no specifications were included. California
Masonic Code Section 32060 states:
"... the unmasonic conduct shall be set forth in a specification or
specifications stating clearly and precisely the facts giving rise to the
offense or offenses ... "

Resolution ADOPTED.
Trial Record No. 2348
In Trial Record No. 2348 a member of Los Angeles Lodge No. 42
was charged with unmasonic conduct alleging sexual battery on four women
in his chiropractic office under the guise of chiropractic treatment.
To these charges the accused entered a plea of not guilty. A Masonic
Trial by Commission was held and he was found guilty. The Commission
fixed the penalty at reprimand.
Your Committee on Trial Review, believes the seriousness of the
crime requires that the penalty be increased to expulsion.

The specification is an essential element of the charges. In the
original charge it was missing. Thus the finding of guilt and imposition of
penalty were invalid.
An attempt was made to correct things. The amended charge did
contain the essential specifications. But there was thereafter no trial and no
findings. It does no good to correct the charges and add specifications if
thereafter no finding is made on the specifications.
There is one further problem. The specifications contained in the
newly amended charge was itself defective. It was alleged that the member
made representations about the Congressional Medal of Honor and other

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

580

awards for valor. It does not allege that those representations were false.
Ample proof was presented that those representations were false, but that does
not correct the specification.
Where the evidence is as clear as it was in this case, it is very
troublesome to have to recommend that the trial record be reversed. But we
must.
Your Committee on Trial Review therefore submits the following
Resolution:
Resolved, that the findings of the Trial Master in Trial Record No.
2350 be reversed, that the mater be referred back to WestBeach
Lodge No. 616 for such proceedings as may be appropriate under the
California Masonic Code.

Trial Record No. 2352
In Trial Record No. 2352, a member of Fox-Coates Daylight Lodge
No. 842 was charged with two c.ounts of unmasonic conduct. The accused
responded with a not guilty plea. Seven Trial Commissioners were elected,
along with three alternates, on January 19, l 993. On January 20, 1993, service

The Trial commenced on January 26, 1993, and the accused was
found guilty of three specifications of unmasonic conduct and the penalty was
fixed at reprimand.
A review of the proceedings revealed several violations of the
California Masonic Code. Your Committee on Trial Review believes that
these violations resulte.d in a miscarriage of justice.

In Trial Record No. 2355, the accused, a member of Sacramento
Lodge No. 40, was charged with unmasonic conduct in that he did embezzle
certain funds which he had received in a fiduciary capacity . He repeatedly
denied using the funds for his own purposes. However, prior to the charges
being filed the accused sent a letter to this Lodge admitting his guilt. The
Trial Master reviewed the evidence and found the accused not guilty in that
there "was no eviden~e of intention on the part of the accused to cheat or
defraud any individual or any willful disregard of moral or Masonic duty."
In reviewing this case, your Committee found that there were several
violations of the California Masonic Code. We find that a failure by the Trial
Master to consider these violations resulted in a miscarriage of justice,
particularly in view of the existence of a letter from the accused admitting his
guilt.
Your Committee, therefore, after careful review of the records finds
Your
Committee on Trial Review therefore submits the following Resolution:

that there is sufficient evidence to support a trial on the facts.

The specifications of unmasonic conduct served on the accused were
two in number.
In this matter, at the Trial the accuser alleged three
specifications against the accused, where were different specifications than the
two specifications served on the accused. California Masonic Code Section
32130 requires service of the charges upon the accused. In the Trial of this
matter, the accused was not served with the charges presented by the accuser
at the Trial. California Masonic Code Section 32130 provides that the accused
has 30 days after service of the charges to file a statement in writing that he

Resolved, that in Trial Record No. 2355, that the findings of not
guilty of unmasonic c.onduct be reversed and a new trial be conducted
in accordance with the California Masonic Code in a Lodge other than
Sacramento Lodge No. 40.

In Trial Record No. 2357, a member of Golden Rule Lodge No . 479
was charged with three specifications of unmasoni c conduct.
In the Municipa l Court of Santa Clara County the accused pied nolo
contender e to two counts of child molestation.
The accused, already suspende d from the Lodge for non-paym ent of
dues, failed to answer the charges and the Trial Master found him guilty and
set the penalty at expulsion .
Your Committe e, in reviewing this case, found it full of errors and
omissions . The specificat ions were not properly worded, the Trial Master
relied on uncertific ated court records and failed to document the reasons for
his finding of guilt as to the charges. While these errors are serious and could
warrant a new trial your Committe e finds, after extensive review, that the
errors do not violate any substantial right of the accused to a fair trial under
our Code. Therefore , without setting a precedent to overlook serious
procedural errors in future trials, we are recomme nding that this case be
affirmed.
Your Committe e therefore submits the following Resolution:
Resolved, that in Trial Record No. 2357 the finding of guilty be
affirmed and the Penalty be affixed at expulsion.
Resolutio n ADOPTE D.

The Trial Master found the accused guilty of unmasonic conduct and
of the three specificat ions and fixed the penalty at expulsion .
The basis for the finding of guilt was court document s, including a
certified coy of the abstract of judgment in the San Mateo County courts
imposing a sentence of six years on each of three counts.
But the member appealed from the criminal court proceeding. The
criminal convictio n on which the Masonic decision was based is not final until
appellate review is completed . Becaus~ th~ Supreme Court has granted a
bearing, that procedure is not complete in this case.
For this reason we cannot recomme nd affirmanc e at this time. On the
other hand, the charges and procedure appear to be proper and we do NOT
recommend reversal.
The accused stands expelled. We recomme nd that the proceedings in
this matter be continued for one year or until the appellate review is
concluded . The accused will remain expelled until the final judgment .
Your Committe e therefore submits the following Resolution:
Resolved , that the findings of the Trial Master be accepted but that
the action on those findings be continued for one year or until
appellate review is concluded , that the accused stands expelled until
further action by this Grand Lodge.

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
ON

y OUTH ORDERS

To the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge, F.& A.M. of California:

Once again the Masonic Youth Orders have shown unparalleled
enthusiasm, good fellowship and continued cooperation this year, throughout
this jurisdiction. The members of our youth groups have been apart of
"Masonry into the 21st Century". As in the past, the lodges with thriving youth
groups continue to be the ones with gains in membership and community
involvement. There is a direct and unrefutable correlation between the
activities of our youth and the growth of our lodges and Eastern Star.
Your committee on Youth Orders continues to have as its primary
functions two main themes; To develop effective Fraternal relations with the
members and adult leaders of the three Youth Orders and to promote the
increase of youth programs in the lodges. Additionally we encourage the
members of our lodges to provide additional adult leadership to their local
youth groups.
As was reported last year, and l am again pleased to report this year,
the three Masonic Youth Groups represented by four distinct organiz.ations
have again had a very small decline in membership. They are doing the things
that are necessary to tum membership around and get back on the right track
in moving total membership upwards. This trend will continue upwards with
our help and support, but it will take the dedication and support of all of us to
keep it going up. We, my brethren, must not get complacent with letting them
do it by themselves. We must all do our part to help and support them in there
efforts. There are still Assemblies, Bethels and Chapters closing, not because
of the lack of members, but for the lack of volunteer adult support. We ask
you, the members of this Grand Lodge, to go back to your districts and seek
out those youth groups and find out what you can do to help them. Masonry
remains in the hands of our youth, we grow when they grow, and we fail when
they fail.
This year, this committee was charged by Grand Master R. Stephen
Doan with two continuing tasks; ones that we wholeheartedly accepted. The
first was to endeavor to get the lodges involved with the youth, not an easy
task to do considering the ages of some of our lodges. But we did just that, the
members of this committee went out to the lodges and coordinated meetings
and introduced lodge members to the local youth groups with much success.

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

587

The second challenge, was one of getting new adult advisors for every member
on this committee. This continues to be a very large task indeed as several
areas in the state do not have youth groups and others have full boards and
eed no new advisors. The committee is composed of 55 members spread
:aoss the four divisions with each member having approximately 8-10 lodges
and 4-10 youth groups assigned to them. Grand Master Doan this committee
is extremely pleased to report to you that we have acquired a total of 58 new
advisors.
In addition to the increased visitation to the Youth Groups and
constituent lodges, other accomplishments were noted.
Our publication of the Masonic Oriented Scholarships continues to be a most
sought after booklet, with weekly requests for more still continuing to come
in. The new and changed version is now in the Grand Secretary's Office and
is ready for printing. The new format will be a looseleaf 81 /2 x 11" manual so
that it may become a part of every Adult Leaders Leadership book and can
be made readily available to everyone who needs it.
Jn August the Annual MA YO (Masonic Adults of the Youth Orders)
meeting between the Adult Leaders of the four Youth Organiz.ations and the
members of the executive committee was held under the auspices of the Youth
Orders Committee. It continues to serve as an open forum for all attending and
to interact and share mutual areas of concern as well as ideas for growth and
prosperity. It was most pleasing to have the members of the executive
committee and repre~entatives from the four groups in attendance this year.
As in past years, this committee has prepared an information package,
which includes the pamphlet "Putting the YOU in YOUTH", and we urge the
Brethren to visit our booth on "G" floor and pick up one of these booklets.
They will also be available through the supply office. We will be glad to
answer any questions that you might have regarding the Youth .
Our Youth Leaders were featured on the cover of the March issue of
the California Freemason magazine which coincided with the Grand Masters
proclamation of Masonic Youth Month. The Grand Masters Youth Service
Award was given to four deserving brothers during last years annual
communication and four more were presented yesterday at the Youth Program.
This award is the highest award a Master Mason can receive for his devotions
to our Masonic Youth Orders.
Your committee on Youth Orders is pleased to report that it also
represented your Grand Lodge at the following events:

Our committee, as well as others in Grand Lodge, took a large cut in
our budget, but I am pleased to report that we have finished this past year
under budget. Many members of this committee do not submit expense sheets
for there travels and other related expenses, even though they were entitled to
them. For that we thank them sincerely. Also, other expense areas were
reviewed and adjustments were made to help in making this past year a most
successful one.
I wish to thank the Grand Master for his confidence in me and the
members of this committee. It has been a pleasure serving with you and the
other members of the executive committee, and been a part of the great
success that you have made of your year. Also a special thanks to the Very
Worshipful John Cooper, Grand Secretary and his staff for the wonderful
cooperation they continue to give. I wish to thank every member of this
Committee with out whom none of this would be possible. They all serve this
Grand Lodge with distinction, dedication and enthusiasm. Lastly, and most of
all, a very large thank you to the members of the Masonic Youth Orders. They
are a joy to work with and for. They are truly the future. of our Order.
As this is my last year and will be replaced by Worshipful Jim
McDonald as the new Chairman, I wish to thank all those who have so ably
served this committee for the last two years in particular and also those who
have been a member of it at any time. Your dedication to our Youth will never
be forgotten and you cannot know how much your service has been
appreciated.
